## Coptis (Goldthread)
<gloss>Top Grade in the Divine Husbandman's Classic</gloss>
<gloss>Explanatory Names</gloss> King’s Thread <gloss>from the Divine Husbandman's Classic</gloss>; Branch Thread <gloss>from the Treatise on Medicinal Properties</gloss>. Shizhen says: The root is long and has <insert>sprouts</insert> that connect like beads, and the color is yellow, hence the name <term>Huanglian</term> <note>literally "Yellow Successive-Beads"</note>. <gloss>The Miscellaneous Records state:</gloss> Coptis grows in the river valleys of Wuyang, the commanderies of Shu <note>modern Sichuan</note>, and the sunny side of Mount Tai. Roots are gathered in the second and eighth months. Hongjing says: Wuyang is in Jianping. Today, the best roots are shaped like connected beads. The sprouts resemble mustard greens or shepherd's purse. A single stem produces three leaves, standing about a foot high. It does not wither in the depths of winter. The flowers are yellow. Those from the Jiangzuo region have high nodes like connected beads; those from Ezhou have lower nodes that do not connect. Currently, those from the Qin region, Hangzhou, and Liuzhou are considered excellent. Song says: Today it is also found in the Jianghu, Jing, and Kui prefectures. The variety from Xuancheng, which has nine nodes and is hard and heavy—clinking when struck together—is superior. Those from Shiqian are next, followed by those from Dongyang, Shezhou, and Chuzhou. The sprouts are about a foot high with leaves like sweet chrysanthemum. It flowers in the fourth month with yellow blossoms and fruits in the sixth month, resembling small slices. Regarding the Jiangzuo variety, the roots are yellow and beaded, the sprouts survive winter, and the leaves resemble small chicken-tail ferns. It flowers in the first month with fine, pale white to yellowish spikes. The roots are firm enough to harvest in the sixth or seventh month. Qin says: The variety from the Shu Road is thick and large with an extremely bitter taste; it is best for treating thirst. The Jiangdong variety has nodes like beads and is excellent for treating dysentery. The Lizhou variety is even better. Shizhen says: In the late Han dynasty, Li Dangzhi’s herbal only took the yellow, fat, and firm roots from Shu as the best. In the Tang dynasty, the Lizhou variety was superior. Today, although it grows in both Wu and Shu, the variety from Yazhou and Meizhou is considered the finest medicine. The rise and fall of medicinal sources varies like this. Generally, there are two types: one has thick roots without hairs, with bead-like growths shaped like eagle or chicken claws, firm and deep yellow; the other has no beads, many hairs, a hollow center, and a lighter yellow color. Each has its appropriate use.

<margin>Processing the Roots</margin> Xiao says: To use it, wipe away the "fleshy hairs" with a cloth. Soak in rice-sour water for one full day <note>approx. 24 hours</note>, filter out, and roast dry over a willow-wood fire. Shizhen says: The five viscera and six bowels all possess "fire" <note>pathogenic heat/energy</note>. When balanced, there is health; when agitated, there is disease. Thus, there are theories of "Sovereign Fire" and "Ministerial Fire," but in reality, they are of one essence. Coptis enters the Hand Lesser Yin Heart Meridian and is the primary medicine for governing fire. To treat fire in its "home" organ <note>the Heart</note>, use it raw. To treat excess fire in the Liver and Gallbladder, stir-fry it after soaking in pig fat juice. To treat Lung fire, stir-fry with vinegar. To treat fire in the Upper Burner <note>chest area</note>, stir-fry with wine. To treat fire in the Middle Burner <note>stomach area</note>, stir-fry with ginger juice. To treat fire in the Lower Burner <note>pelvic area</note>, stir-fry with salt water or Glauber's salt. To treat damp-heat fire in the Qi level, stir-fry after soaking in a decoction of medicinal Evodia. To treat "hidden fire" within blood masses, stir-fry with dry lacquer powder. To treat fire from food stagnation, stir-fry with yellow earth. These various methods do not merely serve as "guides" for the medicine; rather, acrid heat can restrain its bitter cold, and salty cold can restrain its drying nature. The practitioner must weigh these options carefully.

<margin>Flavor and Nature</margin> Bitter, cold, non-toxic. <gloss>The Miscellaneous Records state:</gloss> Slightly cold. <gloss>Pu says:</gloss> Shennong, the Yellow Emperor, Lei Gong, and Tong Jun say it is non-toxic. Li Dangzhi says it is "lesser cold." <gloss>Zhicai says:</gloss> Scutellaria, Dragon Bone, and Gypsum serve as its "messengers" <note>assisting herbs</note>. It dislikes Chrysanthemum, Silene, White Dittany, Genkwa, and Silkworm. It fears Coltsfoot and Achyranthes. It overcomes Aconite and detoxifies Croton seed. <gloss>Quan says:</gloss> Avoid pork; it dislikes cold water. <gloss>Xiao says:</gloss> If taking ten ounces of this medicine, one must not eat pork. If taken for three years, one must never eat pork for the rest of one's life. Shizhen says: Taoist books say eating Coptis with pork causes diarrhea, yet medical formulas include "Pig Stomach Coptis Pills" and "Hog Gallbladder Coptis Pills." Is it possible to avoid the meat but not the internal organs?

<margin>Primary Indications</margin> Heat-related eye pain, injury to the corners of the eyes, tearing, and improving vision. Intestinal sores, abdominal pain, and dysentery. Women’s vaginal swelling and pain. Long-term use prevents forgetfulness. <gloss>Divine Husbandman's Classic</gloss>. Cold or heat in the five viscera, chronic diarrhea with pus and blood. Stops "wasting-thirst" <note>diabetes-like symptoms</note>, treats great fright, removes water retention, benefits the bones, harmonizes the stomach, thickens the intestines, and stops abdominal pain. <gloss>Miscellaneous Records</gloss>. Treats the "Five Labors and Seven Injuries," boosts Qi, stops heart and abdominal pain, palpitations, and irritability. Moistens the Heart and Lungs, promotes muscle growth, stops bleeding, treats seasonal heat diseases, stops night sweats, and treats various skin sores and toxic swellings. Made into pills, it treats childhood malnutrition and kills parasites. <gloss>Daming</gloss>. Settles Liver Qi, treats toxic heat sores and fistulas, irritability in the heart, nausea, and the urge to vomit. Treats fullness and oppression below the heart. Governs heart disease where energy is rebellious and overflowing, and accumulations in the heart. <gloss>Zangqi</gloss> <gloss>Zhen Quan</gloss>

<summary>This page details the medicinal properties, varieties, and processing methods of Coptis (Huanglian), emphasizing its role as a primary treatment for "fire" (heat) in the body's various organ systems. It includes historical geographical sources and specific dietary prohibitions, such as avoiding pork while taking the herb.</summary>

# **Compendium of Materia Medica: Volume 13**

# **Goldthread (Huanglian)** <gloss>Haogu says: Remove the core. Apply to malignant blood sores. Antidote for drug overdoses. Treats poisoning from calomel <note>mercurous chloride</note> at the crown of the head and the "bean-sized" points on the feet. Shizhen introduces Yuansu’s teachings, saying:</gloss>

The nature of Goldthread is cold and its flavor is bitter. Both its essence and aroma are potent; it can both ascend and descend, representing the "Yang within Yin." It enters the Hand Lesser Yin <note>Heart</note> Meridian. It has six primary uses: first, to drain fire from the Heart; second, to remove damp-heat from the Middle Burner <note>the digestive region</note>; third, it is essential for all types of sores; fourth, to dispel wind-dampness; fifth, for sudden outbreaks of red eyes; and sixth, to stop bleeding in the middle part of the body. Zhang Zhongjing treated nine types of "stuffiness below the heart" <note>epigastric distension</note>, and his five types of "Heart-Draining Decoctions" all utilized it. <gloss>Huo Wuyi says</gloss>: Bitterness enters the Heart, and cold overcomes heat. Goldthread possesses the ultimate bitterness among bitter things; its coldness guides away the "empty heat" <note>deficiency heat</note> below the heart. If it meets sweetness, it moves; if it meets bitterness, it settles. The bitterness of Goldthread and Reed Pith is used to settle this condition. <gloss>Haogu says</gloss>: Goldthread is bitter and drying. Bitterness enters the Heart, and the ultimate result is dryness. To drain the Heart is actually to drain the Spleen. This is "draining the son when the mother organ is in excess" <note>a Five Elements theory principle where the Heart is the mother of the Spleen</note>. <gloss>Zhenheng says</gloss>: Goldthread removes damp-heat from the Middle Burner and drains Heart fire. However, if the Spleen and Stomach Qi are too weak to transport nutrients, Scutellaria <note>Huangqin</note> should be used instead. In the past, I stir-fried it with pig gall juice and assisted it with Gentian <note>Longdancao</note> to powerfully drain fire from the Liver and Gallbladder. For dysentery where the stomach opening is hot and the patient cannot eat, use a decoction of Goldthread and Ginseng. Sip it throughout the day; if vomited, force yourself to drink again. If even one sip passes the throat, recovery is possible. <gloss>Liu Wansu says</gloss>: Ancient formulas regarded Goldthread as the supreme treatment for dysentery. The proper treatment for dysentery requires pungent, bitter, and cold medicines. Pungency can disperse and open up stagnant clusters; bitterness can dry dampness; cold can overcome heat and balance the Qi. While most bitter-cold drugs cause purging, only Goldthread and Phellodendron <note>Huangbo</note> are cold yet drying in nature, able to lower fire and remove dampness to stop diarrhea and dysentery. Thus, it is the "sovereign" <note>lead ingredient</note> for treating dysentery. <gloss>Zongshi says</gloss>: People today often use Goldthread for dysentery, strictly adhering to the principle of "bitterness dries dampness." But commoners, seeing only intestinal weakness and leakage with a hint of blood, use it without considering the balance of cold and heat. They only wish to stop the dysentery, which often leads to dangerous exhaustion. If the Qi is robust at the onset of illness with high heat and bloody stools, it stops upon taking it, and the full dose is unnecessary. For those who are weak and cold, be cautious and do not use it lightly. <gloss>Gao says</gloss>: All pain, itching, and sores belong to Heart fire. For all sores, Goldthread and Angelica <note>Danggui</note> should be the sovereign ingredients, with Licorice and Scutellaria as assistants. For unbearable sudden redness and swelling of the eyes, Goldthread and Angelica should be infused in wine and decocted. Furthermore, for undigested food and epigastric fullness, one must use Goldthread and Bitter Orange <note>Zhishi</note>. <gloss>Song says</gloss>: There are many formulas using Goldthread for the eyes, but the "Sheep Liver Pill" is particularly marvelous. I now instruct physicians to wash the eyes using equal parts Goldthread, Angelica, and Peony, decocted in snow water or sweet spring water. Wash while hot; if it cools, reheat it. This is extremely beneficial for the eyes. For "wind-toxin" red eyes where other medicines have failed, this is invariably miraculous. Eye diseases are caused by blood stagnation; therefore, blood-moving herbs are combined with Goldthread. Blood moves when it encounters heat, which is why the wash is used hot. <gloss>Han Mao says</gloss>: For diseases of the "five portions," Goldthread is the primary agent. It does not only drain Heart fire; this is why it is ranked alongside Scutellaria and Phellodendron. For those with eye ailments, soak it in human milk and steam it, then use as drops or take internally. Use it raw as the sovereign, assisted by a little Cinnamon <note>Guan gui</note>. Boil it a hundred times, add honey, and take on an empty stomach; this can cause the Heart and Kidney to communicate in an instant. Added to "Five-Ling Powder," it treats nocturnal emissions. When stir-fried with yellow earth, ginger juice, wine, and honey as the sovereign, with Rangoon Creeper <note>Shijunzi</note> as the minister, and White Peony, wine-processed Ophiopogon <note>Maidong</note>, and Aucklandia <note>Muxiang</note> as assistants, it treats the "five types of malnutrition" in children. Stir-fried with Evodia <note>Zhuyu</note> and equal parts Aucklandia, with double the amount of raw Rhubarb, made into water pills, it treats the "five types of dysentery." These are all examples of the proper method of formulating prescriptions. <gloss>Shizhen says</gloss>: Goldthread is an essential medicine for treating the eyes and dysentery. Ancient formulas like the "Fragrant Goldthread Pill" use Goldthread and Aucklandia. "Ginger-Goldthread Powder" uses Dried Ginger and Goldthread. "Transformation Pill" uses Goldthread and Evodia. "Ginger-Yellow Powder" uses Goldthread and Fresh Ginger. For "wasting and thirst" <note>diabetes-like symptoms</note>, use wine-steamed Goldthread. For "hidden summer heat," use wine-boiled Goldthread. For blood in the stool, use Goldthread and Garlic. For Liver fire, use Goldthread and Evodia. For mouth sores, use Goldthread and Asarum <note>Xixin</note>. These all pair one cold with one hot, one Yin with one Yang—using cold because of heat, or heat because of cold. Sovereign and minister assist each other, Yin and Yang complement each other; this is the pinnacle of the art of formulation. Thus, they achieve success without the harm of one-sided excess. <gloss>Hongjing says</gloss>: Common formulas often use Goldthread for dysentery and thirst. Daoist formulas use it for longevity. <gloss>Wei says</gloss>: Wang Wei of the Liu Song Dynasty wrote a "Praise of Goldthread":

> Goldthread’s flavor is bitter, left and right supporting each other. It cuts through cold and cleanses summer heat, extending life and lightening the body.

The scriptures say: In the past, when the Emperor used flying pellets, he could no longer walk, until he heard of this. Furthermore, Jiang Hai of the Liang Dynasty wrote a "Hymn to Goldthread":

> Goldthread is the supreme herb, second only to Cinnabar. It guards the walls and wards off evil, granting long life and eternal vision. Like a mottled dragon traversing the sky, or a tamed horse leaving the earth. Soaring with grace, following the Way brings profit.

<gloss>Shizhen says</gloss>: Neither the *Classic* <note>Shennong Bencao Jing</note> nor the *Additional Records* mention that long-term consumption of Goldthread leads to immortality. Only Tao Hongjing mentions that Daoist formulas use it for longevity and becoming a transcendent. Records state that Feng Junda and Heixue Gong both took Goldthread for fifty or ten years and became immortals. However, I believe Goldthread is a medicine of extreme bitterness and extreme cold, used to lower fire and dry dampness. Once the illness is cured, one should stop. How can it be taken for a long time? That would allow the "energy of execution" <note>the harsh, killing cold of autumn/winter</note> to constantly operate, thereby damaging the generative and harmonious Qi of life. The *Basic Questions* <note>Suwen</note> records Qibo saying: "The five flavors enter the stomach, each returning to what it prefers. Attacking for a long time increases the Qi; this is the natural transformation of things. If the Qi increases for too long, it follows the course of Heaven." Wang Bing’s commentary says: Sour enters the Liver as warmth, bitter enters the Heart as heat, pungent enters the Lung as coolness, salty enters the Kidney as cold, and sweet enters the Spleen as ultimate Yin. The four energies are combined, and each increases its flavor and benefits its Qi. Thus, each follows the Qi of its home organ. Therefore, long-term consumption of Goldthread or Sophora <note>Kushen</note> actually results in *heat*. This is because it transforms into fire. The same applies to other flavors. Over time, the Qi of an organ becomes excessively dominant, leading to the exhaustion of others and the path to sudden death. This is why those who abstain from grain and take elixirs do not die suddenly—because they do not have the one-sided assistance of the five flavors. Furthermore, Qin Guan wrote to Qiao Xisheng regarding Goldthread: "I hear you are taking Goldthread for an eye ailment, even after ten ounces you have not stopped. This is likely unacceptable. Medical classics state that long-term use of Goldthread or Sophora actually causes heat. Although it is extremely cold, its flavor is extremely bitter; upon entering the stomach, it first returns to..."

# Compendium of Materia Medica: Volume 13, Herbs
## [Section on Coptis chinensis / Goldthread]

If the heart remains in a state of distress for a long time without ceasing, the "Heart Fire" <note>In Traditional Chinese Medicine, the Heart is associated with the Fire element; "Heart Fire" refers to inflammatory or over-active states</note> becomes overly dominant, resulting in heat. This is the underlying principle. Furthermore, eye diseases are rooted in "Liver Heat." The Liver and Heart stand in a "Mother and Son" relationship <note>The Five Elements theory: Wood (Liver) fuels Fire (Heart)</note>; if the Heart is fire, the Liver is also fire. The Kidney, however, is a solitary organ of Water. When a person suffers from a condition where one part Water cannot overcome two parts Fire, how can they long endure bitter medicines? Such medicines cause the Heart to become overly dominant in its specific nature. To use fire to save fire—how can that be acceptable? 

Qin Yueren <note>The legendary physician Bian Que</note> wrote his book based on the theories of the Duke of Wang, expanding upon them in detail. In our own Ming Dynasty, Prince Duan of Jing suffered from many "fire" illnesses. His physicians ordered him to take "Golden Flower Pills," a cooling medicine consisting of four ingredients including Coptis. He took these for several years, but the fire only grew more intense, eventually leading to internal cataracts and loss of sight. Observing this, we see that bitter, cold medicines not only prevent a person from achieving longevity, but if taken for a long time, they cause the vital energy to become unbalanced. This imbalance is the very reason for a premature death. We should <gloss>formerly page 22</gloss> take the words of the *Suwen* <note>The Basic Questions of the Yellow Emperor's Inner Canon</note> as our law. The claims in Master Tao’s Daoist books regarding long-term consumption for immortality are entirely mistaken. These errors harm people most severely; physicians must be aware of this. Yang Shiying stated: Coptis is able to remove "evil blood" from the orifices of the heart.

<insert>Excess Heat in the Heart Meridian</insert> Use "Heart-Purging Decoction" (Xiexin Tang). Use seven *qian* <note>approx. 26 grams</note> of Coptis, one and a half cups of water. Boil down to one cup. Take warm, far from mealtimes. Reduce the dose for children. <gloss>From: Formulas from the Imperial Grace Formulary</gloss>

<insert>Sudden Heat and Heart Pain</insert> Eight *qian* of Coptis, chopped. Decocted in water. <note>From: Secret Essentials from the Outer Terrace</note>

<insert>Liver Fire causing Pain</insert> Coptis stir-fried with ginger juice and ground into powder. Mix with rice paste to make pills the size of a parasol tree seed. Take thirty-nine pills per dose with plain boiled water.

<insert>Vomiting</insert> Take thirty or forty-nine pills per dose. <gloss>Prepared as "Hidden Nourishment Pills"</gloss> For nausea, as well as red and white dysentery, "wasting-thirst" <note>diabetes-like symptoms</note>, intestinal wind <note>bloody stools</note>, alcohol poisoning, and various diarrheal diseases, all are suitable. <gloss>Mastered by "Yellow Dragon Pills" boiled in wine; use one jin of Sichuan Coptis</gloss> To change the yellowing of the hair <gloss>suitable if the condition is unstable</gloss>, take with plain water. <gloss>Formula from Danxi</gloss>

# Dysentery and Abdominal Pain
Red and white dysentery <note>refers to bloody or mucoid stools</note> causes pain and heaviness in the lower body, hence it is called "heavy descent." One may go dozens of times a day and night with twisting pain in the umbilical region.

# Picrorhiza (Huhuanglian) <gloss>From the Song Dynasty Kaibao Era</gloss>
<gloss>The flavor is bitter and "cutting."</gloss> <gloss>Shizhen says: Its nature, flavor, and effects are similar to Coptis (Huanglian), hence the name. "Guluze" is the foreign name for it.</gloss>

### Collection and Preparation
<gloss>Gong says: Picrorhiza comes from the country of Persia. It grows on the edges of fields. The sprouts resemble Prunella (Xiakucao). The tip of the root looks like a bird's beak. When broken, the inside looks like a withered willow branch—the center is black and the outside is yellow. It can be harvested at any time. When broken, if dust rises like smoke, it is genuine.</gloss>

## Root
### Properties
<gloss>Bitter, balanced, and non-toxic. Gong says: It is very cold. It is incompatible with Chrysanthemum, Scrophularia (Xuanshen), and Dictamnus (Baixianpi). It counteracts Croton seed poisoning. Avoid pork while taking it, as it may cause leakage of essence.</gloss>

### Primary Indications
<gloss>Supplements the Liver and Gallbladder, brightens the eyes. Treats "bone-steaming" tidal fever <note>chronic consumptive fever</note>, the "three wastings" <note>diabetes-like symptoms</note>, irritability with heat in the palms and soles, fetal heat in women, fright in children, cold or heat-related dysentery, the five types of hemorrhoids, and strengthens the intestines.</gloss>

# Baikal Skullcap (Huang Qin) <gloss>Middle Grade</gloss>

<gloss>Aliases: Rotten Intestine, Golden Scutellaria, Internal Intestine, Hollow, Carved Stone, Lady Gui, Medicine</gloss> <gloss>Aliases: Carved, Page, Wu, Bitter, Overseer, Master, Record</gloss> **Those with solid interiors are "Larval Scutellaria" (Ziqin)** <gloss>Striped Scutellaria, Network</gloss> **"Supporting House Scutellaria"** <gloss>Tang Dynasty; Tao Hongjing says they are round</gloss>
Those that are broken are called "Old Scutellaria" (Suqin). Because their centers are all decayed, they are named "Rotten Intestine." Shizhen <note>Li Shizhen</note> says: The character for *Qin* in the *Shuowen Jiezi* dictionary is written as "yellow herb," referring to its color. Some say *Qin* means *Qian* (dark/black), as the old roots are often hollow, yellow outside and black inside. This is what is now called "Piece Scutellaria" (Pianqin). It has names like "Rotten Intestine" because of its decayed core. "Larval Scutellaria" (Ziqin) refers to the new roots which are mostly solid; these are what are now called "Striped Scutellaria" (Tiaoqin). Some say Western Scutellaria is mostly hollow and deep in color, while Northern Scutellaria is mostly solid and deep. <gloss>The "Separate Records" says: Scutellaria grows in the valleys of Zigui and Yuanju. Collect the roots on the third day of the third month and dry in the shade.</gloss> <gloss>Tao Hongjing says:</gloss> Zigui belongs to Jianping Prefecture. Now the best comes from Pengcheng. Pengzhou also has it. Only those that are deep in color and firm are good. **Huang** <gloss>Collection: Common formulas use it often. Taoists do not require it. Feng says: Those now from Yizhou, Kuochuan, and Jingzhou are excellent. Those with solid exteriors are also good and called "Pure Tail Scutellaria."</gloss> **Su Song says:** Nowadays, it is found in all nearby prefectures of Sichuan, Hedong, and Shaanxi. The seedlings are over a foot long. The stems are as thick as chopsticks. The leaves grow in clusters from the ground on four sides, resembling Gromwell. It grows about a foot high. Some have single stems. The leaves are slender, long, and green, growing in opposite pairs. In the sixth month, it blooms with purple flowers. The root is like Anemarrhena, four to five inches long. Collect the roots in the second and eighth months and dry in the sun. Wu Pu’s Materia Medica says: In the second month, it grows reddish-yellow leaves in opposite pairs on four sides. The stem is hollow or square, three to four feet high. In the fourth month, the flowers are purplish-red. In the sixth month, the seeds are black and the root is yellow. Collect from the second to the ninth month.

# Root
<gloss>(The *Miscellaneous Records* states) Extremely cold. (Pu states) The Divine Farmer, Tong Jun, and Lei Gong describe it as bitter and non-toxic. Li Dangzhi notes it is slightly warm. (Gao states) It can rise or descend; it is Yin in nature. (Hao Gu states) Its energy is cold, its flavor is slightly bitter and sweet. It is the "minor Yang within Yin." It enters the Hand Greater Yin <note>Lung</note> blood division. Yuan Su states its energy is cool, its flavor is bitter and sweet. Its energy is thick while its flavor is thin. It floats and rises; it is the "Yin within Yang." It enters the Hand Lesser Yang <note>Triple Burner</note> and Foot Bright Yang <note>Stomach</note> meridians. If stir-fried with wine, its effects move upward. (Cai states) Cornelian cherry and Dragon Bone serve as its "messengers" <note>herbs that guide or assist</note>. It dislikes Onion seeds and fears Cinnabar, Peony, and Veratrum. It suppresses Magnolia bark and Coptis to stop abdominal pain. When combined with Schisandra and Oyster Shell, it helps a woman conceive. When combined with Astragalus, Rice water, and Small Red Beans, it treats scrofula <note>lymph node swelling</note>. (Shi Zhen states) With wine, it moves upward. With pig gall juice, it clears Liver and Gallbladder fire. With Bupleurum, it dispels alternating chills and fever. With Peony, it treats dysentery. With Mulberry bark, it drains Lung fire. With Atractylodes, it calms the fetus.</gloss>

-> Flavor: Bitter; Nature: Balanced; Non-toxic <-

Mainly used for various heat-related illnesses, jaundice, intestinal dysentery, and diarrhea. It expels excess water and moves blood blockages. It treats malignant sores, erosive ulcers, and burns. <gloss>(Yuan Su states) It treats redness and heat, "excess-type" internal heat, twisting pain in the lower abdomen, and supports the Small Intestine. (Cai states) It detoxifies silver and treats "red toxins" and bone-steaming fever <term>chronic internal heat associated with wasting diseases</term>.</gloss> It treats alternating chills and fever, gastrointestinal discomfort, and breaks up stagnant energy. It treats the "five types of strangury" <note>painful urinary disorders</note> to ensure smooth flow, removes irritability in the joints, and resolves heat toxins. <gloss>Tao Hongjing notes it directs energy downward and treats epidemic heat diseases.</gloss> It treats swelling, discharges pus, and heals breast abscesses and back carbuncles. <gloss>Da Ming states</gloss> it clears the Heart, treats damp-heat in the Lungs, and drains upward-reversing Lung fire. It heals upper-body heat, redness and swelling in the eyes, and excessive blood stasis. It clears accumulated blood in the upper body, supplements the "cold water" of the Bladder, nourishes Yin, and causes excess Yang to recede. <gloss>Yuan Su states</gloss> it treats wind-heat and damp-heat headaches, dizziness, "running piglet" energy <note>a sensation of gas or energy rushing from the abdomen to the throat</note>, heat-induced pain, fire-based coughing, lung atrophy, and a "fishy" smell in the throat, as well as various types of bleeding. <gloss>Shi Zhen states</gloss> that on the second day of the second month, Scutellaria is highly effective for smoothing energy, resolving phlegm, removing wind-heat, and clearing heat from the skin and muscles. The thin, solid, and firm roots <note>known as "Twig Scutellaria"</note> drain fire from the Large Intestine, nourish Yin to recede Yang, and supplement the Bladder’s cold water to nourish the source of transformation. Its distinction between upper and lower body applications follows the same logic as Bitter Orange and Hawthorn. <gloss>Yuan Su states</gloss> there are nine primary uses for Scutellaria: 1. Draining Lung heat. 2. Treating wind-heat and damp-heat in the upper body and skin. 3. Dispelling various types of heat. 4. Benefiting the energy in the chest. 5. Clearing phlegm from the diaphragm. 6. Removing various dampness from the Spleen meridian. 7. It is essential for use in the summer months. 8. Nourishing Yin and receding Yang for women after childbirth. 9. Calming the fetus. When stir-fried with wine, it moves upward to treat blood accumulation in the upper body; nothing else can remove it. For those with dysentery, bloody stools, abdominal pain, heaviness, and persistent body fever, it should be used alongside Peony and Licorice. For intolerable pain from ulcers and sores, bitter and cold medicines like Scutellaria and Coptis are appropriate, though one must carefully consider which part of the body is affected to guide the medicine correctly. <gloss>Zhen Heng states</gloss> Scutellaria’s ability to descend phlegm relies on its fire-draining property. To remove damp-heat from the upper burner, it must be washed with wine. To drain Lung fire, it must be assisted by Mulberry bark. If the Lungs are deficient, overusing it will damage them; one must first use Asparagus root to stabilize the Lung energy before administration. Scutellaria and Atractylodes are "sage-like" medicines for calming the fetus. Common folk consider Scutellaria too cold and dare not use it, not realizing that pregnancy requires clearing heat and cooling the blood. When blood does not move recklessly, the fetus is nourished. Scutellaria treats the upper and middle burners and can direct fire downward, while Atractylodes tonifies the Spleen. <gloss>Luo Tianyi states</gloss> the Lungs govern energy; heat damages energy and causes numbness in the body. Furthermore, "fishy smells" are associated with the Lungs. The bitterness of Scutellaria can drain fire, supplement energy, benefit the Lungs, and treat a fishy odor in the throat. <gloss>Su Song states</gloss> that Zhang Zhongjing’s four "Heart-Draining Decoctions" for treating fullness and congestion below the heart all use Scutellaria because it governs various heats and benefits the Small Intestine. Also, for "Great Yang" disease where purging leads to persistent diarrhea, panting, and sweating, there is the Pueraria, Scutellaria, and Coptis Decoction. It is also frequently used in "Fetal Calming Powders" for pregnancy. <gloss>Shi Zhen states</gloss> Zhang Jiegū said Scutellaria drains Lung fire and treats Spleen dampness. Li Dongyuan said "Plate Scutellaria" <note>older, hollow roots</note> treats Lung fire, while "Twig Scutellaria" <note>young, solid roots</note> treats Large Intestine fire. Zhu Danxi said Scutellaria treats fire in the upper and middle burners. Zhang Zhongjing used it in "Minor Bupleurum Decoction" for "Lesser Yang" syndrome, in "Scutellaria Decoction" for combined "Great Yang" and "Lesser Yang" diarrhea, and in "Heart-Draining Decoction" for fullness without pain after purging in "Lesser Yang" syndrome. Cheng Wuyi said Scutellaria is bitter and enters the Heart to dissipate congested heat. This means Scutellaria can enter six meridians: the Hand and Foot Lesser Yang, the Hand and Foot Greater Yin, and the Hand and Foot Bright Yang. Because Scutellaria is cold in nature, bitter in flavor, and yellow-green in color, if it enters the Heart, its cold overcomes heat to drain Heart fire and treat Spleen damp-heat. Thus, the "Metal" <note>Lungs</note> is not punished by fire, and Stomach fire does not flow into the Lungs—this is how it "saves" the Lungs. It is unsuitable for Lung deficiency because its bitter cold damages the Spleen and Stomach, thereby harming the "Mother" <note>the Spleen is the mother of the Lungs in Five Elements theory</note>. In "Lesser Yang" syndrome, there are symptoms like alternating chills and fever, pain and fullness in the chest and ribs, being withdrawn and having no desire to eat, irritability, vomiting, thirst, or difficulty urinating. Although the illness is said to be between the exterior and interior, the congestion in the chest and ribs actually involves pathogens in the Heart, Lungs, and upper burner.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the therapeutic applications of Baikal Skullcap (Huangqin), moving from its general properties to specific clinical debates and a personal account from the author, Li Shizhen, followed by a list of classical formulas for various ailments.</meta>

Irritability, vomiting, and a silent lack of desire for food and drink are symptoms of the Spleen and Middle Burner <term>Zhong Jiao; the central metabolic region of the body</term>. Therefore, Baikal Skullcap <term>Huangqin</term> is used to treat the "Ministerial Fire" <term>Xiang Huo; a type of internal heat related to the liver and gallbladder</term> of the Hand and Foot Lesser Yang <term>Shao Yang</term> meridians. Baikal Skullcap is indeed a primary medicine for the Lesser Yang meridian. 

In his annotations on the *Treatise on Cold Damage* <note>original: "Shanghan Lun"</note>, Cheng Wuyi simply states: "The bitterness of Bupleurum <term>Chaihu</term> and Baikal Skullcap serves to release the heat of invading pathogens. The bitterness of Baikal Skullcap also firms and constrains the energy of the intestines and stomach." However, he missed the subtlety of how it treats fire. Yang Shiying stated in his *Direct Guide to Prescriptions* that Bupleurum is not as effective as Baikal Skullcap at reducing fever. This is because he did not realize that Bupleurum’s heat reduction comes from its bitter nature "releasing" and "dispersing" the manifestation <term>the "branches"</term> of the fire. Baikal Skullcap's heat reduction comes from its "cold" nature overcoming the heat, striking at the very source <term>the "root"</term> of the fire. 

The master physician Zhongjing also said: "If there is abdominal pain in the Lesser Yang stage, remove Baikal Skullcap and add Peony." This appears to contradict the *Miscellaneous Records* <note>original: "Bie Lu"</note> which states that it treats "acute pain in the lower abdomen" and "benefits the small intestine." Cheng Wuyi explained that because Baikal Skullcap is bitter and cold, and bitterness can "firm" the Kidneys, it should be removed. This explanation is also not quite right. At this point, one must rely on intuition and differentiate based on the pulse and symptoms. If the abdominal pain is caused by food intake or catching a cold, or if there is palpitations below the heart from drinking water or difficulty urinating—all without a rapid pulse—this indicates a "non-heat" internal syndrome. In such cases, Baikal Skullcap must not be used. However, if there is "heat-reversal" <term>Jue</term> abdominal pain, or if the Lungs are hot and urination is blocked, how could one not use Baikal Skullcap? 

Therefore, a skilled observer first seeks the underlying principle and does not simply cling to the literal text. Previously, a person from Xuan who was prone to excessive drinking suffered from unbearable acute pain in the lower abdomen and painful, dripping urination <term>Lin syndrome</term>. Various medicines failed. By chance, they used a decoction of a single herb—Baikal Skullcap—and the pain stopped. Wang Haizang mentioned someone who took Aconite <term>Fuzi</term> incorrectly while in a deficient state, leading to many illnesses and urinary blockage. Their pulse was surging and rapid; they were cured with Baikal Skullcap. Both these cases involved "pain from intense heat." How can a scholar be restricted by narrow rules? 

When I was twenty years old, I caught a cold. After coughing for a long time and failing to observe health precautions, I fell seriously ill. I suffered from "bone-steaming" heat <term>Gu Zheng; a deep-seated fever typical of chronic illness</term>, and my skin felt as if it were scorched by fire. Every day I spat up phlegm and suffered from night sweats. In the summer months, I was parched with irritability and thirst, and my appetite almost vanished. My six pulses were floating and flooding. I took various medicines—Bupleurum, Ginseng, Ophiopogon, Schizonepeta, and others for "consumption" <term>Zhai</term>—for over a month, but the condition grew worse. Everyone thought I would surely die. My late father happened to recall Li Dongyuan’s method for treating Lung heat that feels like scorching fire: the "Guided Drinking" formula. He realized that my condition was heat in the "Qi division" <term>Qi Fen; a stage of febrile disease</term> and that I should use a single-herb "Baikal Skullcap Decoction" to drain the Lung fire. Following the formula, he used one ounce of "sliced" Skullcap <note>original: "Pian Qin"</note>, added two cups of water, and boiled it down to one cup. I drank it all at once. The next day, my body heat completely subsided, and my phlegm and cough were both cured. <gloss>The wonder of the treatment reaching the Lung meridian was as remarkable as this!</gloss>

### Three Tonics Pill (San Bu Wan)
Treats the Triple Burner <term>San Jiao</term>. Yellow Pills. It treats the "Five Taxations" and "Seven Injuries" in men <term>chronic physical and emotional exhaustion</term>, wasting-thirst <term>diabetes-like symptoms</term>, and failure to build muscle. For women, it treats vaginal discharge <term>Dai Xia</term>, cold or heat in the hands and feet, and diarrhea. It drains fire from the five viscera. 
**Spring (3 months):** Baikal Skullcap 4 oz, Rhubarb 3 oz, Coptis 4 oz. 
**Summer (3 months):** Baikal Skullcap 6 oz, Rhubarb 1 oz, Coptis 7 oz. 
**Autumn (3 months):** Baikal Skullcap 6 oz, Rhubarb 3 oz, Coptis 3 oz. 
**Winter (3 months):** Baikal Skullcap 3 oz, Rhubarb 5 oz, Coptis 2 oz. 
Grind the three substances according to the season. Sift and make pills with honey the size of a black bean. Take with rice water. Take 5 pills per dose, three times a day. If no effect, increase to 7 pills. After one month, the illness will be cured. Long-term use allows one to "run as fast as a horse." This has been proven effective. Do not eat pork. (*Illustrated Materia Medica*)

# Large-leaf Gentian
->Pronounced *Jiao*. Intermediate grade in the *Divine Husbandman's Classic of Materia Medica*<-

<insert>Explanation of Names</insert> Qin Jiu <gloss>Tang Dynasty name</gloss>, Qin Gua <gloss>Xiao Bing’s name</gloss>. ○ <gloss>Gong says:</gloss> Large-leaf Gentian <note>original: "Qinjiao"</note> is commonly written as "Qin Jiao" [using the character for 'glue'], but the original name was "Qin Jiu" [meaning 'entwined']. <gloss>Shizhen says:</gloss> Its roots are earthy yellow and intertwined with net-like patterns. Those that are long, large, and yellowish-white are considered superior. When using it, one should break it open and remove the core. <insert>Collection of Notes</insert> <gloss>says:</gloss> Nowadays, those produced in Jingzhou, Binzhou, and Qizhou are best. <gloss>Su Song says:</gloss> It is found in many prefectures of the Yellow River and Shaanxi regions today. Its roots are yellowish and intertwined, about one foot long, and vary in thickness. The stems and branches are five to six inches high. The leaves are lush and connected to the stalk; both are green, resembling lettuce leaves. It flowers in the sixth month with deep purple blossoms like those of the Sweet Flag <term>Acorus</term>. It produces seeds in both spring and autumn. Harvest the roots and dry them in the shade.

<insert>Preparation of Roots</insert> <gloss>Lei Xiao says:</gloss> One must distinguish the pattern at the base of the root: those with leftward-twisting patterns are called "Qin" for treating illnesses, while those with rightward-twisting patterns are called "Jiao." <note>This likely refers to the spiral growth direction of the root fibers.</note> It is used for "leg qi" <term>swelling or weakness of the legs</term>. When using Qin, wipe away the yellow dust with a cloth. It is slightly warm with a bitter and acrid taste. It removes internal pathogens; as a "minor Yang" herb, its energy can both rise and descend. It enters the Hand Yang Brightness <term>Large Intestine</term> meridian. Wu Zicai says: Sweet Flag <term>Acorus</term> acts as its envoy; it fears cow's milk.

<insert>Flavor and Nature</insert> Bitter, neutral, non-toxic. <gloss>The *Miscellaneous Records* says:</gloss> Acrid, slightly warm. <gloss>Da Ming says:</gloss> Bitter and cold. <gloss>Zhang Yuansu says:</gloss> [Text regarding its medicinal movement].

<insert>Main Indications</insert> Chills and fever, malicious energy, damp-wind painful obstruction <term>arthritis/arthralgia</term>, and pain in the joints of the limbs. It promotes water metabolism and benefits urination. <gloss>*Divine Husbandman's Classic*</gloss> Treats wind-related ailments regardless of whether they are new or chronic, and tightness or spasms of the whole body. <gloss>*Miscellaneous Records*</gloss> Consumptive "bone-steaming" fever <term>chronic internal heat often seen in tuberculosis</term>, childhood malnutrition, and seasonal epidemic energy. <gloss>Da Ming</gloss> Mixed with cow's milk and used as eye drops; benefits the large and small intestines; treats "wine jaundice" <term>jaundice exacerbated by alcohol</term>, detoxifies alcohol, and removes "head wind" <term>chronic headaches or facial pain</term>. <gloss>Zhen Quan</gloss> For wind-dampness in the Great Yang and Yang Brightness meridians, paralysis of the hands and feet, locked jaw, toothaches, lack of taste in the mouth, "intestinal wind" <term>bloody stools</term>, and bleeding. It nourishes the blood and benefits the tendons. <gloss>Zhang Yuansu</gloss> Highly effective treatment for heat.

<gloss>Shizhen says:</gloss> Large-leaf Gentian is a medicine for the Hand and Foot Yang Brightness meridians, and it also enters the Liver and Gallbladder. Therefore, it is essential for paralysis of the limbs, jaundice, and excessive thirst. It is chosen for its ability to clear damp-heat from the Yang Brightness. Yang Brightness energy is effective at treating "bone-steaming" heat and fever from exhaustion. <gloss>Shizhen says:</gloss> When there is dampness, the body feels heavy, sore, and painful, with irritability and heat, afternoon tidal fever, and "bone-steaming." Thus, the *Formulas of Divine Grace* treats irritable heat from acute exhaustion and body soreness using one *liang* <term>approx. 37.5g</term> each of Large-leaf Gentian and Bupleurum, with five *qian* of Licorice. Grind into powder, and for each dose, take three *qian* mixed with plain hot water. To treat childhood bone-steaming and tidal fever leading to wasting and weakness: <insert>Appended Formulas</insert> <gloss>Five old, six new</gloss>.

Boil until reduced to 70% of the original volume. Divide into portions and take while warm. This formula is from Xu Renzhe; Master Sun Simiao's formula adds six *qian* of Mirabilite.

# Bupleurum <gloss>Superior Class of the Divine Husbandman's Classic</gloss>

<gloss>Explanation of Names</gloss> Earth Fragrance <gloss>from the Miscellaneous Records</gloss>, Rue-scented Wormwood <gloss>Wu Pu’s name</gloss>, Tamarisk-like Herb.
<margin><gloss>Su Gong says:</gloss> *Zihu* [茈胡] is the ancient form of the character *Chai* [柴]. The *Rhapsody on the Imperial Park* <note>A famous Han Dynasty poem by Sima Xiangru</note> mentions "Purple Ginger" [Zijiang], and the *Erya* dictionary says this herb is written with the character *Zi* [茈]. The root of this herb is purple in color. It is currently used frequently by the Imperial Medical Office.</margin>
<margin><gloss>The Compendium [Gangmu] says:</gloss> This is indeed *Chaihu*. It has been called *Chaihu* since the Tang Dynasty. Shizhen notes that the character *Chai* has two pronunciations: *yu* and *zi*. The "purple" in the Gromwell plant is always pronounced *zi*, but the *zi* in *Zihu* is pronounced *chai*. *Zihu* grows in the mountains; when young, its shoots are edible; when old, they become woody like brushwood [*chai*]. Thus, the shoots have a beautiful name <gloss>Wu Pu’s records say: Bupleurum is also called "Rue." Its shoots are flat, fragrant, and edible. It grows in the river valleys of Hongnong and Yuanju. Roots are collected in the second and eighth months and sun-dried</gloss>, while the root is called "Brushwood-root" [*Chaihu*]. Su Gong’s explanation lacks clarity regarding the ancient texts. Zhang Zhongjing’s *Treatise on Cold Damage* <note>A foundational text of Chinese medicine from the 2nd century AD</note> still uses the ancient character *Zi*.</margin>
<gloss>Zongshi says:</gloss> It is extremely cold. Major and Minor Bupleurum Decoctions are the essential formulas for phlegm-qi. It would be a great error to use the roots of Rue-scented Wormwood instead. <gloss>Su Song says:</gloss> It is found today throughout the Guanzhong and Shaanxi regions and near the Yangtze and Huai rivers. Those from Silver Prefecture <note>Yinzhou</note> are superior. In the second month, it sprouts; it is very fragrant. The stems are blue-purple, hard, and slightly striated. The leaves resemble bamboo leaves but are slightly tighter and smaller. Some resemble "Slanted Wormwood" [*Xiehao*], while others resemble the leaves of *Ophiopogon* but shorter. In the seventh month, it blooms with small yellow flowers. The root is pale red, resembling *Peucedanum* <note>Qianhu</note> but tougher. Those from Danzhou produce green seeds and differ from other varieties. The root resembles a reed head with red hairs like a rat's tail. Those with a single long leaf are best. <gloss>Zhen Quan says:</gloss> It is produced in Pinzhou. When the "White Crane" <note>likely a poetic reference to a type of bird or movement</note> flies there, the fragrance of Bupleurum rises straight into the clouds. Anyone passing through feels refreshed. <gloss>Li says:</gloss> Bupleurum from Yinxia is the most excellent. The roots are like rat tails, one to two feet long, with a fine fragrance. Modern people often do not recognize the true variety and use roots from Tonghua as substitutes; however, their efficacy is still better than those from other regions because the soil there is sandy. <gloss>Ji says:</gloss> For dispersing pathogens, use "Northern Bupleurum." For deficiency heat, use the soft "Ocean Bupleurum" from the south. Shizhen says: Silver Prefecture is modern-day Shenmu County. The variety produced there is over a foot long, slightly white and soft, and difficult to obtain. The variety from the north is soft like *Peucedanum* and is called "Northern Bupleurum"; it is excellent for medicine. The southern variety is tough like wormwood roots and unsuitable for use. Those with leaves like leeks or bamboo are superior; those like "Evil Wormwood" are the lowest grade. Note: The *Lesser Annals of Xia* <note>an ancient ritual calendar</note> states that in the second month of spring, the Rue begins to grow. The *Cangjie* dictionary explains that Rue resembles wormwood and is edible. It is related to Bupleurum but not as good for medicine. Therefore, Su Gong believed it was not true Bupleurum. Recently, there is a type with roots like *Platycodon* or *Adenophora*, white and large, called "Qiang Bupleurum" or "Silver Bupleurum," but it has no medicinal qi or flavor and must be distinguished.

# The Root
<gloss>Lei says:</gloss> When you obtain Silver Prefecture Bupleurum, remove the neck and head. Use a silver knife to scrape off the thin red skin.
<gloss>Qi and Flavor:</gloss> Bitter, non-toxic. <gloss>Miscellaneous Records say:</gloss> Slightly cold. <gloss>Wu Pu says:</gloss> The Divine Husbandman, Qibo, and Leigong say it is bitter and non-toxic. <gloss>Daming says:</gloss> Sweet. <gloss>Yuansu says:</gloss> The qi is warm, the flavor is slightly bitter. It is "Yang within Yin" <term>a substance that has descending properties but rising potential</term>. It draws the clear qi to rotate to the left. <gloss>He also says:</gloss> Wipe the skin clean with a coarse cloth before use. Do not let it come into contact with fire, or the primary effect will be lost.
<gloss>Gao says:</gloss> Its qi and flavor are both light; it is Yang and ascending. It is a medicine for the Lesser Yang channel <note>Shaoyang, associated with the Gallbladder and Triple Burner</note>, drawing the stomach qi upward. Its bitter and cold nature allows it to disperse pathogens. It is the guiding herb for the four channels of Hand and Foot Lesser Yang and Terminal Yin. In the organs, it governs the blood; in the channels, it governs the qi. To ascend, use the root soaked in wine. To move through the center or descend, use the root tips. <gloss>Rencai says:</gloss> Pinellia [*Banxia*] serves as its messenger. It dislikes Gleditsia pods and fears Aster and False Hellebore. <gloss>Shizhen says:</gloss> To act on the Lesser Yang, use Baikal Skullcap [*Huangqin*] as an assistant. To act on the Terminal Yin, use Coptis [*Huanglian*] as an assistant.

# Main Indications
<gloss>The Classic:</gloss> Knotted qi in the heart, abdomen, intestines, and stomach. Accumulations of food and drink. Pathogenic qi of cold and heat. It "pushes out the old and brings in the new" <term>promotes metabolic turnover and detoxification</term>. Long-term use lightens the body, brightens the eyes, and benefits the essence.
<gloss>Miscellaneous Records:</gloss> Removes vexation and heat under the heart in cold damage. Treats various heat-binding diseases, pathogenic qi in the chest, and wandering qi between the five viscera. Treats accumulations in the large intestine, water swelling, and "damp-bi" <term>dampness-related joint pain or numbness</term> with contractions. Can also be used in medicinal baths.
<gloss>Zhen Quan:</gloss> Treats "heat exhaustion" <term>chronic consumptive fever</term> with aching joints, heat qi, and pain in the shoulders and back. Treats fatigue and emaciation. Lowers qi and aids digestion. Promotes the flow of qi and blood. For seasonal epidemics where internal and external heat do not resolve, decocting this herb alone is effective.
<gloss>Zhen Quan:</gloss> Tonifies the "Five Taxations and Seven Injuries" <term>traditional categories of physical and emotional exhaustion</term>.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Bupleurum (Chaihu) from the previous section, transitioning from its botanical identification to its extensive clinical applications, theoretical underpinnings in Chinese medicine, and specific medicinal formulas.</meta>

Removes irritability and stops fright, <gloss>increases</gloss> strength, resolves phlegm and stops coughing, moistens the heart and lungs, replenishes essence and marrow, <gloss>strengthens</gloss> the will, <gloss>greatly</gloss> clears the vision, removes consumptive exhaustion, and disperses heat in the muscles. It eliminates <gloss>early</gloss> morning tidal fever, alternating chills and fever, malaria, and jaundice. It treats various heat-related conditions in women before and after childbirth, fullness below the heart, and pain in the chest and ribs.

It treats the sinking of Yang Qi <note>The vital energy responsible for warming and activating the body</note>, disorders of the ears, the "Ministerial Fire" of the Liver, Gallbladder, Triple Burner, and Pericardium <note>Technical terms for specific organ systems and their associated energetic pathways</note>, as well as headaches, dizziness, blurred vision with redness and pain, cataracts, deafness, <gloss>nasal</gloss> ringing, various types of scrofula, "fatty qi" <note>abdominal masses</note>, chills and fever, and cases where heat enters the "Blood Chamber" <note>the uterus</note> in women, causing irregular menstruation. It also treats residual fever after smallpox or rashes in children, and the "Five Types of Childhood Malnutrition" <term>Gan</term> <note>A traditional category of pediatric digestive and nutritional disorders</note>. 

<gloss>Shizhen’s</gloss> <gloss>essential</gloss> <gloss>notes</gloss> state: [Xu] Zhicai said that this herb "obtains" <note>works well with</note> Platycodon, Rhubarb, Gypsum, Hemp Seed, Licorice, and Cinnamon. Boil one *dou* <note>about 2 liters</note> of water until four *sheng* remain, then add three square inches of nitre to treat cold damage, chills and fever, headache, and irritability with fullness below the heart. 

[Su] Song says: Zhang Zhongjing <note>The "Sage of Medicine" (150–219 AD)</note> treated Cold Damage <term>Shanghan</term> with formulas such as Major and Minor Bupleurum Decoctions, and Bupleurum with Dragon Bone or with Mirabilite. Therefore, later physicians consider this the most essential medicine for treating chills and fever. 

[Li] Gao <note>Also known as Li Dongyuan (1180–1251), founder of the Spleen and Stomach school</note> says: It can lead the "Clear Qi" upward and travel along the "Yang Path." In cases of Cold Damage, if there is "clumping" or heat, it should be added; if there is no heat, it should not. It can also lead the "Stomach Qi" upward, promoting the "Spring Command" <note>the rising, generative energy of spring</note>; for such purposes, it is appropriate to add it. Furthermore, in treating malaria, Bupleurum is the "King" <note>the primary ingredient</note>; according to the time of onset and the specific meridian involved, it should be assisted by "meridian-leading" herbs. For malaria across all twelve meridians, Bupleurum must be used to disperse blood stasis and qi stagnation; its efficacy in this regard is similar to Forsythia. 

[Wang] Haogu says: Bupleurum can remove both internal and external deficiencies of the organs. It leads "Clear Qi" upward to follow the "Yang Path" and enters the Foot Shaoyang <note>Gallbladder</note> meridian. In the meridians, it governs Qi; in the organs, it governs Blood. When moving forward, it treats aversion to heat; when retreating, it treats aversion to cold. Because its nature is slightly cold and its flavor is thin, it can move through the meridians. If paired with herbs like Bur-reed, Zedoary, or Croton, it can dissolve hard accumulations, which means it is governing the Blood. For women whose menstruation suddenly starts or stops during a febrile illness or malaria, [Zhang] Yilao used Bupleurum Decoction added to formulas like the "Four Substances Decoction" <note>Siwu Tang, a primary blood tonic</note>, along with Gentiana macrophylla and Moutan Bark to regulate the menses. He also stated it is an essential medicine for post-partum deficiency heat in women.

[Kou] Zongshi says: The original *Classic* <note>The Divine Husbandman’s Materia Medica</note> does not contain a single word about treating "Labor" <term>Lao</term> <note>Consumptive exhaustion or chronic deficiency</note>, yet few modern prescriptions for "Labor" omit it. Alas! This has misled the world greatly. I have observed that one type of "Labor" occurs when the organs are depleted and damaged, allowing pathogenic heat to enter; because of this deficiency, "Labor" results. "Labor" [*Lao*] means "firm" [*Lao*]. One must use the herb with careful consideration. For example, in classical formulas for treating "Labor Heat," decocting it with Sweet Wormwood is perfectly appropriate. When taken, it is always effective. Once the heat is gone, one must stop. If it is taken when there is no heat, the condition will worsen. Even by the Yuan Dynasty, people could not bear to witness how many were harmed by this. *Rihua Bencao* says it "supplements the Five Labors and Seven Injuries," and the *Treatise on Medicinal Nature* says it "treats labor-fatigue and emaciation." If a physician stubbornly uses it for such diseases without the presence of "Real Heat," what can they expect but the death of the patient? In annotating the Materia Medica, not a single word should be overlooked, otherwise, the errors will be infinite for ten thousand generations; one must be cautious! However, in cases like Zhang Zhongjing's use of Bupleurum Decoction for alternating chills and fever or malaria symptoms, it is perfectly suited to the condition. 

[Li] Shizhen says: There are "Five Labors" <note>Exhaustion of the five major organ systems</note>. If the labor is in the Liver, Gallbladder, Heart, or Pericardium and involves heat, or if there are chills and fever in the Shaoyang meridian, then Bupleurum is a mandatory medicine for the Jueyin and Shaoyang meridians of both hands and feet. If the labor is in the Spleen and Stomach and involves heat, or if the Yang Qi is sinking, then Bupleurum is a mandatory medicine to lead the "Clear Qi" and clear heat. It is only when the labor is in the Lungs or Kidneys that it should not be used. For this reason, Li Dongyuan said it should be added when there is heat and omitted when there is not. He also said that for malaria in all meridians, Bupleurum is the "King." Since malaria of the twelve meridians involves "clumping," then for malaria of the lungs or back, or any of the twelve meridians where heat is present, it can be used skillfully. However, the practitioner must think deeply about the origin of the disease and adjust the dosage to hit the mark. [Kou] Zongshi failed to distinguish between the organs and meridians, or between the presence and absence of heat; his sweeping claim that Bupleurum does not treat "Labor" is an over-generalization and lacks a comprehensive view. For instance, the *Formulas of the Bureau of People's Welfare* treats various bleeding disorders with "Borneol and Water-Hyssop Pills," which use the method of simmering Bupleurum juice into a paste; few people today understand the logic behind this. 

According to Pang Yuanying’s *Talks from the Wilds*: The official Zhang Zhige had suffered from malaria and heat for a long time, becoming so emaciated he was just skin and bones. Doctors used heat-inducing medicines like Deer Antler and Aconite, but the heat only intensified. He summoned the medical official Sun Lin, who diagnosed him and administered one dose of Bupleurum Decoction. The heat decreased by ninety percent. After three doses, he was completely recovered. Sun Lin said: "This is called 'Labor Malaria.' The heat emerges from the marrow. By adding 'Hard' [hot] medicines, the Qi and Blood were further depleted; how could he not become emaciated? Heat can reside in the skin, the organs, or the bone marrow—none of these can be treated without Bupleurum. If you could get 'Silver' Bupleurum <note>A different species, *Stellaria dichotoma*</note>, only one dose would be needed. This southern variety is weaker, so it took three doses to work." Observing this, one can see the subtle beauty of using medicine correctly. Can one rely entirely on Zongshi’s theory?

# Hogfennel (Qianhu)
<gloss>Listed in the Medium Class of the *Miscellaneous Records*</gloss>

**Explanation of Names** <gloss>Shizhen says: According to Sun Shendu’s *Tang Dynasty Rhyme Dictionary*, it is written as "Jian-hu," but the meaning of this name is not yet understood.</gloss>

**Collected Explanations** <gloss>The *Miscellaneous Records* <note>original: 別錄, *Bielu*</note> state: Collect the roots of Hogfennel in the second and eighth months and dry them in the sun. [Tao] Hongjing says: It grows everywhere in nearby regions, typically in low-lying damp ground. Those from Wuxing are considered superior. The root resembles Bupleurum but is softer. Tao [Hongjing] used it for treatments almost interchangeably with Bupleurum. While the "Superior Class" of the *Classic* <note>The *Shennong Bencao Jing*</note> includes "this Hu" <note>Bupleurum/Chaihu</note>, it lacks "this late one" <note>Hogfennel/Qianhu</note>; only later physicians began using it. [The *Materia Medica of*] Daming states: Those from Yue, Qu, Wu, and Mu prefectures are all of good quality. It is collected in the seventh and eighth months. The exterior is black and the interior is white. [Su] Song says: Today, it is found in Shaanxi, Liang, Han, and the regions of the Yangtze, Huai, Jing, and Xiang rivers, as well as Xiangzhou and Mengzhou. In spring, it grows sprouts of a greenish-white color, resembling *xiehao* <note>a type of wormwood or celery</note>. When they first emerge, the white shoots are three to four inches long, with a very fragrant and pleasant taste. It is also called *yunhao*. In the seventh month, it opens white flowers similar to onion flowers. In the eighth month, it bears fruit. The roots are purplish-green and succulent. The variety currently from Fuyan is very similar to Bupleurum, but Bupleurum is reddish and brittle, whereas Hogfennel is yellow and soft—this is the difference. One theory suggests that the Hogfennel used in various regions today varies. Those from the northern lands around the capital (Kaifeng) are yellowish-white, dry, and brittle, with no scent or flavor. In the Jiangdong region, there are two to four types. One resembles Angelica (Danggui) with a mottled black skin and yellow flesh, oily and moist with a strong aroma. Another is yellowish-white with a texture like Ginseng but thinner and shorter, with a slight flavor. Another type resembles Aconite (Caowutou) with a reddish, firm skin and two or three branches from a single root; if eaten, it irritates the throat. People soak and crush it with ginger juice to take for clearing the diaphragm and resolving epidemics; however, these are not true Hogfennel. Today, the finest quality comes from Wuzhong. Those produced in Shouchun all resemble Bupleurum but are larger, with a powerful fragrance and a strong, bitter taste. These are most effective for treating phlegm and "descending the Qi" <note>directing rebellious energy downwards to stop coughing or vomiting</note>. [Zhen] Quan says: Whenever using it, do not use Wild Kudzu root, as it truly resembles Hogfennel but has a coarse, sour taste. If used by mistake, it causes nausea and loss of appetite. True Hogfennel tastes sweet and slightly bitter. Shizhen says: There are several types of Hogfennel. The true one has sprouts a foot tall, colored like *xiehao* with leaves like wild chrysanthemum but thinner. When tender, they are edible. In the autumn months, it opens pale white flowers similar to those of Cnidium (Shechuangzi). The root has black skin and white flesh with a fragrant aroma. Generally, those from the northern regions are superior, which is why medical texts refer to it as "Northern Hogfennel" (Beiqianhu).</gloss>

**Root**
<gloss>Preparation: [Lei] Xiao says: To prepare, first use a knife to scrape away the dark, rough skin and the fine hairs on top. Slice it finely, soak it in sweet bamboo juice until moistened, and then roast it dry over a fire for use.</gloss>

**Flavor and Nature** <gloss>Bitter, slightly cold, and non-toxic. [Zhen] Quan says: It is sweet, acrid, and balanced. [Xu] Zhicai says: Pinellia (Banxia) serves as its messenger. It dislikes Soap Pod (Zaojia) and fears Veratrum (Lilu).</gloss>

**Main Indications** <gloss>Phlegm and fullness in the chest and diaphragm, stagnation and pressure in the heart and abdomen, "wind-type" headaches, and dispersing "all types of Qi." It breaks up abdominal masses, opens the stomach to assist digestion, and regulates the Five Viscera. It treats cholera with cramping, phlegm-induced asthma, and coughing. It stabilizes pregnancy and treats all types of childhood nutritional stagnation <term>Gan</term>. It clears the lungs, transforms phlegm, and disperses pathogenic wind. Shizhen says: Hogfennel is sweet and acrid in taste, and its nature is slightly balanced. It is the "Yin within Yang," possessing a descending quality. It is a medicine for the Lung and Large Intestine (Hand/Foot Taiyin) and the Stomach and Spleen (Hand/Foot Yangming) meridians. It is different from Bupleurum, which is pure Yang and ascends to enter the Gallbladder and Liver (Shaoyin and Jueyin) meridians. Its merit lies in "descending the Qi," thus it can treat phlegm-heat, coughing, wheezing, diaphragmatic pressure, and nausea. When the Qi descends, the "fire" and phlegm follow. Therefore, it has the achievement of "pushing out the old to bring in the new." It is an essential medicine for "Wasting Qi" <note>original: 瘵氣, *zhaiqi*, associated with consumptive diseases like tuberculosis</note>. Tao Hongjing’s statement that it shares the same merit as Bupleurum is incorrect; although the symptoms they treat may be similar, the meridians they enter and the physiological effects they produce are different. Use "wasting" as the standard of measure.</gloss>

**Additional Formulas** <gloss>Old: 1. For pediatric night crying: Grind Hogfennel and sift it. Mix with honey to make pills the size of a small bean. Take one pill daily with warm water, gradually increasing to five or six pills. From the *Formulas for Universal Relief*.</gloss>

<summary>This page details the medicinal properties of Hogfennel (Qianhu), distinguishing it from Bupleurum (Chaihu). While both treat respiratory and febrile issues, Hogfennel is specifically noted for its ability to "descend Qi" to resolve phlegm and digestive stagnation.</summary>

# Saposhnikovia Root (Fangfeng)
<gloss>Listed in the Superior Class of the *Classic* <note>Referring to the *Shen Nong’s Classic of Materia Medica*, the foundational text of Chinese herbology.</note></gloss>

**Explanation of Names:** Copper Rue <gloss>from the *Classic*</gloss>, Fennel Herb <gloss>from the *Miscellaneous Records*</gloss>, Screen <gloss>from the *Miscellaneous Records*</gloss>, Simple Root <gloss>from the *Miscellaneous Records*</gloss>, Hundred Branches <gloss>from the *Miscellaneous Records*</gloss>, White Firefly <gloss>according to Wu Pu</gloss>.
<margin>Shizhen says:</margin> *Fang* means to guard or protect. Its primary power lies in treating "wind" <note>In traditional medicine, "wind" refers to external pathogens causing symptoms like chills, tremors, or wandering pain</note>, hence the name *Fangfeng* (Guarding against Wind). The name "Screen" (Pingfeng) carries the same meaning.

**Collected Explanations**
<margin>The *Miscellaneous Records* state:</margin> Saposhnikovia grows in the river valleys of Shayuan, as well as in Handan, Langya, and Shangcai. Harvest the roots in the second and tenth months and dry them in the sun.
<margin>Wu Pu says:</margin> It sprouts in the first month. The leaves are slender, appearing in colors of green, yellow, and white. It produces yellow flowers in the fifth month and bears black fruit in the sixth month.
<margin>Hongjing says:</margin> It is found in many districts. Those from Shayuan are currently considered the best. Others come from Pengcheng and Lanling (near Langya). It is also found in Yuzhou and Baishi. Those from Zhen, Yi, and Yang counties are also usable. The best quality roots are firm, moist with resin, and have a head with nodes as tough as an "earthworm's head."
<margin>Su Gong says:</margin> Today, those from Longshan in Qizhou are the finest. Those from Zizhou, Yanzhou, and Qingzhou are also excellent. The leaves resemble those of *Artemisia* or Aconite seedlings. Shayuan is located in Tongzhou. Saposhnikovia also grows in the south, but it is light and hollow, not as good as the varieties from the eastern regions.
<margin>Tao says:</margin> To say there is no Saposhnikovia in Shayuan is an error.
<margin>Song Ze says:</margin> Today, it is found across the prefectures of Bian, the East, Huai, and Zhe. The stems and leaves are both bluish-green. The stems are pale and the leaves are sparse, resembling green mugwort but shorter and smaller. In early spring, the tender leaves are reddish. People in Jiangdong, Song, and Bo harvest them as vegetables, which are very refreshing. In the fifth month, it produces small white flowers. They cluster in the center to form a large head, similar to dill flowers. The fruit resembles coriander seeds but is larger. The root is earthy yellow, similar to the root of the hollyhock. It is harvested in the second and tenth months. In the Guanzhong region, it is harvested in the third and sixth months. However, the light and hollow varieties are not as effective as those from Qizhou. Additionally, there is "Stone Saposhnikovia" (Shi Fangfeng) from Hezhong Prefecture; its root is like a mugwort root but yellow, with green leaves and white flowers. It is harvested in the sixth month and used to treat "head-wind" <note>chronic headaches or migraines</note> and abdominal swelling.
<margin>Shizhen says:</margin> Most of what is produced in the Jiang-Huai region is Stone Saposhnikovia. It grows among mountain rocks. In the second month, the tender sprouts are harvested as a vegetable; they are pungent, sweet, and fragrant, and are called "Coral Vegetable." The roots are coarse and unsightly, but the seeds are also usable.

---

**Properties (Qi and Flavor):** Sweet, warm, and non-toxic.
<margin>The *Miscellaneous Records* state:</margin> Pungent and non-toxic. Note: The nodes at the head of the root can make a person feel delirious, while roots with forked tails can trigger old, deep-seated illnesses.
<margin>Wu Pu says:</margin> According to Shen Nong, the Yellow Emperor, Qi Bo, and Tong Jun: Sweet and non-toxic. According to Lei Gong: Salty and sweet, non-toxic.
<margin>Li Dangzhi says:</margin> Slightly cold.
<margin>Zhang Yuansu says:</margin> The flavor is pungent and sweet; the Qi (nature) is warm. Both flavor and nature are thin; it is a "floating and rising" herb, belonging to the Yang category. it is the primary medicine for the *Taiyang* channels <note>The bladder and small intestine networks</note> of both the hands and feet.
<margin>Wang Haogu says:</margin> It also acts on the *Yangming* (Stomach) and *Taiyin* (Spleen) channels. It is a medicine for the "Qi level" of the Liver channel.
<margin>Li Gao says:</margin> Saposhnikovia can restrain Astragalus (*Huangqi*), yet when Astragalus is paired with Saposhnikovia, its effectiveness becomes even greater. They "fear" each other yet "employ" each other <note>A traditional pairing where one herb moderates the side effects of another while boosting its main function</note>.
<margin>Xu Zhicai says:</margin> Paired with the white part of scallions, it can circulate throughout the whole body. Paired with Alisma and Ligusticum (*Gaoben*), it treats wind conditions. Paired with Angelica, Peony, Yangqi Stone, and Limonite, it treats "Womb Wind" in women.
<insert>
Incompatible with: Dried Ginger, Veratrum, White Ampelopsis, and Genkwa.
Neutralizes: Poisoning from Aconite (*Fuzi*).
</insert>

---

### Main Indications
<gloss>From the *Classic*:</gloss> Severe "wind" with vertigo and headache; aversion to wind and wind-related pathogens; blindness where nothing can be seen. Wind circulating through the body, and aching or numbness in the bones and joints. Long-term consumption makes the body feel light.
<gloss>From the *Miscellaneous Records*:</gloss> Pain in the ribs, "wind" in the flanks, and pains that come and go in the head and face. Contractions and spasms in the limbs, postnatal disorders, metal wounds (cuts), and internal tetanus or convulsions.
<gloss>From Da Ming:</gloss> Treats the thirty-six varieties of "wind" disorders and all types of exhaustion and weakness in men; supplements the "middle" (digestive center) and benefits the spirit. Treats red eyes from wind and stops "cold tears." Also treats paralysis and clears the pathways of the five internal organs. Useful for the "Five Taxations and Seven Injuries," wasting illness, and night sweats. Relieves irritability and heaviness in the body; can calm the spirit and steady the mind.
<gloss>Zhang Yuansu:</gloss> Treats wind pathogens in the "Upper Burner" <note>The chest and head area</note> and drains "fullness" from the Lungs. Scatters stagnant Qi in the head and eyes, and removes lingering dampness in the meridians.
<gloss>Wang Haogu:</gloss> Searches out and removes "wind" from the Liver Qi.

---

### Leaf
<gloss>Main Indications:</gloss> Excessive heat in the body with sweating.
<margin>The *Miscellaneous Records* state:</margin> There is a type of Saposhnikovia in Jiangdong with tender sprouts. It is said to "agitate wind," which contradicts the main text. Perhaps it is a different plant entirely?

---

### Flower
<gloss>Main Indications:</gloss> Spasms and stiffness in the limbs, making walking impossible. Weakness of the meridians, pain between the joints, and pain in the heart and abdomen.

---

### Seed
<gloss>Main Indications:</gloss> Even more effective at treating "wind." Should be prepared with food.

---

### Inventions (Commentary)
<margin>Zhang Yuansu says:</margin> Saposhnikovia treats wind and is generally used for the upper half of the body. To treat wind pathogens in the lower body, use the "tail" (bottom part) of the root. It is an "immortal medicine" for treating wind and removing dampness. Because wind overcomes dampness, it is highly effective.
<margin>Su Gong says:</margin> It can drain "fullness" (excess) from the Lungs. However, if taken incorrectly, it can deplete the original Qi of the "Upper Burner."
<margin>Li Gao says:</margin> Saposhnikovia treats pain throughout the entire body. It acts like a low-ranking soldier: it goes wherever it is led. Among "wind" medicines, it is highly versatile.

It is a moistening agent. If one seeks to supplement the Spleen and Stomach, they cannot be reached without this herb acting as a guide. In all cases of spinal pain or neck stiffness where the patient cannot look back—where the waist feels as if it were breaking and the neck feels as if it were being pulled—these are symptoms of the Hand and Foot Greater Yang <term>Taiyang; the outermost defensive energetic layers of the body</term> channels. In such cases, Saposhnikovia must be used. Even if these specific channel symptoms are absent, it should still be used for muteness caused by blockages in the chest and diaphragm, as it can dissipate stagnation and remove "Wind" from the upper parts of the body. If a patient’s body feels restricted and weary, this is a sign of "Wind." It is also necessary for various skin sores presenting these symptoms. The reason Qian Zhongyang <note>A famous Song dynasty pediatrician</note> doubled the dose of Saposhnikovia in his "Yellow-Draining Powder" was to purge the source of the fire from both the Upper and Middle Burners <note>The functional divisions of the torso</note>.

### Appendix of Formulas <note>2 from old records, 9 new</note>

**Spontaneous sweating that will not stop:** Remove the reed-heads from Saposhnikovia and grind into a powder. Take two *qian* <term>approx. 3.7 grams</term> per dose, boiled in a decoction of floating wheat. <note>From *Zhu’s Collection of Proven Formulas*</note> Alternatively, use Saposhnikovia stir-fried with flour and take with a decoction of pig skin.
**Night sweats during sleep:** Two *liang* <term>approx. 37 grams</term> of Saposhnikovia, one *liang* of Szechuan Lovage, and half a *liang* of Ginseng. Grind into powder. Take three *qian* with a drink before bed. <note>From *Easy and Simple Formulas*</note>
**Clearing Wind and Regulating Qi:** For elderly patients experiencing constipation and convulsions. One *liang* of Saposhnikovia and half a *liang* of Licorice. Grind into powder. Take two *qian* with plain boiled water before meals. <note>From *Convenient Formulas*</note>
**Migraines and Headaches:** Equal parts Saposhnikovia and Dahurian Angelica. Grind into powder and mix with refined honey to form pills the size of a bullet. Chew one pill per dose and wash down with clear tea. <note>From *Formulas for Universal Relief*</note>
**Tetanus (Wind-stroke from wounds):** For lockjaw and emergency symptoms. Equal parts Southern Star (*Tiannanxing*) and Saposhnikovia. Grind into powder. Take two to three spoonfuls. Boil five *sheng* of "boy's urine" <note>A traditional medium believed to clear heat and blood stasis</note> down to four *sheng*, and take in two doses to stop the symptoms. <note>From *Later Formulas of Experience*</note>
**Incomplete closing of an infant's skull:** Equal parts Saposhnikovia, Bletilla Root, and Cypress Seeds. Grind into powder, mix with breast milk, and apply to the head. Change the dressing once a day. <note>From *Treatise on the Maintenance of Life*</note>
**Uterine bleeding in women:** Known as "Single Sage Powder." Use Saposhnikovia with the reed-heads removed. Roast until red and grind into powder. Take one *qian* mixed with warm wine, then drink more medicinal wine. This medicine is highly proven. Another version adds equal parts charred Cattail Pollen. <note>From *Formulas of Experience*</note>
**Antidote for Monkshood (Aconite) poisoning:** For poisoning by *Fuzi* or *Tianxiong* <note>Varieties of processed Aconite</note>. Drink a decoction of Saposhnikovia; it is very effective. <note>From the *Section on Detoxification*</note>
**Antidote for Genkwa poisoning:** Same as above.
**Antidote for Gelsemium (Yellow Jasmine) poisoning:** Even if the person appears dead, as long as the heart is still warm, they have merely been struck by the toxin. Use Saposhnikovia alone, pounded with cold water, and pour it into the patient. <note>From *Wan’s Hall of Accumulated Celebrations*</note>
