# Appendix: Plants Resembling Wild Ginger
<gloss>Su Qi states: The taste is bitter, the nature is warm and toxic. It primarily treats internal accumulations, abdominal masses <term>Zhengjia: hard tumors or masses in the abdomen</term>, and constipation. It "pushes out the old and removes the evil," breaking up cold energy. One must not take it lightly, as it can cause a patient to suffer from severe diarrhea until they are exhausted. It grows on Mount Zhongnan and does not wither in the winter. Its sprouts resemble the **Great Spurge** <note>original: 大戟 (Daji)</note> and its roots resemble **Wild Ginger** <note>original: 細辛 (Xixin)</note>.</gloss>

# Jiyi <note>Chloranthus fortunei</note> <gloss>From the *Supplementary Records*</gloss> <gloss>Low Grade</gloss> [Synonyms] Roebuck-ear Wild Ginger <gloss>Shizhen states: The origin of the name "Jiyi" is unclear. In the second month, it sprouts. It first produces white flowers and then grows three leaves. Because the leaves are shaped like the ears of a roebuck <note>original: 獐耳 (Zhange)</note> and the roots resemble Wild Ginger, it is called **Roebuck-ear Wild Ginger**.</gloss>
<gloss>Collected Explanations</gloss> <gloss>Gong states: Jiyi grows in damp, shaded areas of mountain valleys. The herb has a single stem, with four leaves clustered at the tip. White flowers emerge from the gaps between the leaves. The roots resemble Wild Ginger but are black. It is toxic. People often mistake it for **False Wild Ginger** <note>original: 杜衡 (Duheng)</note>, but this is incorrect. The roots are harvested in the second month and dried in the sun.</gloss>

## The Root
[Scent and Taste] Bitter, neutral, and toxic. <gloss>Gong states: Upon entering the mouth, it causes a person to vomit blood.</gloss>
[Main Indications] Various malignant sores, scabies, crusting skin diseases, leaking ulcers, and various sores on cattle and horses. <gloss>From the *Tang Materia Medica*</gloss>. For head sores, "white baldness" <term>scalp fungal infections</term>, wind-induced itching, and skin scaling, one may decoct the juice to soak the area or apply it topically. <gloss>From Daming</gloss>. It kills parasites. <gloss>Shizhen</gloss>.
->People find it extremely effective when combined for treating scabies and sores.<-
<gloss>Shizhen states: People today do not recognize the Jiyi plant and often mistake it for **False Wild Ginger** or **The Ghost's Superintendent**. Because of this, they use it as a substitute for Wild Ginger. Thus, many formulas calling for False Wild Ginger actually contain Jiyi. The distinction is found in the entries for Wild Ginger and False Wild Ginger.</gloss>

> **Head Sores and Baldness** <gloss>Roebuck-ear Wild Ginger has a fragrant and spicy taste. Grind it into a powder and mix it with oil boiled from glutinous rice to apply to the scalp. From *The Complete Book for Preserving the Young*.</gloss>

# The Ghost’s Superintendent <note>original: 鬼督郵 (Guiduyou)</note> <gloss>Herb</gloss> <gloss>From the *Tang Materia Medica*</gloss> <gloss>Herb</gloss> [Synonyms] Self-shaking Herb <gloss>The *Tang Materia Medica* and Shizhen state: This herb has a single stem with leaves clustered at the end. It moves even when there is no wind, hence the name "Ghost’s Self-shaking Herb." Later generations mistakenly called it "The Ghost’s Superintendent" because it specifically governs "ghost-related" diseases <note>unseen or mental ailments</note>, much like the ancient "Superintendent" <note>original: 督郵 (Duyou)</note> officials who managed postal stations. Both **Xu Changqing** and **Arrow Herb** <note>original: 亦箭 (Yijian)</note> also treat ghost diseases and share this name, but they are different plants.</gloss>
<gloss>Collected Explanations</gloss> <gloss>Gong states: The Ghost’s Superintendent is found everywhere. It grows in clusters, but each sprout has only one stem. At the tip of the stem, leaves grow in the shape of an umbrella. The root is like **Achyranthes** <note>original: 牛膝 (Niuxi)</note> but thinner and black. People who substitute **Xu Changqing** for it are wrong. Baosheng states: The stem resembles a slender arrow shaft, about two feet tall. Leaves grow at the tip like an umbrella, with yellowish-white flowers in the center. The root grows horizontally without fine hairs. Roots are harvested in the second and eighth months. Shizhen states: The Ghost’s Superintendent is of the same category as Jiyi, and their roots and sprouts look similar. However, those with black roots are Jiyi, while those with yellowish-white roots are the Ghost’s Superintendent.</gloss>

## The Root <gloss>Preparation</gloss>
<gloss>Xiao states: After harvesting, slice it finely and boil it in water with raw Licorice for one full day (twelve double-hours), then dry it in the sun for use.</gloss>
[Scent and Taste] Pungent, bitter, neutral, and non-toxic. <gloss>Shizhen states: It is slightly toxic.</gloss>
[Main Indications] Wasting diseases <term>Ghost infusion: a chronic tubercular or parasitic illness</term>, sudden collapse from "evil influence," abdominal qi disorders, various toxic spirits, malaria, and epidemic diseases. It strengthens the lower back and feet and builds physical endurance. <gloss>From the *Tang Materia Medica*</gloss>.
<gloss>Shizhen states: According to Master Shen's formulas from the Eastern Jin, this was used to treat rising qi, coughing, and cold phlegm. The "Forty Surge Pill" uses the Ghost’s Superintendent alongside centipedes, **Genkwa** <note>original: 芫花 (Yuanhua)</note>, and **Sheep Laurel** <note>original: 踟躅 (Chizhu)</note>—all toxic medicines. Therefore, its toxicity is evident. Without toxic properties, it could not treat "ghost-wasting" or evil diseases. The *Tang Materia Medica* claims it is non-toxic, but this is likely incorrect.</gloss>

# Xu Changqing <note>Cynanchum paniculatum</note> <gloss>From the *Classic of Materia Medica*</gloss> <gloss>Low Grade</gloss> Revised <gloss>Now merged with "Stone-bottom Changqing" according to Wu's Materia Medica</gloss> [Synonyms] The Ghost’s Superintendent <gloss>From the *Classic*</gloss>, Parting Ways with the Immortal <gloss>Su Song and Shizhen state: Xu Changqing was a person's name. He often used this herb to treat patients afflicted by "evil influences," so the people named it after him. In the *Supplementary Records of Famous Physicians*, the author no longer recognized the plant. However, checking the two entries shows their effects are similar. Wu Pu’s Materia Medica says Xu Changqing is also called "Stone-bottom Changqing," proving they are the same thing; earlier scholars were simply not observant enough. Tao Hongjing said: The name "Ghost’s Superintendent" is used for many things. Today, common folk use Xu Changqing; its root is exactly like Wild Ginger, but short and flat, with a similar scent. The "Dog-spine Powder" uses the Ghost’s Superintendent for its powerful ability to benefit the lower back and legs, which confirms it is Xu Changqing.</gloss>

# Xu Changqing
<note>The Paniculate Swallow-wort, *Cynanchum paniculatum*</note>

<gloss>The *Supplementary Records* state: Xu Changqing grows in the mountain valleys of Mount Tai and Longxi. It is harvested in the third month. It also states: "Stone-dweller Changqing" <note>original: 石下長卿 (Shixia Changqing)</note> grows in the valleys, ponds, and marshes of Longxi and is harvested in the third month. Su Song states: It is found everywhere near rivers and marshes. Its leaves resemble those of a willow, growing in opposite pairs.</gloss>

**Collected Explanations**

<gloss>The plant has a luster. The roots resemble **Wild Ginger** but are slightly thicker, longer, and yellow in color with a fishy odor. Local people often use it as a substitute for "The Ghost’s Superintendent" <note>original: 鬼督郵 (Gui Duyou)</note>, but this is incorrect; the Ghost’s Superintendent has its own entry. Bao Sheng states: It grows in low, damp river valleys. The sprouts resemble small mulberry leaves and grow in opposite pairs. In the third month, the sprouts are green; in the seventh or eighth month, it bears seeds that look like those of the **Climbing Metaplexis** but are smaller. In the ninth month, the sprouts turn yellow, and in the tenth month, they wither. The roots are harvested in the eighth month and dried in the sun. Su Song states: Today, it is found throughout the regions of Zi, Qi, Huai, and Si. It is harvested in the third or fourth month and is also called "Traces of the Departed Immortal" <note>original: 別仙蹤 (Biexianzhong)</note>. Shizhen states: The Ghost's Superintendent, the *Jiyi*, and the **Duheng** <note>Asarum forbesii</note> are often confused, yet their medicinal powers and foliage differ. Xu Changqing is often confused with the Ghost’s Superintendent; while their foliage differs, their medicinal effects are similar. When Duheng is confused with Wild Ginger, both the roots and foliage are so similar that it leads to great confusion. One must examine them carefully.</gloss>

---

### The Root

<gloss>Preparation: Master Lei states: Once the raw materials are gathered, mix them with a little honey and steam them in a porcelain vessel for three full days and nights <note>original: 三伏時 (Sanfu shi)</note>, then dry them in the sun for use.</gloss>

**Nature and Flavor**
Acrid, warm, and non-toxic. <gloss>The *Supplementary Records* state: Stone-dweller Changqing is salty, balanced, and toxic. In ancient times, Master Lei and the Divine Farmer stated it was acrid. Shizhen notes: Medicines used to treat "ghostly" afflictions are often toxic; therefore, one should follow the *Supplementary Records* on this point.</gloss>

**Primary Indications**
Treats possession by ghosts and spirits, *Gu*-poisoning <note>a form of venomous magic</note>, epidemics, and evil influences. It is also used for "warm malaria." Long-term use makes the body strong, resilient, and light. <gloss>The *Divine Farmer’s Classic* says it boosts *qi* and extends life. It also states: Stone-dweller Changqing governs ghostly spirits and evil qi, kills the hundred spirits and *Gu*-poison, and treats those who are elderly and find it difficult to speak, those who wander off, or those who suffer from crying and overwhelming sorrow or mental confusion.</gloss> <gloss>The *Supplementary Records* and Shizhen state: Ge Hong in the *Baopuzi* mentions that in ancient times, the "Xu Changqing Powder" was highly effective at warding off pestilence, though people today no longer know how to use it.</gloss>

**Appendix of Formulas** <gloss>New</gloss>

> <insert>1</insert> **Urinary Blockage:** The "Trichosanthes and Xu Changqing Decoction" treats blockage of *qi* where the pathways are obstructed, resulting in urinary retention, knots, and a stifling sensation below the navel. Take half an ounce of toasted Xu Changqing, three-tenths of an ounce of thatch grass root, and one ounce each of Akebia, mallow seeds, and two ounces of talc, with a small portion of betel nut and half an ounce of pink-carnation spikes. For every five *qian* <note>approx. 15-20g</note>, decoct in water, stir in one *qian* of Glauber's salt, and drink warm twice a day. <note>From *Sage's Benevolence Formulas*</note>
> **Motion Sickness (Carriage or Boat):** For those who feel dizzy, have headaches, or wish to vomit when boarding a carriage or boat. Use equal parts of Xu Changqing, "Stone Immortal" <note>original: 石長生 (Shi Changsheng)</note>, plantain seeds, and "Plum-under-the-Carriage." Crush them and place them in a square-drawn bag. Tie it to the belt or wear it on the head to avoid this suffering. <note>From *Formulas for Emergencies*</note>

# Baiwei
<note>Black-endened Swallow-wort, *Cynanchum atratum*</note>

<gloss>Classified as "Medium Grade" in the *Divine Farmer’s Classic*. Also called Wei Grass or Spring Grass.</gloss> <gloss>The *Supplementary Records* also call it "Bone Beauty" <note>original: 骨美 (Gumei)</note>.</gloss>

**Collected Explanations**

<gloss>Shizhen states: *Bai* means white, and *wei* means small or delicate; its roots are thin and white. According to the *Erya*, the *Yu* is the Spring Grass. The sounds of *Wei* and *Yu* are similar, so "Baiwei" is likely a phonetic shift from "Yu." The *Supplementary Records* mistakenly used the name *Yu* for the **Great Spurge** <note>original: 莽草 (Mangcao)</note>.</gloss>
<gloss>The *Supplementary Records* state: Baiwei grows in the valleys of the plains. The roots are gathered on the third day of the third month and dried in the shade.</gloss>
<gloss>Tao Hongjing states: It is found everywhere along the roadsides. Su Song states: Today it is found in the prefectures of Shaanxi, as well as Shu, Chu, Run, and Huo. Both the stems and leaves are green and resemble willow leaves. It blooms with red flowers in the sixth or seventh month and bears fruit in the eighth month. Its roots are yellowish-white, resembling **Ox-knee** <note>original: 牛膝 (Niuxi)</note> but shorter and smaller. People today harvest it in the eighth month.</gloss>

---

### The Root

<gloss>Preparation: Master Lei states: Once gathered, soak it in glutinous rice water overnight. Remove the hairy fibers and finely chop it on a locust-wood chopping block. Steam it from the hour of the Monkey <note>3-5 PM</note> until the hour of the Snake <note>9-11 AM</note>, then dry it in the sun. Shizhen states: Later practitioners typically only wash it with wine before use.</gloss>

**Nature and Flavor**
Bitter, salty, balanced, and non-toxic. <gloss>The *Supplementary Records* state: Its nature is "Great Cold." It is said to be incompatible with **Astragalus**, **Rhubarb**, **Great Spurge**, **Dried Ginger**, **Dates**, **Dry Lacquer**, and **Cornelian Cherry**.</gloss>

**Primary Indications**
Treats sudden stroke, fever, fullness in the limbs, and sudden loss of consciousness or delirium. It addresses "evil qi," alternating chills and fever, aching pains, and "warm malaria" that occurs at specific times. <gloss>The *Divine Farmer’s Classic* says it treats internal injuries, urinary difficulty, and vaginal discharge. It regulates water, benefits the "Yin Qi," and boosts the essence. Long-term use is beneficial.</gloss>
<gloss>The *Supplementary Records* state it treats fright-induced evil, madness, malaria, possession by ghostly charms, "wind-warmth" with scorching heat, excessive sleepiness, heat-induced urinary dribbling, and bleeding from metal wounds.</gloss>
<gloss>Shizhen states: According to the *Sage's Benevolence Formulas*, ancient recipes often used this to treat women’s ailments because the *Materia Medica* notes its effectiveness for internal injuries and discharge. Shizhen adds: Baiwei was frequently used by the ancients, but later generations rarely understand it. Zhang Zhongjing used Baiwei alongside Cinnamon Twig in his "Bamboo Bark Pill" formula for treating postpartum restlessness, vomiting, and to harmonize the center and boost *qi*.</gloss>

<vocab>
**Xu Changqing (徐長卿):** Paniculate Swallow-wort; used for spirit-related illnesses.
**Baiwei (白微):** Black-endened Swallow-wort; used for fevers and women's health.
**Gui Duyou (鬼督郵):** The Ghost's Superintendent; a similar-looking medicinal root.
**Nature and Flavor (氣味):** The energetic qualities of a drug.
**Primary Indications (主治):** The main diseases a drug treats.
**Collected Explanations (集解):** Commentary on the plant's appearance and origin.
**Preparation (修治):** Processing methods to enhance efficacy or reduce toxicity.
**Appendix of Formulas (附方):** Specific recipes for clinical use.
**Sage's Benevolence Formulas (聖惠方):** An imperial medical encyclopedia from the Song Dynasty.
**Formulas for Emergencies (肘后方):** Ge Hong's 4th-century handbook for urgent care.
</vocab>

Both are noted for their ability to treat "evil qi" and "ghostly" possessions, with Xu Changqing also being used for urinary issues and Baiwei for postpartum recovery and fevers.</summary>

...one part [of various ingredients], bamboo sap, three parts gypsum, and seven parts licorice. Combine with jujube pulp to form large pills. For each dose, dissolve one pill in a drink. It is said that for those with internal heat, the amount of **Baiwei** <note>White Micro-root, *Cynanchum atratum*</note> should be doubled. Baiwei is cold in nature and is a medicine for the Stomach Meridian. <note>original: 陽明經 (Yangming Jing)</note> Xu Zhicai’s *Materia Medica Pairings* states that Baiwei has an aversion to **Large Jujubes**, yet this formula uses jujube pulp for the pills; this is likely because the various cold and cooling medicines might otherwise injure the Spleen and Stomach. The powdered form can cause dizziness in patients. It is recorded as a treatment for "Wind-Warmth" <note>A traditional category of febrile disease</note> after sweating has been induced, where the body remains scorching hot, spontaneous sweating persists, the body feels heavy, the patient sleeps excessively, snores while breathing, and has difficulty speaking. It is also used in the Solomon’s Seal Decoction. From Master Sun’s *Thousand Golden Formulas*. <insert>Attached Formulas</insert> <gloss>New</gloss>

> **Nasal congestion from Lung Excess** where one cannot distinguish fragrances from stenches. Use one ounce each of Baiwei, Fritillary bulb, and Coltsfoot flower, and one ounce each of Stemona root and Magnolia bud. Grind into a powder. Take one drachm <note>approximately 3.75 grams</note> per dose with rice water. From the *Formulas for Universal Relief*.
> **Urinary incontinence in women** regardless of whether it occurs before or after childbirth. One ounce each of Baiwei and Peony root. Grind into a powder. Take a "square-inch-spoon" dose with wine three times a day for seven days. From the *Thousand Golden Formulas*.

There is also a "Baiwei Powder for Sweating" mentioned in the consulting books. <gloss>Five</gloss>

**Heat Strangury and Urinary Blockage** <insert>Sudden Fainting in Women</insert> When a person who is usually healthy suddenly appears dead—the body does not move, eyes are closed, and the jaw is clenched—or if they have only a slight awareness of people but remain dizzy and take time to wake up, this is called "Blood Syncope" <note>original: 血厥 (Xuejue)</note> or "Depressive Veiling" <note>original: 鬱冒 (Yumao)</note>. This occurs when excessive sweating leads to a deficiency of blood; the Yang Qi rises alone and causes a blockage of Qi that does not circulate. The body appears dead, and the person only wakes once the Qi and Blood return to the Yang vessels. Women are particularly prone to this condition. It is appropriate to take Baiwei Decoction, using one ounce each of Baiwei and Angelica root, half an ounce of Ginseng, and one and a half drachms of Licorice. Take five drachms per dose. <insert>Bleeding from metal wounds</insert> apply powdered Baiwei to the wound. Boil in two cups of water until reduced to one cup, and take while warm. From *Materia Medica Formulas* and *Confucians' Duties to Their Parents*.

# Baiqian
<note>White Front, *Cynanchum stauntonii* or *C. glaucescens*</note>

<gloss>From the *Supplementary Records*</gloss> Middle Grade <gloss>Explanations of Names</gloss> "Stone Indigo" <note>original: 石藍 (Shilan)</note> <gloss>From the *Tang Materia Medica*</gloss> <gloss>Same as above; Shizhen states:</gloss> Hongjing said: Baiqian is produced near roads. The roots resemble **Wild Ginger** but are larger; they are white in color, not flexible, and break easily. Formulas for Qi-coughs use it frequently. <gloss>Su Gong states:</gloss> The sprouts are about a foot high, and the leaves <gloss>The meaning of the name "Cough Medicine" is not yet clear</gloss> <gloss>Collected Explanations</gloss> resemble willow or *Daphne genkwa*. The roots are an inch long, resembling a white version of Wild Ginger. It grows on the sandy banks of islands and not near roads. Common people call it "Stone Indigo" or "Cough Medicine." Nowadays, people use a climbing variety that tastes bitter; this is not the true herb. <gloss>Maozhi states:</gloss> The roots resemble Baiwei or **Cow-knee**. Harvest in the second and eighth months and dry in the shade. <gloss>Su Song states:</gloss> Compared to Cow-knee, the variety that is coarse, long, firm, straight, and easily broken is Baiqian. The variety that resembles Cow-knee but is short, small, soft, and flexible is Baiwei. Both are found near roads. Their shape and color are quite similar; use these characteristics to distinguish them so as not to make a mistake.

**Nature and Flavor** Sweet, slightly warm, non-toxic. <gloss>Quan states:</gloss> Pungent, cold. <gloss>Lei says:</gloss> Slightly cold.

**Main Indications** Reversing Qi in the chest and ribs, coughing with ascending Qi, and breathing so labored that life seems near its end. <gloss>The *Supplementary Records* state:</gloss> It governs all types of Qi, as well as irritability in the Lungs, "running piglet" Qi <note>A sensation of gas rushing up from the abdomen to the throat</note>, and it greatly descends Qi and eliminates phlegm. <gloss>Shizhen states:</gloss> Zongshi said: Baiqian can stabilize Lung Qi and is frequently used to treat coughs. It is best when supported by warm medicines. <gloss>Shizhen states:</gloss> Baiqian is white in color and slightly pungent and sweet in flavor, making it a medicine for the Great Yin <note>Lung</note> channel. It excels at descending Qi; it is suitable for those with congested Lung Qi and phlegm. If the Qi is deficient and the person is gaunt, it should not be used. Zhang Zhongjing used it in formulas for coughs. <insert>Attached Formulas</insert> <gloss>Two old, one new</gloss>

> **Chronic cough with spitting of blood** Three ounces each of Baiqian, Platycodon root, and Mulberry bark, and one ounce of stir-fried Licorice. Boil in six pints of water until one pint remains. Divide into three doses. Avoid pork and cabbage. From *Secret Essentials from the Outside World*.
> **Chronic cough with ascending Qi** with body swelling and fullness, where the patient leans against a wall day and night and cannot lie down, and the throat constantly makes a "water-chicken" sound <note>A rattling or croaking sound caused by phlegm/asthma</note>. Baiqian Decoction governs this: two ounces of Baiqian, three ounces each of Purple Aster and Pinellia, and seven-tenths of a pint of *Euphorbia kansui*. Soak in one gallon of water overnight, then boil down to three pints. Divide into several doses. Forbidden foods: mutton and maltose. Very effective. From *Master Shen’s Formulas*.
> **Chronic asthma and panting** with coughing and sounds in the throat that prevent sleep. Take Baiqian, roast it, and pound it into a powder. Take two drachms with warm wine. From *Master Shen’s Formulas*.
It is also used in the "Lung-Moistening Decoction" <note>original: 肺澤湯 (Feize Tang)</note>; that formula can be found in the *Essential Prescriptions from the Golden Cabinet*, though many medicines are not listed here.

# Caoxi
<note>Grass Rhino, *Cynanchum anthonyanum*</note>

<gloss>From *Supplement to Materia Medica*</gloss> <gloss>Explanation of Names</gloss> Shizhen states: its detoxifying power <gloss>Collected Explanations</gloss> Zangqi states: Caoxi grows in the areas of Qu, Wu, Hong, and Rao. The sprouts are three feet high. It grows solitarily, and the roots resemble Wild Ginger. Those growing on the water's surface are called "Water <gloss>Supplement</gloss> <gloss>Explanation of Names</gloss> is like that of a rhino horn. Thus it is called Grass Rhino. <gloss>Collected Explanations</gloss> Rhino." Li Xun states: The *Records of Guangzhou* say: it grows in the Lingnan region and in the sea. It has a single stalk with leaves growing in opposite pairs, looking like a lampstand. The roots are like Wild Ginger.

**Root** **Nature and Flavor** Pungent, balanced, non-toxic. <gloss>Li Xun</gloss>

**Main Indications** All types of poison, such as wounds from tigers, wolves, or insects, mountain stream toxins, Wild Kudzu <note>A poisonous plant</note>, "Gu" poison <note>A legendary sorcerous poison</note>, and stings. Even if one is near death, they can be saved by burning and consuming it. Also for seasonal epidemics, malaria, chills and fever, chronic cough, phlegm congestion, "Flying Corpse" <note>original: 飛尸 (Feishi); a sudden, severe illness or stroke-like event attributed to ghosts</note>, throat blockage, sores and swelling, pediatric chills and fever, erysipelas, and "Evil Stroke" <note>Sudden loss of consciousness</note>. Boil the juice and consume it. Those poisoned in the Lingnan or Muwu regions are cured by this herb or "Ten-Gold Vine."

# Forked-Twig Root
<gloss>Corrected name: Haisha; incorporated from the Supplement</gloss>

<margin>Names</margin> **Golden Hairpin Root** <gloss>Shizhen says: The *Shihu* <note>Dendrobium orchid</note> is called "Golden Hairpin," and since this herb's shape resembles it, it is given the same name.</gloss>

<margin>Explanations</margin> <gloss>Cangqi says: Golden Hairpin Root grows in the valleys of Lingnan <note>The region covering modern Guangdong and Guangxi</note> and the Southern Seas. The roots look like *Xixin* <note>Wild Ginger</note>. Each stem has thirty to forty roots. Shizhen says: According to the *Records of the Southern Borderlands*, Gu-poison <note>A legendary medicinal poison associated with southern sorcery</note> is prevalent in the Guangzhou region. The locals use the herb Golden Hairpin Root to treat it, saving eight or nine out of ten. Its appearance is like the *Shihu* orchid. It is also called "Vine for Waking from Poison" and also "Golden Hairpin Root," which shares the name with the plant mentioned here.</gloss>

## Root
<margin>Properties</margin> Bitter, balanced, and non-toxic.

<margin>Indications</margin> A divinely effective antidote for various poisons and all types of abscesses and swellings. Decoct in water and consume. For those suffering from itchy obstructions <note>Likely a type of skin reaction or toxic swelling</note> or drug toxicity, decoct the juice and drink. When the raw root is ground, its power is even more intense; it will inevitably cause heavy vomiting and purging. If no poison is present, it will still induce vomiting to clear heat-phlegm, malaria, miasma, epidemic diseases, Gu-poison, and throat obstruction. <margin>Cangqi</margin>

<column-break/>

# Auspicious Grass
<margin>Compendium Explanations</margin> <gloss>Shizhen says: According to Ji Han’s *Flora of the Southern Regions*, this grass grows in the Jiaozhou and Guangzhou regions. It is shaped like Golden Hairpin Root and is similar to the *Shihu* orchid, while its roots resemble the Peony. During the Huangwu era <note>222–229 CE</note> of the Eastern Wu dynasty, Lord Li of Hepu and his servant Jiang Zhen encountered poison. The servant found a plant like small chestnuts, roasted them, and ate them to detoxify; its power was second only to Auspicious Grass. It was first named "Liang" <note>original: 梁 (Liang Dynasty)</note> after a monk from the Liang dynasty, but the name eventually transformed into "Liang" <note>original: 良 (Good/Auspicious)</note>.</gloss> <gloss>Additionally, Gaoliang County produces a "Hard-to-find" grass <note>original: 良難草 (Liangnan cao)</note> that resembles Perilla with yellow flowers and white roots like ox-tails; it bears seeds in late autumn.</gloss>

## Root
<margin>Properties</margin> Bitter, balanced, and non-toxic.

<margin>Indications</margin> Extremely effective for treating Gu-poison. <margin>Shizhen</margin>

<column-break/>

# Hundred Taels of Gold
<margin>Classic Explanations</margin> <gloss>The *Illustrated Records* say: Hundred Taels of Gold grows in Rongzhou and the Yunan military district. The seedlings grow two to three feet high with a woody stem. The leaves look like Lychee leaves; when they first grow, both the front and back are green. After the flowers and fruit appear, the back turns purple while the front remains green. They do not wither in winter. In early autumn, the previous year's flowers remain. Collect the roots in the fifth month; they grow to about one inch in length. Dry in the sun before use.</gloss> <gloss>Su Song says: It blooms with greenish-blue flowers. The fruit is as large as a pea, green when raw and red when ripe. Harvest the root for medicine and remove the core. Those produced in Hezong Prefecture have roots like small turnips, also red in color. The stem is thin and green. In the fourth month, it blooms with tiny yellow flowers that look like stars.</gloss>

## Root
<margin>Properties</margin> Bitter, balanced, and non-toxic.

<margin>Indications</margin> For stagnant heat and swollen, painful throats. Take one inch of the root and swallow the juices. It also treats "wind-saliva" <note>respiratory congestion or phlegm associated with "wind" illnesses</note>. <margin>Su Song</margin>

<column-break/>

# Cinnabar Root
<margin>Compendium Explanations</margin> <gloss>Shizhen says: Cinnabar Root grows in deep mountains. Today, only the people of Mount Taihe <note>Wudang Mountain</note> harvest it. The seedlings are about a foot high. The leaves look like those of the *Jiji* plant <note>Chloranthus fortunei</note>; they are green on top and red underneath. In the summer months, it grows pale red stems as thick as chopsticks, which are also red. This plant is very similar to the Hundred Taels of Gold.</gloss>

## Root
<margin>Properties</margin> Bitter, cool, and non-toxic.

<margin>Indications</margin> For swollen and painful throats. Grind with water or vinegar and swallow the liquid; the effect is excellent. <margin>Shizhen</margin>

## Snake-Repelling Thunder <gloss>From the *Tang Materia Medica*</gloss>
<gloss>Shizhen says: This substance repels snakes, hence its name.</gloss>
**Collected Explanations** <gloss>Gong says: Snake-Repelling Thunder <note>Original: *Bihuilei*</note> appears as coarse, chunky pieces. Within the *Evodia* fruit <note>A common medicinal berry</note>, there are "eyes." Shizhen says: It is currently found in the Emei and Guming mountains of Sichuan. The root resembles *Cangzhu* <note>Atractylodes rhizome, used for digestive health</note>; the large ones are the size of a fist. Locals provide it as a regional tribute. The appearance of the seedlings still needs to be investigated.</gloss>
**Root**
**Properties** Bitter, greatly cold, and non-toxic.
**Primary Healing** Repels a hundred toxins, dissolves scrofula <note>Swelling of the lymph nodes, often in the neck</note>, dispels intense heat and headaches, and wards off epidemic diseases <gloss>Tang Dynasty records</gloss>. It treats sore throats, numbness, and neutralizes the venom of snakes and vipers <gloss>Shizhen</gloss>.

<column-break/>

## Brocade-Ground Net <gloss>From the *Compendium*</gloss>
<gloss>Shizhen says: Brocade-Ground Net <note>Original: *Jindiluo*; likely a species of Sundew or similar ground cover</note> comes from the mountain cliffs of Qingyuan in Guangxi. It is also found in Zhen'an, Guishun, and Liuzhou. The root resembles mushrooms or the *Jiegeng* <note>Platycodon/Balloon flower</note> root. The local people value it highly and provide it as a regional specialty.</gloss>
**Root**
**Properties** Slightly bitter, balanced, and non-toxic.
**Primary Healing** Toxins from miasmic mists <note>Harmful vapors or "swamp gas" thought to cause illness in tropical regions</note>, scrofulous toxins, and various carbuncles or boils. Grind the root and take 1.7 mace <note>Approximately 6 grams</note> with raw wine to immediately resolve the toxin <gloss>Shizhen</gloss>.

<column-break/>

## Purple Golden Bull <gloss>From the *Song Illustrations*</gloss>
**Collected Explanations** <gloss>Song says: Grows in Fuzhou. The leaves are like tea leaves, green on top and purple beneath. It bears round red fruit that look like pearls. Another name is "Dwarf Tea." Shizhen says: It grows in the fields of Wenzhou. The leaves resemble those of the Sheep’s Hoof root <note>A type of dock or sorrel</note>.</gloss>
**Properties** [Missing]
**Primary Healing** Ground into a powder and used as a wash for scrofula; it revives the *Qi* <note>The body's vital energy</note> <gloss>Xiang</gloss>.

<column-break/>

## Fist Ginseng <gloss>From the *Song Illustrations*</gloss>
**Collected Explanations** <gloss>Song says: Grows in Jingzhou. Harvest the root in the third month and dry in the shade. Shizhen says: Today it is commonly called *Xuchu* or "Ironwire Grass," but these are simply shared names for different plants.</gloss>
**Properties** Slightly bitter, balanced, and non-toxic.
**Primary Healing** Treats "Wind" disorders <note>In Chinese medicine, "Wind" causes sudden ailments like tremors, rashes, or strokes</note> and is effective at dissolving swellings and toxins.
**Additional Formulas** <gloss>New</gloss> For various "Wind" conditions in men and women <gloss>Especially miraculous for postpartum Wind; use five mace of Ironwire Grass root.</gloss>

<column-break/>

<gloss>Take one tael <note>approx. 37g</note> of Acanthopanax bark, two mace of *Fangfeng* <note>Siler root</note>, and grind into a powder. Take a black-boned chicken weighing one catty <note>approx. 600g</note>, drown it in water, remove feathers and entrails, and chop the meat. Mix the medicine into the meat, add a little sesame oil, and fry until yellow. Depending on the person's capacity, add wine and boil until cooked. First, bathe the head and body in a decoction of Bittersweet Nightshade. Then drink the wine and eat the chicken. Once a sticky sweat breaks out, the patient is healed. If one does not bathe, a "Wind-rash" <note>Hives or red spots</note> must break out for the cure to be complete. From Hua Boran's *Essentials of the Tranquil Heart*.</gloss>

## Ironwire Grass <gloss>From the *Song Illustrations*</gloss>

<column-break/>

<margin>Shizhen added three formulas</margin>
<margin>For uterine bleeding in women: <gloss>Take equal parts Goldensilk Grass, Sea Cypress branch, Cardamom, Sichuan pepper, silkworm-molt paper, and old silk brocade. Grind to powder and take with wine on an empty stomach. Passed down by Chen Guangji; from the formulas of the Old Man of the Fields.</gloss></margin>
<margin>For carbuncles, ulcers, and boils: <gloss>For all malignant sores, use equal parts Goldensilk Grass, Honeysuckle vine, Five-leaf vine, and Tartary buckwheat. Decoct into a soup and wash while warm. Alternatively, for "scattered miscellaneous sores," use two taels of Goldensilk Grass mixed with vinegar, sun-dried, and powdered. Mix with cool water and apply to the sore; fragrant oil may also be used, or add a small amount of dragon bone <note>fossilized bone</note>.</gloss></margin>
<margin>For scrofula and lower swellings: <gloss>For those that appear dark during the month, add vinegar. Use equal parts Fritillaria <note>Bulb removed</note>, Angelica root, *Luosu* (which is Goldensilk Grass), Honeysuckle vine, Five-leaf vine, Purple Kudzu, and Tartary buckwheat. Chop finely and decoct heavily in high-quality vinegar. First smoke the area with the steam, then wash. From the *Formulas for Emergencies*.</gloss></margin>

## Goldensilk Grass <gloss>From the *Compendium*</gloss>
**Collected Explanations** <gloss>Shizhen says: Goldensilk Grass <note>Original: *Jinsicǎo*</note> comes from the valleys of Qingyang. The appearance of its seedlings should be investigated further.</gloss>
**Properties** Bitter, cold, and non-toxic.
**Primary Healing** Immediately effective for vomiting blood and nosebleeds. Treats bloody stools, uterine bleeding, and carbuncle toxins. It neutralizes various drug poisons, treats malignant sores and boils, cools the blood, and disperses heat.

->## Herbs: Part 3 <gloss>Fragrant Species, 56 types</gloss><-

# Chinese Angelica <note>original: "當歸", Danggui</note>
<gloss>Middle grade in the *Classic of Materia Medica* <note>original: "Benjing"</note>. Also called Dry Return <note>from the *Classic of Materia Medica*</gloss>; Mountain Thistle <note>from the *Erya*</note>; White Qi <note>from the *Erya*</note>; and Without Refinement <note>from the *Compendium*</note>. Master Song said: According to the *Erya* dictionary, one name is Mountain Thistle, and another is White Qi. The character 'Qi' is the ancient word for celery. The scholar Guo Pu noted that this is Danggui, which resembles celery but is thicker and larger. Xu Shen’s *Dictionary of Phrases* <note>original: "Shuowen Jiezi"</note> says those growing in mountains are called *Xiang*, or Mountain Celery. Thus, Danggui is a type of celery; those on level ground are common celery, while the thick, large ones in the mountains are Danggui.</gloss>

Zongshi said: Nowadays in the Sichuan region, the "female" variety is considered best; it is oily and rich. Quality is judged by these traits rather than whether it grows in the mountains or on level ground.

Shizhen said: Danggui is not actually a type of celery, but because its flowers and leaves resemble celery, it earned that name. In ancient times, when a man took a wife, it was for the sake of continuing the lineage. Since Danggui regulates the blood and is the essential medicine for women, it carries the sentiment of "missing one's husband" <note>the name "Danggui" literally means "should return"</note>. This is the same intent found in the Tang poem: "The sesame is ready to plant but no one plants it; it is precisely the time for the husband’s return." The *Notes on Ancient and Modern Things* by Cui Bao says: Ancient people gave peonies <note>original: "Shaoyao"</note> when parting, and used "Without Refinement" <note>original: "Wenwu," a name for Danggui</note> to call someone back. This is because "Without Refinement" is Danggui, and the peony is also called "About to Leave."

Cheng said: Danggui treats postpartum distress in women. <gloss>Collected Explanations</gloss> The *Supplementary Records* <note>original: "Bielu"</note> says: Danggui grows in the river valleys of Longxi. It should be gathered in the second and eighth months. When blood rushes upward, it brings immediate relief. For those with confused vital energy and blood <note>Qi and Blood</note>, taking it settles them immediately, as it enables the Qi and blood to "return" to their proper places. I suspect the name Danggui <note>"Should Return"</note> must come from this effect. <gloss>Collected Explanations</gloss> The roots should be dried in the shade.

Hongjing said: Today, the Danggui from the "Four Sunny Slopes of Black Water" in Longxi is meaty with few branches and a fragrant aroma; it is called "Horse-tail Danggui." The Danggui from northern Sichuan has many thin root-branches. Those grown in sunny spots are white with a thin flavor and are not called "Palm Danggui," but are used when others are scarce.

Gong said: It now comes from Dangzhou, Dangzhou, Jizhou, and Songzhou, with the variety from Dangzhou being superior. There are two types: one with large leaves like Lovage <note>original: "Xiongguang"</note> called "Horse-tail Danggui"; another with fine leaves like Lovage, which people today mostly use, called "Silkworm-head Danggui." Tao claimed the variety from Liyang is unusable; its stems and leaves resemble celery and are inferior to Lovage.

Song said: It is now found in various districts of Sichuan, Shaanxi, Jiangning, and Chuzhou, with the Sichuan variety being the best. The sprouts emerge in spring, with green leaves having three lobes. It flowers in the seventh or eighth month, resembling dill but light purple. The root is blackish-yellow. The thick, meaty ones that are not dried out are superior.

Shizhen said: Nowadays, people in Shaanxi, Sichuan, Qinzhou, and Wenzhou cultivate it for trade. The "Qin Angelica" <note>from Qinzhou</note> has a round head and many tails, is purple-colored, fragrant, and oily; it is called Horse-tail Angelica and is superior to other regions. Those with large heads and thick tails that are white and dry are called Silkworm-head Angelica; these are only suitable for medicines that disperse pathogens. The *Erya* notes say the Sichuan variety has a strong power and is good for "attacking" <note>purging/moving</note>, while the Qin variety has a gentle power and is good for "supplementing" <note>tonifying</note>. This is correct.

### The Root <gloss>Processing and Preparation</gloss>
Zhen Quan said: For all use, remove the "reed head" <note>the top crown</note> and soak it in wine overnight before adding to medicine. Its effects for stopping blood versus breaking up blood <note>resolving stasis</note> differ depending on whether you use the head or the tail. To break up blood stasis, use the hard, firm first section of the head. To stop pain or stop bleeding, use the tail. If you use the whole root together, it may be ineffective; it is best to use it skillfully.

Yuansu said: The head stops bleeding, the tail breaks up blood stasis, and the body harmonizes the blood. Using the whole root means one part stops and one part moves. First, wash away the soil with water. To treat the upper body, soak in wine. To treat the exterior, wash with wine. Then dry it by fire or sun for use.

Gao said: The head stops bleeding and moves upward; the body nourishes blood and stays in the center; the fine tips break up blood and flow downward; the whole root enlivens the blood without letting it dissipate.

Shizhen said: Masters Lei Xiao and Zhang Yuansu spoke of different effects for the head and tail. For any plant root, the pulse of vital energy <note>Qi</note> in the upper half moves upward, following the Law of Heaven; the pulse in the lower half moves downward, following the Law of Earth. Since the human body mirrors Heaven and Earth, one should use the head to treat the upper body, the body to treat the middle, and the tail to treat the lower body. Using the whole root for a general treatment is a fixed principle of nature. Master Zhang’s explanation is the most excellent. When sun-dried, seal it in paper while still warm and store it to prevent insect damage.

### <gloss>Flavor and Nature</gloss>
Bitter, warm, non-toxic. <gloss>The *Supplementary Records* says: Pungent, greatly warm. Master Pu says: According to Shennong, the Yellow Emperor, Tong Jun, and Bian Que, it is sweet and non-toxic. Qi Bo and Lei Gong say: Pungent, non-toxic. Li Dangzhi says: Slightly warm. Hongjing says: Sweet, pungent, warm, non-toxic. Zhang Yuansu says: The flavor is thin and the Qi <note>aroma/energy</note> is thick; it can ascend or descend. It is the "Minor Yin" within the "Yang." It enters the blood portions of the Heart, Spleen, and Liver channels. Zhicai says: It dislikes *Luru* <note>Sheep's Ear</note> and *Shuyu* <note>Water Plantain</note>. It fears Calamus, Seaweed, and *Mumeng*. House-grown ginger can be used to process realgar.</gloss>

### Primary Indications
<gloss>For coughing and reversal of Qi, "warm malaria" with alternating chills and fever, and the sensation of "washing" <note>creeping cold/numbness</note> within the skin. For women with uterine bleeding or infertility, and for various malignant sores, ulcers, and metal wounds: boil into a juice and drink.</gloss> <note>from the *Classic of Materia Medica*</note> <gloss>Warms the center and stops pain; removes stagnant blood blocked internally; treats stroke and convulsions.</gloss>

<summary>This page details the origins, etymology, and preparation of Danggui (Chinese Angelica), emphasizing its vital role as a "blood medicine" for women and explaining how different parts of the root (head, body, tail) target different areas of the human body.</summary>
<keywords>Danggui, Chinese Angelica, blood tonic, women's health, plant anatomy in medicine, Longxi, Sichuan herbs, Li Shizhen</keywords>

It treats the absence of sweating, damp numbness, strokes caused by "evil winds" <note>original: "中惡", refers to sudden illness attributed to external pathogens or spirits</note>, and "guest qi" <note>pathogenic factors entering from outside</note>. It addresses deficiency-cold, tonifies the five internal organs, and helps build muscle. <gloss>From the *Additional Records* <note>original: "Bielu"</note></gloss> It stops vomiting and reflux, treats "taxation" <note>chronic fatigue or consumption</note>, chills and fever, diarrhea, abdominal pain, and toothaches. For women, it treats blood loss and waist pain, and tonifies various deficiencies. <gloss>From Zhenquan</gloss> It treats all forms of "wind" and "qi" disorders. <gloss>From *Daming*</gloss>

It tonifies all forms of exhaustion, breaks up "evil" <note>clotted or stagnant</note> blood, and nourishes new blood. It treats abdominal masses <note>original: "癥癖", likely tumors or cysts</note> and coldness in the intestines and stomach. <gloss>From *Daming*</gloss> It treats headaches and various pains in the heart and abdomen. It moistens the intestines, stomach, tendons, bones, and skin. It treats carbuncles and sores, expels pus, stops pain, and harmonizes and tonifies the blood. <gloss>Shizhen</gloss> It primarily treats abdominal masses, excessive sleepiness, and heat and pain in the soles of the feet. <gloss>Shizhen</gloss>

Because the Thoroughfare Vessel <note>original: "Chong Mai"</note> is the "Sea of Blood," and this herb treats urgency in the lower abdomen, as well as diseases of the Girdle Vessel <note>original: "Dai Mai"</note> where the abdomen is painful and the waist feels heavy, as if sitting in water. <gloss>Haogu</gloss>

## Theoretical Development <note>original: "Faming"</note>

<gloss>Zhenquan stated: For patients suffering from deficiency-cold, increase the dosage. Cheng stated: Common folk often believe this herb only treats blood. However, the formulas in the *Golden Chamber*, *Outer Platform*, and *Thousand Gold Pieces* all use it to tonify various deficiencies in people, and it is a medicine that produces immediate results. Ancient formulas used it to treat women’s postpartum "evil blood" rushing upward; nothing is more urgent or effective than this. For any case where the "qi" and blood are chaotic, taking this will stabilize them. It is an essential postpartum medicine. Zongshi stated: The *Treatise on Medicinal Properties* says it tonifies all "deficiencies" in women; this single statement sums up the use of Danggui. Cheng Wuji stated: The pulse is the "mansion of blood," and all blood belongs to the Heart. To open the pulse, one must first tonify the Heart and benefit the blood. Therefore, when Zhang Zhongjing treated cold limbs and a pulse so faint it was nearly gone, he used the bitter-warm property of Danggui to assist the Heart blood. Yuansu stated: It has three main uses: first, as a primary medicine for the Heart meridian; second, to harmonize the blood; third, to treat various diseases that worsen at night. Whenever the blood is diseased, this must be used. When blood is congested and does not flow, it causes pain; the sweet-warm nature of Danggui harmonizes blood, while its acrid-warm nature disperses internal cold. Its bitter-warm nature helps the Heart disperse cold, allowing the "qi" and blood to each "return" to their proper place. Haogu stated: It enters the Hand Lesser Yin <note>Heart</note> because the Heart generates blood; it enters the Foot Greater Yin <note>Spleen</note> because the Spleen contains the blood; and it enters the Foot Absolute Yin <note>Liver</note> because the Liver stores the blood. The head of the root can break up stagnant blood, the body can nourish blood, and the tail can move blood. If the whole root is used with Ginseng and Astragalus, it tonifies qi and generates blood. If used with Morning Glory seeds and Rhubarb, it moves qi and breaks up blood. If followed by Cinnamon, Aconite, or Notopterygium, it follows heat; if followed by Rhubarb or Mirabilite, it follows cold. The practitioner must know these distinctions. When steamed in wine, it treats headaches—all pains are related to "fire," so a blood-nourishing medicine is used as the primary agent. Ji stated: To treat headaches, boil it in wine and drink the clear liquid; this takes advantage of its ability to float upward. To treat heart pain, mix the powder with wine and drink; this takes advantage of its "turbid" nature to remain suspended between sinking and floating. To treat blood in the urine, decoct it in wine; this takes advantage of its ability to sink to the lowest point. The distinctions of height are as such. Wang Haizang asked: Danggui is a blood medicine, so how can it treat coughing and upward-rushing qi in the chest? I note that Danggui’s flavor is acrid and dispersing; it is a "qi medicine within the blood." Furthermore, for coughing and upward-rushing qi caused by Yin deficiency where Yang has nothing to attach to, using a blood medicine to tonify Yin harmonizes the blood and causes the qi to descend. Han Mao stated: Danggui governs diseases of the "blood portion." That produced in Sichuan is strong and can attack; that produced in Shaanxi <note>original: "Qin"</note> is gentle and suitable for tonifying. For its primary use, it should be prepared with wine. If there is phlegm, prepare it with ginger to guide the blood back to its source. For blood deficiency, use Ginseng and Halloysite as assistants. For blood heat, use Raw Rehmannia and Scutellaria as assistants. It is the source of life and transformation; for blood accumulation, pair it with Rhubarb. As an essential blood medicine, one cannot omit Danggui. Thus, the ancient "Four-Substance Decoction" <note>Siwu Tang</note> uses it as the "sovereign" <note>primary</note> herb, with Rehmannia as the "minister" <note>assistant</note> and Chuanxiong as the "envoy" <note>guide</note>.</gloss>

## Attached Formulas <gloss>8 old, 19 new</gloss>

**Fever from Deficiency** <gloss>Danggui Blood-Tonifying Decoction. Treats skin heat, dry heat, exhaustion, thirst, red eyes, and a flushed face that persists day and night. The pulse is flooding and large but empty; if pressed hard, it has no strength. This is a sign of blood deficiency. It may result from hunger, exhaustion, or overwork. The symptoms resemble those of a "White Tiger Decoction" case, but the pulse is not long or solid. If one mistakenly takes White Tiger Decoction, they will die. This formula governs it. Use 2 mace <note>approx. 7.5g</note> of Danggui body (washed in wine) and 1 ounce <note>approx. 37g</note> of Astragalus (honey-roasted). Make one dose with 2 cups of water, boil down to 1 cup. Drink warm on an empty stomach twice a day. From *Dongyuan’s Secrets from the Orchid Chamber*.</gloss>

**Dizziness from Blood Loss** <gloss>For any case of blood loss from miscarriage, postpartum, tooth extraction, or any excessive bleeding leading to irritability, dizziness, fainting, or unconsciousness. Danggui 1 ounce, Chuanxiong 1 ounce. For each use, take 5 mace with 7 parts water and 3 parts wine. Boil to 7 parts and drink hot. From *Fine Formulas for Women*.</gloss>

**Unceasing Bleeding** <gloss>Roasted Danggui ground into powder. Take 1 mace per dose mixed with rice water. From *Holy Benevolence Record*.</gloss>

**Blood in Urine** <gloss>Chop 4 ounces of Danggui. Boil in 3 pints of wine until 1 pint remains. Drink all at once. From *Emergency Formulas Kept up the Sleeve*.</gloss>

**Skin Tumors and Scrofula** <gloss>Prepare 2 ounces of Danggui. Boil in 1 pint of wine until 0.6 pints remain. Drink twice a day. From *Secret Essentials from the Outer Platform*.</gloss>

**Dim Vision from Cold and Deficiency** <gloss>To nourish qi and blood. Use 6 ounces of sun-dried Danggui and 2 ounces of fire-prepared Aconite. Grind into powder and mix with refined honey to make pills the size of a parasol tree seed. Take 30 pills per dose with warm wine. Named "Six-One Pill." From *Comprehensive Record of Holy Benevolence*.</gloss>

**Pain Below the Heart** <gloss>Grind Danggui into powder. Take one square-inch spoonful with wine. From *Proven Formulas*.</gloss>

**Cold Pain in Arms and Hands** <gloss>Cut 3 ounces of Danggui. Soak in wine for three days. Drink warm. When finished, warm more wine and soak another 3 ounces until cured. From *Broad Records of the Forest of Matters*.</gloss>

**Persistent Warm Malaria** <gloss>Decoct 1 ounce of Danggui in water. Drink once a day. From *Comprehensive Record of Holy Benevolence*.</gloss>

**Unceasing Severe Dysentery** <gloss>Fry 2 ounces of Danggui and 1 ounce of Evodia until fragrant. Discard the Evodia. Grind the Danggui into powder and mix with honey to make pills the size of a parasol tree seed. Take 30 pills per dose with rice water. Named "Victorious Gold Pill." From *Universal Relief Formulas*.</gloss>

### Difficulty with Urination or Bowels
<gloss>Mix equal parts of Chinese Angelica and Dahurian Angelica <note>original: "Baizhi"</note> into a powder. Take two "qian" <note>approximately 8 grams</note> per dose with rice water. From the *Comprehensive Record of Divine Assistance*.</gloss>

### The Hundred Ailments of Women
<gloss>For those suffering from various forms of deficiency and exhaustion: combine four ounces of Chinese Angelica and two ounces of Rehmannia root <note>original: "Dihuang"</note>. Grind into a powder and mix with honey to form pills the size of parasol tree seeds. Take fifteen pills with rice water before meals. From *Nineteen Formulae*.</gloss>

### Retrograde Menstruation
<gloss>If blood exits through the mouth or nose: first, grind a high-quality ink stick <note>original: "Jingmo", traditional pine-soot ink used medicinally to stop bleeding</note> into juice and drink it to stop the flow. Formula from the Great Physician Zhi Facun.</gloss>

### Blocked Menstruation
<gloss>Follow the previous treatment by using three "qian" each of Chinese Angelica "tails" <note>the fine tips of the root, believed to be more effective at breaking blood stasis</note> and Safflower. Boil in one cup of water until reduced to eighty percent, and drink warm. The menses will then flow. From *Simple Formulas*.</gloss>

### Amenorrhea in Adolescent Girls
<gloss>Use one "qian" of powdered Chinese Angelica tail. Steep Safflower in wine, boil it, and add a few drops of white wine. Drink this once a day. From *Formulas for Universal Relief*.</gloss>

### Blood and Qi Disorders in Women
<gloss>For abdominal distension below the navel, irregular menstruation, or "blood-qi" attacking upwards causing nausea and insomnia: take four "qian" of Chinese Angelica and two "qian" of dried lacquer <note>carbonized/charred to retain its properties</note>. Grind into powder and mix with refined honey to form pills the size of parasol tree seeds. Take fifteen pills with warm wine. From *Formulas of Eternal Class*.</gloss>

### Bleeding During Miscarriage
<gloss>If bleeding does not stop: roast one ounce of Chinese Angelica and take a handful of scallion whites. Take five "qian" per dose. From *Excellent Formulas for Women*.</gloss>
<gloss>Administer the dose; in the time it takes a person to walk five "li" <note>about 2.5 kilometers</note>, give another. It is usually effective within three to five doses. From Zhang Wenzhong’s *Formulas for Emergencies*.</gloss>

# Szechuan Lovage
<gloss>Pronounced: *Xiong-Qiong*</gloss>

## Names
**Qiong** <gloss>From the *Additional Records*</gloss>, **Fragrant Fruit** <gloss>From the *Compendium*</gloss>, **Mountain Juqiong** <gloss>From the *Compendium*</gloss>

<margin>Shizhen says:</margin> The character *Xiong* was originally written differently; its meaning is not entirely clear. Some say it refers to the "vault of heaven" <note>original: "穹窿", qionglong</note>, which symbolizes the human head. Since this medicine travels upward specifically to treat ailments of the head and eyes, it was named *Xiongqiong*. Those from the western regions are considered best and called **Hu-Xiong** <note>Western Xiong</note>. Because the root joints resemble a horse's bit, ancient people called it **Horse-Bit Xiong**. Later generations called it **Sparrow-Brain Xiong** because of its shape. Those from the capital of Shu <note>modern Sichuan</note> are called **Jing-Xiong** or **Xi-Xiong** <note>Western Xiong</note>. Those from elsewhere in Sichuan are **Chuan-Xiong**, those from Tiantai are **Tai-Xiong**, and those from south of the Yangtze are **Fu-Xiong**. These are all named after their place of origin. In the *Zuo Zhuan* <note>a historical chronicle</note>, it is mentioned alongside wheat leaven as a remedy for dampness-related abdominal ailments. Zhu Danxi used "Yue-Tao" and "Ju-Qiong" in his "Pill for the Six Depressions," which is how it got that name. The *Golden Light Sutra* calls it **Jyamaka** <note>Sanskrit name</note>.

<margin>Collected Explanations</margin> <gloss>The *Additional Records* states: The leaves of Xiongqiong are called "Miwu." It grows in the valleys of Wugong and the western ridges of the Slanted Valley. The roots are harvested in the third and fourth months and dried in the sun. Master Pu says: It grows on Mount Huwutao or Mount Tai. The leaves are fine and uniquely fragrant. The surface is bluish-black with red veins. It grows in clusters through winter and summer. It flowers in the fifth month (red) and fruits in the seventh (black). Tao Hongjing says: The areas mentioned are near Xi'an. Today it is found in Liyang and is widely cultivated. The leaves resemble Cnidium but are more fragrant. The thickest stalks look like horse bits. It is harvested in the ninth or tenth months when the roots are heavy and full of resin; those harvested in spring are hollow and of poor quality. Su Song says: It is found throughout Sichuan and the eastern mountains.</gloss>

<meta>This page continues from the previous discussion on Chinese Angelica (Danggui), transitioning into the detailed entry for Szechuan Lovage (Xiongqiong), focusing on its botanical description, medicinal properties, and its specific role as a "holy medicine" for headaches.</meta>

->**Compendium of Materia Medica, Volume 14: Herbs**<-

Szechuan Lovage <note>original: "Xiongqiong"</note> is found in many regions, but that from the Shu region <note>modern-day Sichuan</note> is considered superior. In the fourth or fifth month, it grows leaves resembling water celery, coriander, or *Cnidium monnieri*. It grows in clusters with thin stems; its leaves are exceptionally fragrant. People in the Jiangdong and Shu regions harvest the leaves to make drinks. In the seventh or eighth month, it produces tiny white flowers like those of the *Cnidium* seed. The root is firm and thin, yellowish-black in color. Those roots that grow with a heavy, solid interior and a shape resembling a "sparrow’s brain" are known as "Sparrow Brain Lovage" <note>original: "Quenaoxiong"</note>, and these are the most potent. **Shizhen states:** In the Sichuan region, where it is less cold, people cultivate it extensively. Even in late autumn, the stems and leaves do not wither. After the Qingming Festival, the old roots sprout; one can take the branches and bury them horizontally, and roots will grow from every node. In the eighth month, the Szechuan Lovage <note>original: "Chuanxiong"</note> begins to form under the roots and can then be harvested, steamed, and dried for sale. The *Famine Relief Materia Medica* says: The leaves resemble celery but are finer and narrower with clefts. They also resemble Dahurian Angelica leaves but are finer, and like coriander leaves but slightly more robust. One variety resembles *Cnidium* leaves but is coarser. The tender leaves can be blanched and eaten. **Zongshi states:** For medicinal use, large chunks from Sichuan that are white inside, not oily, and slightly sweet when chewed are best. Other varieties are not used in medicine and are only suitable for grinding into powder to make a decoction for bathing.

---

### **The Root**
<gloss>Flavor and Nature:</gloss> **Piquant, warm, and non-toxic.** <gloss>Lu states: According to Shennong, the Yellow Emperor, Qibo, and Leigong, it is piquant and non-toxic. Bian Que says it is sour and non-toxic. Li Dangzhi says it is warm when raw and cold when cooked. Yuansu says: Its nature is warm, and its flavor is both piquant and bitter. Its Qi is thick and its flavor is thin; it is buoyant and rises, belonging to the Yang energy. It is the guiding herb for the Gallbladder Meridian <note>original: "Shaoyang"</note> and enters the Liver and Pericardium Meridians. Cai says: Dahurian Angelica <note>original: "Baizhi"</note> serves as its envoy. It fears Coptis <note>original: "Huanglian"</note> and can neutralize Realgar. When combined with Asarum <note>original: "Xixin"</note>, it heals metal wounds and stops pain. Combined with Oyster shell, it treats chronic headaches <note>original: "Toufeng"</note> and vomiting.</gloss>

### **Treatments**
Wind entering the brain causing headaches, numbness from cold, muscle spasms and stiffness, metal wounds, and women with menstrual blockages or infertility. <gloss>From the *Divine Husbandman's Classic*.</gloss> Internal cold and stagnation, "wandering wind" on the face, excessive tearing, runny nose, feeling dazed as if drunk, various cold Qi ailments, hardness and pain in the heart and abdomen, sudden abdominal distress, swelling and pain, pain in the ribs, and internal cold in the nose. <gloss>From the *Supplementary Records*.</gloss> Weakness in the legs, coughing with reflux <note>hiccups or belching</note>, paralysis of the limbs, and retained placenta. <gloss>According to Zhen Quan.</gloss> All types of "wind" and "Qi" disorders, all forms of exhaustion and chronic damage, and all blood disorders. It tonifies the "Five Exhaustions," strengthens muscles and bones, regulates the pulses, breaks up internal masses and old blood, and nourishes new blood. It treats vomiting blood, nosebleeds, blood in the urine, brain fistulas, back sores, scrofula, goiters, hemorrhoids, and itchy skin sores. It promotes tissue growth, drains pus, and clears blood stasis. <gloss>According to Daming.</gloss> It scours Liver Qi, tonifies Liver blood, moistens Liver dryness, tonifies "wind-void" <note>deficiency caused by wind pathogens</note>, dries dampness, stops diarrhea and dysentery, moves Qi, and opens up "stagnation" <note>emotional or physical blockages</note>.

During the Jin Dynasty, the "Shenhe Pill" was taken at night to treat dizziness caused by wind. <gloss>According to Hong.</gloss> **Min** states: For bleeding gums, holding a decoction in the mouth often cures it. <gloss>According to Hongjing.</gloss>

### **Elucidation**
<gloss>Zongshi states: Modern physicians use this herb most frequently; it is indispensable for "wind" ailments of the head and face. However, it must be supported by other herbs. Yuansu states: Szechuan Lovage is the "holy medicine" for headaches involving the Yin meridians and headaches due to blood deficiency. It has four primary uses: first, as a guide for the Gallbladder Meridian; second, for headaches involving any meridian; third, to assist the "clear Yang" energy to rise; and fourth, to remove dampness from the head. Gao states: Szechuan Lovage must be used for headaches. If it does not cure the ailment, add the specific "guiding herb" for the affected meridian: for the forehead <note>Taiyang</note> use *Qianghuo*; for the face <note>Yangming</note> use Dahurian Angelica; for the sides of the head <note>Shaoyang</note> use Bupleurum; for the top of the head <note>Taiyin</note> use *Cangzhu*; for the vertex <note>Jueyin</note> use Evodia. The Gallbladder Meridian accounts for half of these cases. Zhenheng states: Szechuan Lovage should be used with "Fuxiong" <note>a specific variety of Lovage</note> to lift and open the Qi. When Qi rises, stagnation naturally descends. Thus, Fuxiong resolves all types of stagnation and reaches the Triple Burner, acting as an envoy to connect Yin and Yang, Qi and Blood. Shizhen states: Szechuan Lovage is a "Qi-moving medicine within the Blood." When the Liver is "distressed by urgency," use piquant flavors to tonify it; thus, those with Blood deficiency should use it. Piquant flavors disperse; thus, those with Qi stagnation should use it. The *Zuo Zhuan* mentions using millet, yeast, chrysanthemum, and lovage to treat abdominal ailments caused by dampness. I have found that adding these two ingredients when treating damp diarrhea works like an echo <note>meaning it is instantly effective</note>. If dysentery has been cleared but pain persists, it is due to Yin deficiency and Qi stagnation; adding Szechuan Lovage as a support will move the Qi and harmonize the Blood, stopping the illness immediately. These are the subtle mysteries of medicine that can only be discussed with those of flexible mind. Zongshi states: Shen Kuo’s *Dream Pool Essays* mentions a relative who frequently took Szechuan Lovage. The physician Hao Shu saw this and warned that it should not be taken long-term as it could cause sudden death. Later, the relative indeed died suddenly despite having no prior illness. Also, the wife of official Zhang Zitong suffered from "brain wind" and took Szechuan Lovage for a long time; she too died suddenly one day. These were eyewitness accounts. These stories refer to taking the herb alone for too long, which dissipates the "True Qi." If supported by other herbs and stopped once the illness is cured, how could it lead to this? Yu Tuan states: People who sweat excessively or have weak Qi should not take it long-term. Its piquant and dispersing nature causes the True Qi to leak out, making the Yin deficiency even worse. Shizhen states: The "Five Flavors" enter the stomach and return to their respective functions. Taking any single one for too long causes an imbalance of Qi, which inevitably leads to decline and the risk of sudden death. But if a medicine is formulated with all five flavors and four natures, with "Prince, Minister, Assistant, and Envoy" herbs properly balanced, how could such harm occur? Szechuan Lovage is a Liver Meridian medicine; if taken alone for too long, then...</gloss>

# Fragrant Lovage Leaves
<gloss>original: "Miwu"</gloss>
Listed in the *Divine Husbandman's Classic* as a superior grade medicine under the name **Weiwu**. In the *Additional Records*, it is called **Mi**.
<gloss>The *Additional Records* <note>original: "Bielu"</note> states: The leaves of Szechuan Lovage are called Miwu. It is also called Jiangli. It is the sprout of the Lovage plant. It grows in the rivers and marshes of Yongzhou and Yuanju. The leaves are harvested in the fourth or fifth month and dried in the sun. Tao Hongjing says: It is now produced in Liyang; many households grow it. The leaves resemble *Cnidium* <note>original: "Shechuang"</note> and are fragrant. People use them as a perfume, but they are rarely used in medicine. Su Gong says: There are two types. One has leaves like celery, the other like *Cnidium*. Their fragrances are similar, and their uses do not differ. Shizhen states: The *Additional Records* says Miwu is another name for Jiangli, the sprout of Szechuan Lovage. Yet in Sima Xiangru's *Rhapsody of Sir Vacuous*, he lists Szechuan Lovage, Sweet Flag, Jiangli, and Miwu separately. In the *Rhapsody of the Imperial Park*, he says, "Clothed in Jiangli, perfumed with Miwu," making them seem like different things. Why? It is because when the tender sprouts have not yet formed a root, they are called Miwu. After the root forms, they are called Chuanxiong. Those with large leaves like celery are Jiangli; those with fine leaves like *Cnidium* are Miwu. With this distinction, it becomes clear. The *Huainanzi* says: "Those who confuse people are like Szechuan Lovage and Miwu, or *Cnidium* and..."</gloss>

The name *Miwu* <note>the leaf of Szechuan Lovage</note> specifically refers to the variety with thin leaves. The *Guangzhi* <note>Comprehensive Records</note> states that *Miwu* is a fragrant herb that can be stored among clothes to scent them. *Guanzi* <note>an ancient philosophical and political text</note> mentions that it grows in the most fertile of the "five types of soil." In his eulogy, Guo Pu <note>a Jin Dynasty scholar</note> praised it, saying: "The fragrant herb *Miwu* is often confused with Snake’s Bed, yet its true nature is never diminished; it splits open to reveal its own fragrance." Additionally, a type of seaweed found in the ocean called *Tafa* is also known as *Jiangli* <note>Gracilaria</note>, which happens to share a name with this plant.

<margin>Nature and Flavor: Acrid, warm, and non-toxic.</margin>

**Main Indications:** It treats coughing and "rebellious qi," calms "fright-qi" <note>agitation caused by sudden shock</note>, wards off evil and pestilence, eliminates insect toxins and "ghost-infestation" <note>a traditional term for wasting diseases or infectious conditions</note>, and expels the "three worms" <note>parasites</note>. Long-term consumption allows one to communicate with the spirit world <gloss>from the Shennong’s Classic of Materia Medica</gloss>. It treats chronic "wind" <note>pathogens causing wandering pain or neurological symptoms</note> in the chest and head, as well as dizziness <gloss>from the Miscellaneous Records</gloss>. It can be made into a drink to stop diarrhea <gloss>according to Chen Zangqi</gloss>.

# Snake’s Bed <gloss>Top Grade in the Shennong’s Classic</gloss>

<gloss>Also known as:</gloss> Snake Millet <gloss>from the Classic</gloss>, Snake Rice <gloss>from the Classic</gloss>, Viper’s Bed <gloss>from the Erya</gloss>, Horse’s Bed <gloss>from the Erya</gloss>, Broad-Matted Herb <gloss>from the Miscellaneous Records</gloss>. Also named *Siyi* <gloss>from the Compendium</gloss> and Longevity Bramble. <gloss>Li Shizhen says:</gloss> Snakes and vipers enjoy lying beneath this plant and eating its seeds, hence names like "Snake’s Bed" and "Snake Millet." Its leaves resemble those of *Miwu*, so it is also called "Wall *Miwu*." The *Erya* commentary explains that the name *Chuang* <note>bed</note> refers to the way the plant spreads out.

<gloss>Collective Notes:</gloss> <gloss>The Miscellaneous Records state:</gloss> Snake’s Bed grows in Lin-yue. Harvest the seeds in the fifth month and dry them in the shade. <gloss>Tao Hongjing says:</gloss> It is very common in fields and rural settlements. The flowers and leaves look exactly like *Miwu*. <gloss>Han Baosheng says:</gloss> The leaves resemble the small-leaved Szechuan Lovage. The flowers are white, and the seeds are like yellowish-white millet. It grows in low, damp places everywhere. Those from Yangzhou and Xiangzhou are considered of the highest quality. <gloss>Su Song says:</gloss> The sprouts appear in the third month, growing two to three feet high. The green leaves are finely divided and grow in clusters like wormwood stalks. Each stalk bears over a hundred flower heads forming a cluster, similar to cumin. In the fifth month, white flowers bloom in umbrella-like shapes <term>umbels</term>. The seeds are yellowish-brown, like millet, and are very light and hollow. <gloss>Li Shizhen says:</gloss> The flowers look like clusters of broken rice. The seed consists of two halves joined together, resembling dill seeds but smaller and with fine ridges. Generally, plants with flowers and seeds similar to Snake’s Bed include Angelica, Szechuan Lovage, Water Celery, Lovage, and Carrot.

### The Seed <gloss>Preparation</gloss>

# **Chinese Lovage** <note>original: *Gaoben*</note>
<gloss>Listed as Top Grade in the *Classic*. Also known as Ghost Minister <gloss>from the *Classic*</gloss>, New Ghost <gloss>from the *Compendium*</gloss>, or Tattered Stem <gloss>from the *Miscellaneous Records*</gloss></gloss>

<gloss>Because the shoots above the root resemble rice straw (*gao*), it is named *Gaoben*, meaning "straw-root." Li Shizhen states: Chinese Lovage grows in the valleys of high mountains. In the first and second months, its appearance and vital energy are similar to Szechuan Lovage (*Xionggong*). However, *Tong Jun’s Records* notes that while the shoots of Szechuan Lovage look like Chinese Lovage, their flowers and fruits differ, and they grow in different regions. Currently, there is a variety in the Eastern Mountains that is very similar in appearance and nature, only larger. Su Gong says the shoots, leaves, roots, and flavor of Chinese Lovage differ slightly from Szechuan Lovage. Those from Yaozhou are considered best today. Su Song says it is found in Sichuan, Hedong, Yanzhou, and Hangzhou. The leaves resemble Angelica (*Baizhi*) and the fragrance is like Szechuan Lovage, but it is more bitter. It resembles water celery but is larger. Its leaves are fine, it has white flowers in the fifth month, and seeds in the seventh or eighth month. The root is purple. Shizhen adds: It grows in deep mountains south of the Yangtze. The root is like Szechuan Lovage but lighter and hollower; its flavor is numbing and unsuitable for making drinks.</gloss>

## **Root**

### **Nature and Flavor** Acrid, warm, and non-toxic.
<gloss>The *Miscellaneous Records* say it is slightly cold. Zhen Quan says it is slightly warm. Yuan Su says the energy is warm, the flavor is bitter and very acrid, it is non-toxic, and its energy is "thick" <note>meaning it has a strong physiological effect</note>.</gloss>

### **Main Indications** For women's "hernia-like" abdominal masses <note>original: *shanjia*</note>, cold-induced swelling and pain within the abdomen, and abdominal urgency. It eliminates "wind" pathogens, treats headaches, and promotes the growth of muscle and flesh while brightening the complexion.

It treats 160 types of "evil wind" and "ghost-infestation" <note>infectious or wasting diseases</note>, lower back pain where the cold moves through the body, and it can transform and clear the urine. It clears the head and darkens the skin <note>likely referring to evening out skin tone</note>. Zhen Quan says it treats skin blemishes, brandy-nose <note>rosacea</note>, acne, and epilepsy.
<gloss>It is excellent for treating "Greater Yang" <note>original: *Taiyang*</note> headaches, vertex <note>top of the head</note> pain, and extreme cold that attacks the brain and spreads to the teeth and cheeks.</gloss>
<gloss>According to Yuan Su</gloss>
Wind-dampness of the head, face, body, and skin; diseases of the "Governor Vessel" <note>the spinal meridian</note> where the spine is stiff and the limbs feel cold and inverted; it effectively treats spasms, boils, and expels pus while closing sores.

## White Angelica
<gloss>Top Grade in the Divine Husbandman's Classic</gloss>
Named *Baizhi* <gloss>pronounced "zhi" or "hai"</gloss>. It is fragrant. <margin>Alt. Name</margin> *Fuli*. <margin>Alt. Name</margin> *Bi* <gloss>pronounced "ji"</gloss>. *Qiong* <gloss>pronounced "qiong"</gloss>. *Li* <gloss>pronounced "li"</gloss>. *Guan* <gloss>pronounced "guan"</gloss>. <gloss>Shizhen says: Xu Kai stated that when the root and stem first grow, it is called "Zhi." The meaning of White Angelica (Baizhi) is derived from this. The pronunciation "zhi" implies nourishment. Xu Shen’s dictionary (Shuowen) says the sound is like "ginger." The Classic of Poetry (Erya) calls it "Zhai." In the state of Chu, it was called "Li" or "Yue." It grows in low-lying wetlands; its leaves are called "Li" and its flowers are also called "Li."</gloss>

<margin>Collected Explanations</margin>
<gloss>The Miscellaneous Records (Bielu) state: White Angelica grows in the river valleys and wetlands of Hedong. The roots are gathered in the second and eighth months. Its fragrance is as noble as that of the orchid; thus, poets often sang of "Orchids and Angelica." In the Materia Medica, it is called "Fragrant Marsh." The ancients called it "Fragrant White Angelica," noting that its surface should be dried in the sun. Tao Hongjing said: It is found everywhere today, especially in the eastern regions. The leaves can be used to make incense. Zhen said: It is found in many places, especially in the Wu region. The roots are over a foot long and vary in thickness; they are white. The stems rise more than five inches from the ground. In spring, the leaves grow opposite each other in a lush, swaying fashion; they are purple and about three fingers wide. The flowers are white with a hint of yellow. After the "dog days" of summer, it produces seeds. After the beginning of autumn, the sprouts wither. Roots are gathered in the second and eighth months; those that are yellow and solid are of high quality. Lei Xiao says: Do not use the roots of "Four-Hoof" or "Guangsheng" plants, which are actually called "Supreme Duke’s Vine," nor use the roots of the Horse Orchid.</gloss>

<margin>Root</margin>
<margin>Preparation</margin>
<gloss>Lei Xiao says: After gathering, scrape off the outer skin and slice finely. Use equal parts of Solomon’s Seal (Huangjing) slices and steam them together for one full day (twelve double-hours). Dry in the sun and remove the Solomon’s Seal before use. Shizhen says: For all gathering...</gloss>

<margin>Flavor and Nature</margin>
Pungent, warm, and non-toxic. <gloss>Yuan Su says: The nature is warm, the flavor is bitter and very pungent. Both its nature and flavor are "light," making it a Yang-type medicine. It is the guiding herb for the Hand Yang Brightness (Large Intestine) meridian. When used with Cimicifuga (Shengma), it clears both the Hand and Foot Yang Brightness meridians. It also enters the Hand Great Yin (Lung) meridian.</gloss>

<margin>Main Indications</margin>
Treats women’s red and white vaginal discharge, blood stasis, swelling of the labia, chills and fever, and tearing eyes due to wind invasion. It promotes muscle growth, moistens the skin, and improves the complexion; it can be used to make facial powders and creams. —— *Divine Husbandman's Classic*

Treats chronic thirst due to wind pathogens. <gloss>Angelica sinensis (Danggui) acts as its messenger. It is incompatible with Inula flowers and is processed with Scutellaria and Sulfur.</gloss>

Treats vomiting, fullness in the sides of the chest, dizziness, and itchy eyes. It can be used in ointments to treat red eyes and fleshy growths (pterygium). It removes facial spots and scars, moistens the skin, and treats thirst and diabetes. It supplements new blood and treats breast abscesses, back sores, scrofula <note>swelling of the lymph nodes</note>, hemorrhoids, fistulas, and abdominal masses. It stops pain and expels pus; it is highly effective at draining pus. It stops stabbing pain in the heart and abdomen, as well as blood loss, lower back pain, and heavy uterine bleeding in women. —— *Zhen*

It is pungent and benefits the Hand Yang Brightness meridian. It treats headaches, wind-cold fevers, and wind-heat in the Lung meridian. It treats itching of the face and skin, sinus infections, nosebleeds, toothaches, and pain in the eyebrow bone. It treats abdominal distension, constipation, and blood in the urine. It treats "Blood Wind" <note>postpartum or menstrual wind disorders</note> in women with dizziness, vomiting after eating, and acts as an antidote for arsenic poisoning, snake bites, and wounds from blades or arrows. —— *Shizhen*

Shizhen says: White Angelica is a universal remedy for treating "wind." Because its scent is aromatic, it can open the nine orifices <note>the eyes, ears, nostrils, mouth, etc.</note>. It is an essential herb for inducing sweating and dispersing pathogens from the surface. 

Liu Wansu says: It treats "Pure Yang Brightness" headaches and fevers.

<term>Shizhen</term> <note>Li Shizhen, the primary author</note> says: White Angelica is white in color and pungent in flavor, which allows it to act upon the "Geng-Metal" <note>The Large Intestine</note> of the Hand Yangming.
