The Lung is considered the "younger brother" of Geng and the "son" of Wu <note>In Five Elements theory, Earth (Stomach/Wu) creates Metal (Lung/Large Intestine/Geng)</note>. Therefore, the diseases it governs are never far from these three channels. For example, ailments of the head, eyes, eyebrows, and teeth are caused by "wind-heat" in these three channels. Ailments like scrofula, sores, and rashes are caused by "damp-heat" in these three channels. For wind-heat, we use its pungency to disperse it; for damp-heat, we use its warmth to remove it. As the primary medicine for the Yangming channels, it can also treat blood disorders and pregnancy-related illnesses, as well as drain pus, generate new flesh, and stop pain. 

According to a selected formula by <term>Wang Qiu</term>, the Prince of Dingguo suffered from "wind-headache" <note>a sharp, wandering headache</note>. He went to the capital, Duliang, to seek the physician <term>Yang Jie</term>. Yang administered three doses of a pill, and the illness vanished immediately. When the Prince asked for the recipe, it was found to use only one ingredient: fragrant White Angelica. It was washed, dried, ground into powder, and mixed with honey to form pills the size of a bullet. One pill was chewed at a time, washed down with tea or a decoction of Schizonepeta (*Jingjie*). The Prince thereafter named it the **Duliang Pill**. This medicine treats dizziness, and it is effective for women’s headaches before or after childbirth, as well as "blood-wind" headaches. <term>Dai Yuanli</term> says its secret is that it is most suitable for those whose headache feels "soft" or warm, or if the pain is centered in the forehead and teeth. 

Furthermore, the *Book of Spiritual Seclusion* mentions that planting White Angelica can repel snakes. This matches a formula in the *Records of the Strange* (*Yijian Zhi*) for treating viper bites, suggesting the herb is something snakes fear, though earlier herbal manuals did not mention this. <term>Zongshuang</term> <note>Kou Zongshi</note> says: The *Treatise on Medicinal Nature* states that White Angelica can "eat away" at pus. People use it to treat vaginal discharge. When the intestines contain "defeated pus" that leaks out continuously with a foul smell, leading to cold pain in the umbilical region, it is caused by stagnant pus and blood. One must use this herb to drain the pus. Take one tael <note>about 37 grams</note> of White Angelica and two roots of single-leaf red hollyhock.

Take two doses in succession. — *From Prescriptions for Universal Relief (Puji Fang)*

**For unstoppable nosebleeds:** Take the blood that has just come out of the nose and mix it with White Angelica powder. Apply this paste to the <term>Mountain Root</term> <note>the bridge of the nose between the eyes</note> and the bleeding will stop immediately. — *From Simple and Convenient Prescriptions (Jianbian Fang)*

**For blood in the urine:** Take equal parts of White Angelica and <term>Chinese Angelica</term> (Danggui) and grind into a powder. Take two <term>qian</term> per dose with rice water. — *From Proven Prescriptions (Jingyan Fang)*

**For "Intestinal Wind" (blood in the stool):** Use fragrant White Angelica ground into a powder. Take two <term>qian</term> per dose with rice water. It is divinely effective. — *Layman Yu’s Selected Rare Prescriptions*

**For bleeding from hemorrhoids or fistulas:** Use the same formula as above, but also boil the herb in water to use as a medicinal steam and wash. — *From Straightforward Directions (Zhizhi Fang)*

**For painful, swollen hemorrhoids:** First, fumigate the area with the smoke of <term>Honey Locust</term> (Zaojiao). Then, mix White Angelica powder with rouge juice and apply it to the area.

**For the onset of breast abscesses:** Grind two <term>qian</term> each of White Angelica and <term>Fritillaria</term> (Beimu) into a powder. Take it with warm wine.

**For the onset of furuncles (clove-like sores):** Take one <term>qian</term> of White Angelica and one ounce of fresh ginger. Crush them and add one cup of wine. Drink it warm to induce sweating, and the sore will dissipate. This formula is from Commander Chen. — *From Pocket Prescriptions (Xiuzhen Fang)*

**For red, swollen carbuncles:** Use equal parts White Angelica and <term>Rhubarb</term> (Dahuang) ground into a powder. Take two <term>qian</term> with rice water. — *From Proven Prescriptions (Jingyan Fang)*

**For "Danliu" (erysipelas or red rashes) in children:** If the rash moves into the abdomen, it is fatal. At the first sign, use "Wind-Interrupting Powder" to stop it. Grind White Angelica and <term>Cold Water Stone</term> (Hanshuishi) <note>a form of gypsum or calcite</note> into a powder and apply it mixed with fresh green onion juice. — *From Mirror of Pediatric Hearts (Quanyou Xinjian)*

**For wounds from knives or arrows:** Chew fragrant White Angelica into a pulp and apply it to the wound. — *From Collected Simple Prescriptions (Jijian Fang)*

**For venomous snake bites:** Take White Angelica powder with well water in two <term>qian</term> doses. — *From Forest of Forest of Records (Shilin Guangji)*

**For bones stuck in the throat:** Use equal parts White Angelica and <term>Pinellia</term> (Banxia) ground into a powder. Take one <term>qian</term> with rice water; the person will vomit the bone out. — *From Prescriptions for Universal Relief (Puji Fang)*

In Linchuan, a person was bitten by a viper. In a short time, their whole body skin swelled up and turned a yellowish-black color. A Taoist mixed one pound of fragrant White Angelica powder with freshly drawn water and poured it down the person's throat. After a while, they felt a "slippery" sensation in their navel, and a foul-smelling, fishy yellow water poured from their mouth. Eventually, the swelling receded. It is said that mixing it with a decoction of Ginseng and Ophiopogon (*Mendong*) is even more miraculous; one should also sprinkle the powder on the wound.

Furthermore, a monk in a mountain temple was bitten by a snake on his foot. The wound rotted and festered, and a hundred medicines failed to cure it. A traveling monk washed the area clean of rot with fresh water until the white tendons were visible. After drying it, he applied White Angelica powder mixed with a little <term>Verdigris</term> (Danfan) and Musk. Foul water gushed out of the wound. He did this daily, and in one month, the leg was fully healed. — *From Hong Mai’s Records of the Listener (Yijian Zhi)*

<gloss>Mainly used to make a medicinal bath to remove "corpse worms" <note>parasites or unseen pathogens</note>. Boiling them for a bath also treats erysipelas, heat rashes, and wind-related itching. <insert>Appended Formula</insert> For a child's fever: boil White Angelica seedlings and <term>Bitter Ginseng</term> (Kushen) in equal parts with starch-water and a little salt. Use this to wash the child. — *From Comprehensive Treatise on Health (Weisheng Zongwei)*</gloss>

# Peony (Shaoyao)
<gloss>The name "Shao" is pronounced like "shao" <note>original: "芍音勺"</note>. It is also called "General Leaving" (*Jiang-li*). <insert>Compendium</insert> Also called *Lishi* <insert>Separate Records</insert>, White Peony <insert>Separate Records</insert>, *Jinrong* <insert>Separate Records</insert>. The white variety is called "Golden Peony" <insert>Illustrated Classic</insert>, while the red variety is called "Wood Peony" <insert>Illustrated Classic</insert>. Shizhen says: The name *Shaoyao* is like *chuoyue* <note>meaning "graceful and beautiful"</note>. Because the flower’s appearance is so graceful and lovely, it was given this name. Luo Yuan, in his *Supplement to the Erya*, says that for neutralizing toxins in food, nothing is better than the Peony, so the name "Medicine" (*Yao*) is also appropriate. In the "Odes of Zheng" in the *Classic of Poetry*, it says "They tease each other and present each other with peonies." The *Outer Tradition of Han Poetry* says: "The Peony is the herb of parting." Dong <insert>Qizhen</insert> explains: "One name for the Peony is 'General Leaving,' which is why it is gifted when people are about to part." Common folk call the variety with many petals the "Little Tree Peony" <note>Mudan</note>, often shortened to "Wood Peony," which shares a name with the Tree Peony. <insert>Su Gong</insert> says: It is harvested in the second and eighth months, and the roots are dried in the sun. Tao Hongjing says: Those now coming from Baishan, Jiangshan, and Maoshan are the best; they are white and about a foot long. They grow elsewhere too but are mostly red; the red ones are slightly more purgative. <insert>Zhi</insert> says: There are two types, red and white, and the flowers also come in red and white. <insert>Song</insert> says: It is found everywhere now; those from Huainan are superior. In spring, it grows red buds in clusters. On the stems are three branches with five leaves, similar to a Tree Peony but narrower and longer. It grows one to two feet high. In early summer, it blooms in white, red, and purple varieties. It produces seeds similar to Tree Peony seeds but smaller. The roots are harvested in autumn. Cui Bao, in his *Notes on Ancient and Modern Matters*, says: "There are two kinds of Peony: the Herbaceous Peony and the Wood Peony. The Wood Peony has larger, deeper-colored flowers and is commonly called the Tree Peony (*Mudan*), but this is incorrect." In An Qisheng’s *Methods of Refinement*, it is said: "Golden Peony is white and oily; Wood Peony is purple and has many veins." Now, the *Classic* says Peony grows in the hills, but today most people use those cultivated in gardens. Because the flowers and leaves are so lush, they must be heavily fertilized. Every year in the eighth or ninth month, the roots are divided. Because they are cultivated for profit, they are used as medicine. Today, they are most abundant in Zhenyang, Huainan. Although the roots are thick, their fragrance is poor and they are less effective as medicine. Shizhen says: People of old said "The Tree Peonies of Luoyang and the Herbaceous Peonies of Yangzhou are the finest under heaven." Most Peonies used in medicine today are from Yangzhou. In the tenth month the buds appear, growing through the spring. They bloom in the third month. There are over thirty varieties, including single-petaled, multi-petaled, and "hidden-center" types. For medicine, the single-petaled root is best, as its energy and flavor are thick and complete. Whether the root is "red" or "white" follows the color of its flower.</gloss>

### **The Root** 
<gloss>Lei Fu says: Whenever the roots are gathered, use a bamboo knife to scrape away the outer skin and the "mustache" at the head of the root. Slice it finely, mix it with honey water, and steam it from the hour of the Snake until the hour of the Sheep <note>original: "from Si to Wei," approximately 9:00 AM to 3:00 PM</note>. Then, sun-dry it.</gloss>

**Preparation and Processing**

**Nature and Flavor** 
<gloss>It is bitter, slightly cold, and non-toxic. The physician Qi Bo and the text *Bin* say it is "sour." Lei Gong says it is "sour." Li Dangzhi says it is "slightly cold." Zhang Yuansu says: Its nature is cold, its flavor is sour; its <term>Qi</term> <note>vital energy or aromatic quality</note> is thick while its flavor is thin. It rises but also slightly descends; it is the "Yin within Yang." Kou Zongshi says: White Peony is sour and neutral, possessing a slight toxicity. It can rise or descend and belongs to Yin. Wang Haogu says: The flavor is sour and bitter, the Qi is thin and the flavor thick. It is Yin. It acts as a medicinal messenger for the Hand and Foot <term>Taiyin</term> <note>Lung and Spleen</note> meridians, entering the blood divisions of the Liver and Spleen. It requires <term>Xu Jiu</term> <note>original: "須九", likely a transcription error for "Lei Wan" or similar medicinal</note> as an assistant. It dislikes <term>Dendrobium</term> (Shichuhu) and <term>Glauber’s Salt</term> (Mangxiao). It fears <term>Saltpeter</term> (Xiaoshi), <term>Turtle Shell</term> (Biejia), and <term>Small Thistle</term> (Xiaoji). It is incompatible with <term>Veratrum</term> (Lilu). Zhu Danxi says: Other editions say "Xu Jiu" should be <term>Lei Wan</term> (Omphalia). Li Shizhen says: To tonify the Spleen, use it with <term>Atractylodes</term> (Baishu). To drain the Liver, use it with [Red] Peony. To tonify Qi, use it with <term>Ginseng</term>. To tonify the blood, use it with <term>Chinese Angelica</term> (Danggui). When stir-fried with wine, it tonifies Yin. With <term>Licorice</term> (Gancao), it stops abdominal pain. With <term>Coptis</term> (Huanglian), it stops diarrhea and dysentery. With <term>Ledebouriella</term> (Fangfeng), it helps erupting pox and rashes. With Ginger and Jujubes, it warms the meridians and disperses dampness.</gloss>

**Primary Indications** 
It treats "evil Qi" and abdominal pain, removes blood stasis, and breaks up hard accumulations or cold-heat masses and hernias. It stops pain, promotes urination, and clears the blood vessels. It relaxes the "Middle" <note>the digestive center</note>, disperses "evil blood," and expels "thief blood" <note>stagnant or harmful blood</note>. It removes water retention and benefits the bladder, small intestine, and large intestine. It dissipates carbuncles and swellings. It treats seasonal fevers and chills, "middle-evil" <note>sudden demonic or toxic strike</note> abdominal pain, and back pain. The *Additional Records* (Bielu) state it treats congestion of Qi in the viscera, strengthens the five internal organs, and tonifies Kidney Qi. It treats seasonal epidemic bone-heat and "blood closure" <note>amenorrhea</note> in women, and it can "eat away" pus.

**Elucidations** 
<gloss>Zhen Quan says:</gloss> It treats all women’s illnesses, including all disorders before and after childbirth. It treats "wind" disorders, tonifies for exhaustion, clears heat, and removes irritability. It treats nosebleeds, red eyes (improving vision), "intestinal wind" <note>bloody stools</note>, diarrhea, hemorrhoids, fistulas, back sores, and scabies. It strongly drains the Liver and calms the Spleen and Lungs, gathering the Stomach Qi to stop diarrhea. 
<gloss>Zhen Quan says:</gloss> It firms the <term>interstices</term> <note>striae or skin pores</note>, harmonizes the blood vessels, gathers the Yin energy, and restrains counterflow. 
<gloss>Zhang Yuansu says:</gloss> It regulates the "Middle Qi," treats Spleen deficiency with abdominal fullness, distension below the heart, and pain under the ribs. It is good for belching and tightness in the lungs with distension, gasping, and coughing. In the <term>Taiyang</term> <note>Bladder</note> meridian, it aids the eyesight. For insufficient Liver blood and <term>Yangwei</term> channel diseases characterized by bitter chills and fever, or <term>Daimai</term> <note>Girdle vessel</note> diseases with abdominal pain and a waist that feels heavy "as if sitting in water." 
<gloss>Wang Haogu says:</gloss> It treats dysentery with abdominal pain and a heavy feeling in the rectum <note>tenesmus</note>. 
<gloss>Li Shizhen says:</gloss> To clarify, the red variety benefits urination and lowers Qi, while the white variety stops pain and disperses blood. 
<gloss>The *Grand Clarity* (Daming) says:</gloss> The red variety tonifies Qi, and the white variety tonifies blood. 
<gloss>Tao Hongjing says:</gloss> White tonifies while red drains; white gathers while red disperses. Its sourness gathers, and its sweetness relaxes. Thus, when sour and sweet are combined, it is used to tonify the Yin blood, open the Qi, and remove dryness in the Lungs. It is also said that the sourness of Peony restrains body fluids to benefit the <term>Ying</term> <note>Nutritive</note> Qi and drain "evil heat." 
<gloss>Zhang Yuansu says:</gloss> White tonifies and red drains. It drains the Liver and tonifies the Spleen and Stomach. When soaked in wine, it moves through the upper and middle parts of the body. For abdominal pain, it is used with Silkworm to warmly disperse dampness and unblock stagnation. When Qi is blocked and does not flow naturally, it enters the Spleen meridian to tonify the "Middle Burner." It is an essential medicine for diarrhea. Since both diarrhea and dysentery are <term>Taiyin</term> <note>Spleen</note> diseases, this herb cannot be omitted. When paired with honey-fried Licorice, it is excellent for abdominal pain. If there is heat, add <term>Scutellaria</term> (Huangqin); if there is aversion to cold, add <term>Cinnamon</term> (Gui). This is a divine formula of Zhang Zhongjing. Its uses are sixfold: first, to settle the Spleen; second, to treat abdominal pain; third, to gather Stomach Qi; fourth, to stop diarrhea; fifth, to harmonize the blood vessels; sixth, to firm the interstices. 
<gloss>Kou Zongshi says:</gloss> Peony with single-petaled red flowers is best. However, people with Qi deficiency and cold must avoid it. The ancients said, "Reduce the Peony to avoid internal cold"—this truly cannot be ignored. 
<gloss>Zhu Zhenheng says:</gloss> Peony drains Spleen fire. Its nature is sour and cold. In winter months, it must be stir-fried with wine. Most abdominal pain is due to blood stasis and stagnation, so it must also be stir-fried with wine for those cases. However, it can only treat abdominal pain from blood deficiency; it does not treat other types because its sour-cold astringency lacks the power to warmly disperse. For dysentery with abdominal pain, it must be used stir-fried. If there is a heavy feeling in the rectum, do not stir-fry it. It should not be used after childbirth because its sour-cold nature attacks the "generative Qi." If it absolutely must be used, it must be stir-fried with wine. 
<gloss>Li Shizhen says:</gloss> White Peony benefits the Spleen and can "drain Wood from within Earth" <note>restrain the Liver from overacting on the Spleen</note>. Red Peony disperses "evil" and can move stagnation within the blood. The author of *Rihuazi* said red tonifies Qi and white treats blood—this is incorrect. After childbirth, Liver blood is already deficient and should not be further drained, which is why it is forbidden. There are many sour-cold medicines; why single out Peony? Looking at this, Zhang Zhongjing used Peony frequently in treating "Cold Damage" (Shanghan) because it governs chills and fever and benefits urination. 
<gloss>Li Gao says:</gloss> Some say the ancients used sour and astringent flavors for "gathering" (astringing). Why does the *Classic* say it benefits urination? White Peony can benefit Yin and nourish moisture, allowing body fluids to settle, and thus urination occurs naturally; it is not because it is a diuretic. He also asks: why is it said to "relax the Middle"? The answer: to reduce the center is to regulate the blood. Therefore, the *Four-Substance Decoction* (Siwu Tang) uses Peony. Generally, sour and astringent things are agents that gather and settle moisture. Thus, it governs the "gathering" function of the Hand and Foot <term>Taiyin</term> meridians. It can also treat the "Sea of Blood" and enter the "nine levels of the earth" <note>the deepest parts of the body</note>, reaching the <term>Jueyin</term> <note>Liver</note> meridian. White is the color of the West (Metal), so it tonifies; Red is the color of the South (Fire), so it drains.

It highlights the herb's essential role in treating abdominal pain, women's health, and Spleen-Liver disharmony when combined with other substances like Licorice or Wine.</summary>

**Formula Eleven: Methods for Consumption** <gloss>Su Song says: Regarding the method for preparing Peony for longevity, the "Record of Refining Peony" states: There are two types of Peony. For curing illness, use the "Gold Peony" <note>original: "Jin Shaoyao," likely referring to the high-quality white herbaceous peony</note>, which is white in color and rich in "fatty" flesh. The "Wood Peony" <note>likely referring to the wild or tree variety</note> is purple, thin, and very fibrous. When selecting, one must look carefully to avoid error. Once gathered, wash them clean, remove the skin, and boil them in "east-flowing water" <note>water from a stream flowing eastward, traditionally thought to possess "Yang" energy</note> for one hundred boils. Dry in the shade. After three days, steam it in a wooden steamer, covering the top with clean yellow earth. After one day and night, it will be thoroughly cooked. Remove, dry in the shade, and grind into a powder. Take three coins' weight <note>approx. 9-10 grams</note> with wheat drink or wine. Taking it three times every seven days for three hundred days will result in [great benefit].</gloss>

### **Clinical Applications**

**Abdominal pain due to deficiency** <gloss>White Peony three coins, honey-fried Licorice one coin. In summer months, add Scutellaria five fen. If there is an aversion to cold, add Cassia bark <note>Cinnamon</note> one coin.</gloss>

**Bone pain from Wind-Poison** <gloss>When the pain is deep in the marrow. Peony two parts, Tiger Bone one ounce <note>original: "Hugu"; modern conservation laws prohibit this, but it was historically used for joint/bone ailments</note>. Roast and grind into powder. Place in a silk bag and soak in three pints of wine for five days. Take a dose regularly.</gloss>

**Abdominal pain due to deficiency and swelling from Beriberi** <gloss>White Peony six ounces, Licorice one ounce. Used for wasting-thirst <note>diabetes-like symptoms</note>.</gloss>

**For Wasting-Thirst (Diabetes)** <gloss>Take White Peony and honey-fried Licorice in equal parts. Grind to a powder. Use one coin's weight per dose, decocting in water. Take three times a day.</gloss> <note>This entry appears to overlap with the beriberi formula in the source transcription.</note>

**Swelling and pain from Beriberi** <gloss>From the *Proved Formulas* (Jingyan Fang): Take a decoction of Red and White Peony.</gloss>

**Chronic ailments of nine years** <gloss>From the *Comprehensive Records of the Forest of Affairs* (Shilin Guangji): A patient suffered for nine years; medications would stop the pain, but it always returned. Master Bu Bian taught this formula: after seven days of use, the patient was suddenly cured. The prescriptions of the ancients are sometimes incomprehensible at first; one must not ignore them simply because they seem common or easy.</gloss>

**The Five Urinary Blockages (Strangury)** <gloss>From Chen Rihua's *Proved Formulas*: Red Peony one ounce, one Betel Nut. Pound and sieve into a powder. Take two coins per dose, decocting in a cup of water until reduced by 10-20%. Take on an empty stomach.</gloss>

**Unstoppable Bleeding** <gloss>From *Formulas for Universal Relief* (Boji Fang): Red Peony powder, two coin-spoons taken with water.</gloss>

**Nosebleeds and Coughing Blood** <gloss>From *Comprehensive Records of the Forest of Affairs*: White Peony one ounce, Betel Nut half an ounce. Grind to a powder. Take one coin-spoon with water.</gloss>

**Uterine Hemorrhage with Severe Abdominal Pain** <gloss>Peony one ounce, stir-fried until yellow. Cypress leaves six ounces, lightly stir-fried. For each dose, use two coins in one pint of water, decocting until reduced by 40%.</gloss>

**Unstoppable Menstrual Discharge** <gloss>White Peony, Cyperus (Xiangfuzi), and aged Mugwort leaves, 1.5 coins each. Decoct in water and drink.</gloss>

**Uterine Flooding and Vaginal Discharge** <gloss>From the *Sage's Beneficence* (Shenghui Fang): Red Peony and Cyperus in equal parts. Grind to powder. For each dose, take two coins with a pinch of salt in water.</gloss>

**Chronic Red and White Vaginal Discharge** <gloss>From *Guangli's Formulas*: For cases that have persisted for years without healing. Take White Peony three ounces, Dried Ginger half an ounce. Chop and roast until yellow. Grind to powder and take with wine.</gloss>

**Bleeding from Metal Wounds** <gloss>White Peony one ounce, roasted yellow and ground to powder. Take two coins with wine or rice water.</gloss>

**Abdominal Pain from Smallpox or Rashes** <gloss>White Peony and honey-fried Licorice. Grind to powder. Take two coin-spoons with water on an empty stomach twice a day. From the *Formulas for Wide Relief* (Guangji Fang): Simply use Peony stir-fried until black, grind to powder, and take with wine.</gloss>

**Swelling of the "Wooden Tongue"** <gloss>A condition where the tongue swells to fill the mouth, which can be fatal. Red Peony and Licorice. Decoct in water and use as a hot gargle.</gloss>

**Bone Stuck in the Throat** <gloss>From the *Sage's General Record*: Chew White Peony finely and swallow the juice.</gloss>

# Tree Peony (Mudan)
<gloss>Ranked as a Middle Grade herb in the *Divine Husbandman's Classic*. Also named: Mouse-Aunt, Deer-Leek, Hundred-Taels-Gold. <gloss>The *Tang Herbals* call it "Peony" (Shaoyao); the *Compendium* (Gangmu) calls it the "King of Flowers."</gloss></gloss>

<gloss>Li Shizhen says: The Tree Peony (*Mudan*) with cinnabar-red color is superior. Although it produces seeds, new shoots sprout from the roots, hence it is called "Mu" (Male/Progenitor) "Dan" (Cinnabar/Red). People of the Tang Dynasty called it the "Wood Peony" because its flowers resemble the herbaceous Peony (*Shaoyao*), but its old stems are woody. In the *Manual of a Myriad Flowers*, the Tree Peony is ranked first and the Herbaceous Peony second; thus, the world calls the Tree Peony the "King of Flowers" and the Herbaceous Peony the "Prime Minister of Flowers." Ouyang Xiu’s *Flower Manual* records over thirty varieties, named after locations, people, colors, or unique traits. Details can be found in that book.</gloss>

<gloss>Explanatory Notes: The *Additional Records* (Bielu) state: The Tree Peony grows in the valleys of Hongjun and Hanzhong. Gather the roots in the second and eighth months and dry them in the shade. Tao Hongjing says: It is now also found in the east, and many varieties are grown for their beauty. It grows in Hanzhong and Jiannan. The shoots resemble the "sheep-peach" <note>likely Actinidia/Kiwi relative</note>. It produces white flowers in summer and round green fruit in autumn, which turn red in winter. It does not wither in the cold. The root has the flesh of a Peony, white with a red skin. The locals call it "Hundred-Taels-Gold." What the people of Chang'an call the "Wu Mudan" is the true variety. What is commonly used today has no other special scent. Su Song says: The best now comes from Hezhou; those from Xuanzhou are also good. The white variety is tonifying, while the red variety is draining. Da Ming says: This is the root of the Tree Peony flower. Those from the Sichuan regions are secondary. Su Song continues: Today, it is found in the mountains of Danyan, Qingyue, and Chuhezhou. However, the flowers come in several colors: yellow, purple, red, and white. These are likely wild Tree Peonies. The stems are dry and blackish-white. In the second month, shoots and leaves grow from the stems. In the third month, it flowers. The flowers and leaves are similar to those planted in gardens, but the wild variety has only five or six petals. In the fifth month, it produces black seeds as large as Foxnuts (Gorgon fruit). The roots are yellow-white, five to seven inches long, and as thick as a brush handle. In recent times, people value them highly and desire strange, exotic flowers; they graft them in autumn and winter and nourish them with rich soil so they bloom magnificently in spring, taking a hundred different forms. Therefore, the nature of the roots...</gloss>

<meta>This page continues the detailed study of the Tree Peony (Mudan), transitioning from its cultivation and physical selection to its specific pharmacological properties, preparation methods, and clinical applications for blood-related conditions and "bone-steaming" fevers. It also begins the entry for Wood Fragrance (Muxiang).</meta>

If a plant loses its true essence, it cannot be used in medicine as it will have no potency. Song Zhong says: Tree Peony flowers come in crimson and deep green, but only the red, single-petaled variety found in the mountains provides root bark suitable for medicine. Market sellers often use the bark from the branches or stems to fill their stock, which is particularly dishonest. 

Li Shizhen states: For medicinal use, one should only select Tree Peonies with white or red single petals. The elaborate, multi-petaled varieties are products of human ingenuity; their "Qi" <note>the vital energy or essence of the plant</note> and flavor are impure and should not be used. Regarding its habitat, it grows most abundantly west of Yanzhou and in the Baoxie mountain passes, where it is as common as brambles. The locals even use it for firewood. However, its root is excellent for medicine. Gardeners who cultivate these flowers use powdered *Bailian* <note>original: "Bailian," likely *Ampelopsis japonica*</note> at the base of the root to deter pests; if insects bore holes, they apply sulfur to kill them. This acts like a "bone-needle" for the tree. These characteristics of the plant's nature are essential to understand.

## Root Bark
<gloss>Preparation</gloss>
<note>
Tao Hongjing <note>referred to here as "Yinjue" or the Hermit</note> says: Whenever you gather the roots, dry them in the sun. Use a copper knife to split them open and remove the woody core, then chop them into pieces.
</note>
<gloss>Nature and Flavor</gloss>
Acrid, cold, and non-toxic.
<note>
The *Record of Famous Physicians* <note>original: "Bielu"</note> says: Bitter and slightly cold. Pu Jing says: According to the emperors Shennong and Qi Bo, it is acrid. According to Lei Gong and Tong Jun, it is bitter and non-toxic. Tong Jun also noted that some varieties are bitter and toxic. Wang Haogu <note>original: "Haogu"</note> says: The flavor is bitter and acrid; it possesses "minor Yang within Yin" <note>a quality of rising or moving energy within a cooling substance</note> and acts upon the Pericardium and Kidney channels.
</note>
<gloss>Contraindications</gloss>
<note>
The *Materia Medica of the Ming Dynasty* states: Avoid Garlic, Cilantro, Ginger, and Arsenic.
</note>

# Tree Peony
<gloss>Incompatible with Fritillaria and Rhubarb</gloss> <gloss>Incompatible with Dodder Seed and Rhubarb</gloss>
**Main Indications** Chills and fever, stroke, convulsions, and epilepsy. It expels "evil qi" <note>pathogenic influences</note>, removes hard masses, and clears stagnant blood lodged in the stomach and intestines. It stabilizes the five internal organs and heals abscesses and sores. <gloss>Classic of Materia Medica</gloss> It treats seasonal headaches, "guest heat" <note>temporary, external fevers</note>, the five types of exhaustion, "labor qi" <note>exhaustion from overwork</note>, and pains in the waist and knees. <gloss>Record of Famous Physicians</gloss> Taken over a long period, it lightens the body and extends life. <gloss>Pu Jing</gloss> It treats "cold qi" <note>internal cold causing stagnation</note>, disperses various pains, and manages women's menstrual blockages, blood spotting, and back pain. <gloss>Zhen Quan</gloss> It opens the channels to move blood, drains pus, dissolves bruises from falls, knits together tendons and bones, and removes "wind-damp" numbness. It helps expel a retained placenta and treats various postpartum conditions.

## It is highly effective for all types of "cold" and "heat" blood-related disorders, lack of mental clarity, and "bone-steaming" fever without sweating. It also stops nosebleeds and the vomiting of blood.
<gloss>Zhang Yuansu</gloss>
## It harmonizes, generates, and cools the blood. It treats "hidden fire" within the blood and removes irritability and heat.
<gloss>Li Shizhen's Elaboration</gloss>
<note>
Li Shizhen, Cheng Yanyi, and Zhang Yuansu state: The Tree Peony is the essence of Heaven and Earth, the leader of all flowers. Its leaves represent "Yang" growth, while its flowers represent "Yin" completion. The color "Dan" <note>meaning red or cinnabar</note> represents fire; thus, it can drain fire from the "Yin womb" <note>the lower abdomen/reproductive system</note>. When added to the "Four Substances Decoction" <note>original: "Siwu Tang," a primary blood-tonifying formula</note>, it treats women's bone-steaming fever. It is said that Tree Peony bark enters the Pericardium and Kidney channels, so it treats bone-steaming fever *without* sweating. In contrast, Wolfberry root bark <note>original: "Digupi"</note> enters the Heart and Triple Burner channels and treats bone-steaming fever *with* sweating. Since the Heart governs the spirit and the Kidneys govern the will, Master Zhang Zhongjing used it in his "Kidney Qi Pill" <note>original: "Shenqi Wan"</note> to treat deficiencies of spirit and will. It is also an essential medicine for stagnant blood in the Yang channels and for bleeding from the nose or mouth; hence its use in "Rhino Horn and Rehmannia Decoction" <note>original: "Xijiao Dihuang Tang"</note>.
</note>
<gloss>Zhu Zhenheng says:</gloss>
<note>
For those with Heart deficiency, heat accumulation in the intestines/stomach, blazing heart-fire, or insufficient Heart Qi, use Tree Peony bark as the "sovereign" <note>primary</note> ingredient. Li Shizhen adds: Tree Peony bark treats "hidden fire" in the four blood-related channels. This hidden fire is "Yin fire," also known as "Ministerial Fire." Ancient formulas used it specifically for this. While later doctors relied solely on *Phellodendron* <note>original: "Huangbai"</note> to treat Ministerial Fire, they did not realize the power of Tree Peony is even greater. This is a secret of a thousand years that I now reveal. Note that red flowers favor "draining" while white flowers favor "tonifying"—a distinction few people realize.
</note>

# Wood Fragrance
<gloss>Classic of Materia Medica</gloss> <gloss>Also called Honey Fragrance</gloss> <gloss>Record of Famous Physicians</gloss> <gloss>Green Wood Fragrance</gloss> <gloss>Zhang Zhongjing</gloss>
## Five Wood Fragrances
<gloss>Illustrated Classic</gloss>
## Southern Wood Fragrance
<gloss>Compendium</gloss>
<note>
Li Shizhen says: Wood Fragrance <note>original: "Muxiang," *Aucklandia costus*</note> is a type of herb. It was originally called "Honey Fragrance" because its scent resembles honey. Because *Aquilaria* <note>Agarwood</note> also contains a variety called Honey Fragrance, this was mistakenly called Wood Fragrance. Former writers called it "Green Wood Fragrance," but later people called the root of Birthwort <note>original: "Madouling"</note> "Green Wood Fragrance," so they renamed this "Southern Wood Fragrance" or "Guang Wood Fragrance" <note>indicating it came from Guangzhou or abroad</note>.
</note>

# Wood Fragrance
<note>original: "Muxiang"; refers primarily to the root of *Aucklandia costus*, also known as Costus root.</note>

To distinguish it, modern people also call a type of rose "Wood Fragrance," which further confuses the true plant. *The Pearl Satchel of the Three Caverns* <note>original: "Sandong Zhunang," a Daoist encyclopedia</note> states that the "Five Fragrances" is actually Green Wood Fragrance. A single plant has five roots, one stem with five branches, and each branch has five leaves with five nodes between them; thus, it is named "Five Fragrances." When burned, its scent is said to reach the "Nine Heavens" <note>the highest realms of the spirit world</note>. Ancient formulas for treating carbuncles and ulcers, such as the "Five Fragrances and Forsythia Decoction," utilized Green Wood Fragrance. Ancient folk songs also mention "viewing the hairpin of five-wood fragrance," all referring to this plant. <gloss>Song says: Books on self-cultivation state that taking a bath in a decoction of the five-wood fragrances on the first day of the first lunar month will keep one's hair and beard black even in old age. Xu Kai’s commentary notes: Daoists call this "Green Wood Fragrance."</gloss> <gloss>The *Record of Famous Physicians* <note>original: "Bielu"</note> states: Wood Fragrance grows in the valleys of Yongchang. Hongjing says: This is Green Wood Fragrance. Yongchang no longer sends it as tribute; now it all comes on foreign ships. It is also called "Five Wood" and is frequently used for bathing. The *Golden Light Sutra* <note>original: "Jin Guang Ming Jing"</note> calls it *Jupihua* fragrance. Only later was it said to come from the country of Daqin <note>the Roman Empire or the Near East</note>. Today it is used in blended incenses and rarely in medicine. Gong says: There are two types; that which comes from the Kunlun Mountains is superior, while that from the "West Lake" is not as good. The leaves resemble those of the Dock plant <note>original: "Yangti"</note> but are longer and larger. The flowers are like chrysanthemums, and the fruit is yellow-black. It grows in many places and has numerous uses. Tao’s claim that it is not used in medicine is incorrect. Huo says: The *Records of Exotic Things from the Southern Provinces* <note>original: "Nanzhou Yiwu Zhi"</note> states that Green Wood Fragrance comes from India <note>original: "Tianzhu"</note>; it is a grass root shaped like licorice. Song says: Today it only comes via ships to Guangzhou; it is found nowhere else. The root crown resembles an eggplant, and the leaves are like those of the Dock plant but larger. There is also a variety like the Mountain Yam but with a larger root and purple flowers. The roots are harvested regardless of the season. For medicine, those shaped like dry bones that taste bitter and stick to the teeth are best. A variety found in the Yangtze and Huai regions called "Local Green Wood Fragrance" is unsuitable for medicine. The *Sichuan Materia Medica* <note>original: "Shu Bencao"</note> notes that Meng Shen once grew it in his garden; he said the seedlings reached three to four feet, with wrinkled, soft, hairy leaves nine inches long and yellow flowers. This was likely the "Earth Wood Fragrance" variety. Shen says: Its fragrance comes from the vine-like rootlets that spiral to the left. It takes twenty-nine days to harden like rotted bone. Those with a distinct "reed head" <note>rhizome top</note> and a bluish color are the "spirit" of the Wood Fragrance. Zongshi says: I once traveled beyond the border at Minzhou and obtained Green Wood Fragrance to bring back to Luoyang. The leaves are like Burdock but narrower and longer. The stem is two to three feet high, and the flowers are yellow like gold coins. The root itself is the incense. Chewing it raw reveals a spicy fragrance that is excellent for circulating Qi. Cheng says: Wood Fragrance now comes entirely from abroad. Tao's description is correct. The Guangzhou variety mentioned by Shen and Song in the *Illustrated Classic* is a woody type, and the varieties from Chuzhou and Haizhou are actually the roots of Birthwort <note>original: "Madouling"; Aristolochia</note> used for treating sores and heat, which do not resemble the true plant at all. These were errors in the illustrations. Shizhen says: Wood Fragrance is found in many countries across the southern provinces.</gloss> The *Continued Annals* states the leaves resemble those of the silk gourd; the roots are harvested in winter and dried in the sun.

---

### Root
<gloss>Preparation: Shizhen says: When used in medicines to regulate Qi, use it raw and do not expose it to fire. If the goal is to strengthen the Large Intestine, it should be wrapped in dough and roasted until ripe.</gloss>

**Nature and Flavor**
Spicy, warm, and non-toxic. <gloss>Yuan-su says: The Qi is hot and the flavor is acrid and bitter. Both Qi and flavor are thick; it is a "sinking and descending" substance, belonging to Yin. Bing says: Bitter, sweet, spicy, and slightly warm; it descends and belongs to Yin. Haogu says: Acrid, bitter, and hot. The flavor is thicker than the Qi; it is the "Yang within Yin."</gloss>

**Primary Indications**
Expels evil Qi and protects against pestilence, epidemics, and malevolent spirits. It strengthens the will and treats urinary blockages. Long-term use prevents nightmares and sleep paralysis <gloss>from the *Divine Husbandman's Classic*</gloss>. It neutralizes toxins, kills "ghost essences," and treats "warm malaria" <note>a type of fever</note>, poisoning, and Qi deficiency. It warms the interior when the muscles are cold and draws out the essence of other medicines <gloss>from the *Record of Famous Physicians*</gloss>. It treats all types of Qi stagnation in the heart and abdomen, cold pain in the bladder, vomiting, acid reflux, cholera, diarrhea, and dysentery. It strengthens the spleen, aids digestion, and calms the fetus <gloss>according to Daming</gloss>. It treats nine types of heart pain, chronic cold Qi, abdominal masses, bloating, and the "surging up" of Qi in cholera. For women with unbearable stabbing pains from blood-Qi disorders, it should be powdered and taken with wine <gloss>according to Zhen Quan</gloss>. It disperses stagnant Qi, harmonizes all forms of Qi, regulates Stomach Qi, and drains Lung Qi <gloss>according to Yuan-su</gloss>. It moves the Qi of the Liver meridian and dries/strengthens the Large Intestine <gloss>according to Zangqi</gloss>. It treats disorders of the "Thrusting Vessel" <note>original: "Chongmai"; one of the eight extraordinary vessels in TCM</note>, upward-rushing Qi, abdominal urgency, and difficulty urinating <unclear>below</unclear> the navel <gloss>according to Haogu</gloss>.

<gloss>Inventions and Elaborations: Hongjing says: The people of Daqin <note>Rome/West</note> use Green Wood Fragrance to treat toxic swellings; bathing in its juice is excellent. Zongshi says: Wood Fragrance specializes in discharging stagnant Qi and cold blockages in the chest and abdomen; its other uses are secondary. It is exceptionally effective and fast-acting when aided by orange peel, nutmeg, and fresh ginger. Yuan-su says: Wood Fragrance removes stagnant Qi from the Lungs. If treating Qi blockages or poor circulation in the Middle or Lower Burners <note>term: "Burners" (Sanjiao); the three functional divisions of the body's torso</note>, betel nut must be used as a guiding herb. Zhenheng says: When regulating Qi, use Wood Fragrance because its spicy flavor can cause Qi to rise, making it suitable for stagnant Qi that cannot circulate. However, if "Yin fire" is surging upward, Wood Fragrance will instead fuel the fire; in such cases, one should use Phellodendron and Anemarrhena, with only a tiny amount of Wood Fragrance as an assistant. Haogu says: The *Materia Medica* says it "governs Qi," meaning it supplements when Qi is insufficient. It also "clears blockages," meaning it breaks down all stagnant Qi. It "calms the fetus and strengthens the Spleen/Stomach," which is tonifying, yet it "removes abdominal masses," which is breaking down. Its functions are diverse. Zhang Jiegu only spoke of it regulating Qi, not tonifying it. Ji says: When used as an assistant to tonifying drugs, it tonifies; when used as the lead for purgative drugs, it purges. Shizhen says: Wood Fragrance is a medicine for the Qi portion of the Triple Burner. It can raise or lower all forms of Qi, as well as harmonize the protective and nutritive levels <note>original: "Wei" and "Ying"; the outer defense and inner nourishment systems of the body</note>.</gloss>

<meta>This page concludes the medicinal applications of Wood Fragrance (Muxiang, *Aucklandia costus*) and begins the entry for Spikenard (Gansongxiang, *Nardostachys jatamansi*). It focuses heavily on "Attached Formulas"—specific recipes for various ailments collected from historical medical texts.</meta>

All [stagnation in the upper torso] belongs to the Lungs; therefore, using this herb for Qi stagnation in the Upper Burner <note>The "Upper Burner" (shangjiao) refers to the chest area, including the heart and lungs.</note> follows the principle that when the "Metal" element is depressed, it must be drained. When the "Middle Qi" does not circulate, it belongs to the Spleen; thus, Wood Fragrance is suitable for Qi stagnation in the Middle Burner <note>The mid-torso, involving digestion.</note> because the Spleen and Stomach delight in aromatic fragrances. For Qi stagnation in the Large Intestine, which causes a heavy feeling in the rectum, or when Bladder Qi fails to transform, leading to urinary blockage or painful urination, or when Liver Qi is depressed, leading to pain—in all these cases of stagnation in the Lower Burner <note>The lower abdomen and pelvic region.</note>, this herb is appropriate. This follows the principle that when the "Wood" element is depressed, it must be reached and dispersed.

<gloss>Luo says: The *History of Sui* mentions Qidan Zigai, the Governor of Wuwei, who accompanied the Emperor into the territory of the Tuyuhun people. Because that region was filled with "miasma" <note>harmful environmental vapors</note>, Zigai presented Green Wood Fragrance to protect against the evils of fog and dew. Song says: The *Supplement to the Formulas of Proven Credit* records Zhang Zhongjing’s <note>the "Sage of Medicine" (150–219 CE)</note> Green Wood Fragrance Pill. It is primarily for "Yang fatigue" and various deficiencies. It uses Gleditsia pods, Green Wood Fragrance, "Six-Paths" bark, and Myrobalan fruit—twenty ounces of each. These are crushed and sifted, mixed with sugar into pills the size of a parasol tree seed. Take with wine on an empty stomach. After thirty-nine days, the effects are profound. When Lord Consort Guo used this, he replaced the sugar with white honey and added twelve ounces of Antelope horn. These ingredients are unlike typical ancient formulas, and though it is attributed to Zhongjing, it is unknown where this recipe originated.</gloss>

One new formula: For "Sudden Qi Stagnation" <gloss>Symptoms: eyes closed, unable to speak, appearing like a stroke. Grind Southern Wood Fragrance into a powder. Boil winter melon seeds into a soup. Take three to five mace (approx. 10–15g). If the patient has a cold, add bamboo sap and pour it down the throat. From *Formulas for Universal Relief*.</gloss>

### All Wandering Pains
For disharmony and pain caused by Qi: Grind Guangzhou Wood Fragrance in warm water to a thick juice. Mix into hot wine and drink. <gloss>From *Simple Formulas*.</gloss>

### Internal "Hooking" Abdominal Pain
<gloss>Equal parts Wood Fragrance and Frankincense, ground into powder. Place inside a fat pig’s large intestine, tie both ends tightly, and boil until extremely soft. Alternatively, for ear pain: take Wood Fragrance powder, dip the yellow heart of a scallion into fat, then into the powder, and insert deep into the ear. From the *Sage's Benevolent Formulas*.</gloss>

For pediatric abdominal pain: One mace of Wood Fragrance with Papaya juice. <gloss>From *General Records of Sage-like Assistance*. For "stagnant heat," mix with hot wine and take.</gloss>

### All Types of Dysentery
<gloss>Regardless of whether the patient is a man, woman, or child. Take a piece of Wood Fragrance one inch square and half an ounce of Coptis (Huanglian). Boil the two in half a liter of water until the water is gone. Remove the Coptis and the Wood Fragrance. Slice the Wood Fragrance, roast it dry, and grind it into powder. Divide into three doses. The first dose is taken with orange peel soup; the second with aged rice water; the third with licorice soup. This was passed down by Li Jingchun. A woman who was dying of chronic dysentery was allegedly given this formula by Guanyin <note>the Bodhisattva of Compassion</note> in a dream and was cured. From *Sun Bei's Secret Treasure Formulas*.</gloss>

### Blood in Stool (Intestinal Wind)
<gloss>Equal parts Wood Fragrance and Coptis ground into powder. Place inside a fat pig’s large intestine, tie both ends, and boil until very soft. Mash and form into pills the size of a parasol tree seed. Before meals, take thirty to ninety pills with salt water. From *Prescriptions for Universal Relief*. The "Fragrant Coptis Pill" formula can also be found under the "Coptis" entry.</gloss>

[Formula continuation]: Boil until soft, remove residue, and eat the intestine; or grind the ingredients into pills. <gloss>From *Liu Songshi’s Formulas for Preserving Longevity*.</gloss>

For stool resembling semen: Equal parts Wood Fragrance, Myrrh, and Angelica. Grind into powder. Mix with the natural juice of Jujube thorn hearts to form pills the size of a parasol tree seed. Take thirty to ninety pills with salt water before meals. <gloss>From *Prescriptions for Universal Relief*.</gloss>

### Pediatric Genital Swelling
<gloss>Caused by the collision of Wind-Heat and Damp-Qi in the Stomach Meridian (Yangming). The penis swells or shrinks without an obvious cause. This formula cures that specific meridian. Two and a half mace of Guangzhou Wood Fragrance and Bitter Orange (Zhike, bran-fried), and two mace of Licorice. Decoct in water and take. From *Zeng’s Pediatric Formulas*.</gloss>

### Pediatric Epidemics
For intense fever and headache: Six parts Wood Fragrance and three parts White Sandalwood. Grind into powder and take with fresh water. Also, mix the powder with warm water and apply to the fontanelle <note>the soft spot on a child's head</note> to effect a cure. <gloss>From the *Sage's Benevolent Formulas*.</gloss>

For epidemic skin spots <gloss>Red or black spots. Boil one ounce of Green Wood Fragrance in two liters of water until one liter remains. Drink. From *Arcane Essentials from the Imperial Library*.</gloss>

### All Carbuncles and Ulcers
<gloss>For sores, boils, pain, scrofula <note>swelling of lymph nodes</note>, malignant sores, and "dripping" scrofula. Also for wounds that have been infected by wind or cold after bursting. Mix the powder with oil and apply. For bites from venomous snakes or vipers: Boil any amount of Green Wood Fragrance in water and apply internally and externally. This also treats foul-smelling, non-healing discharge from any carbuncle or ulcer. A combination of Wood Fragrance, Coptis, and Areca nut is effective. From *Formulas from the Bureau of Harmonious Medicines*. The effects are beyond description. From *Pocket-Sized Formulas*. For damp, foul odors or sores under the armpits or in the groin: Soak Green Wood Fragrance in good vinegar, or mix the powder with a little Musk and apply to the area. From *Arcane Essentials from the Imperial Library*.</gloss>

### Toothache
Grind and apply to the gaps between teeth, then rinse with salt water.

# Spikenard
<note>original: "Gansongxiang"; *Nardostachys jatamansi*.</note>
<margin>Song Kaibao edition. Interpretation of name: Also called "Kumi." Shizhen says: It is produced in Songzhou, western Sichuan. Because its taste is sweet (gan), it is so named. The *Golden Light Sutra* calls it "Kumiduo."</margin>
<gloss>The *Materia Medica of the Kaibao Era* says: Spikenard comes from the mountains of Guzang and Liangzhou. It has fine leaves and creeping vines. It lives long and can be blended into various perfumes or used to scent clothing collars. It is said that it is now also found in various prefectures of Guizhou, Sichuan, and Liaozhou. It grows in clusters in the mountains and fields. The leaves are as fine as thatch grass, and the roots are extremely numerous and tangled.</gloss>

Collected in the eighth month and prepared with honey; used in a decoction for bathing, it makes the person’s body fragrant.

## Root
<gloss>Nature and Flavor: Sweet, warm, and non-toxic</gloss> <gloss>Hao-gu</gloss> <note>Wang Haogu, a physician of the Yuan Dynasty.</note> Primarily treats <term>Cholera (Huoluan)</term> <note>In historical Chinese medicine, this refers to sudden, violent vomiting and diarrhea rather than the specific bacterial disease known today.</note>, pain and fullness in the heart and abdomen, and helps "descend the Qi" <note>Moving rebellious energy downward to relieve bloating or hiccups.</note>. <gloss>Kaibao Materia Medica</gloss> The black-skinned wild ginger variety is excellent when paired with Aconite. <gloss>Zangqi</gloss> <note>Referring to the Tang dynasty pharmacologist Chen Zangqi.</note> Regulates the "Original Qi" (Yuanqi) and removes stagnation caused by "evil" environmental factors. <gloss>Hao-gu</gloss> For "Beriberi" <note>Jiaoqi, often referring to swelling, numbness, or pain in the legs.</note> where the knees are swollen and protruding.

Wash the area with a decoction of the herb. <gloss>Shizhen</gloss>
**Invention** <gloss>Shizhen says: Spikenard is fragrant and can open the stagnation of the Spleen. If a small amount is added to Spleen and Stomach medicines, it greatly awakens the Spleen Qi. Du Bao’s "Supplement to the Record of Forgotten Matters" says: Zen Master Shou was a brilliant physician who created</gloss> <insert>Attached Formula</insert> <gloss>New</gloss> a recipe for consumption (tuberculosis): boil six ounces of Spikenard into a powder. ## Sand Ginger
<gloss>Compendium of Materia Medica</gloss>
**Explanation of Names:** Mountain Spice (Shanla). <gloss>Compendium</gloss> Three-Nai. <gloss>Shizhen says: Sand Ginger is commonly mispronounced as "Three-Nai" or "Three-Lai" due to local dialects. Some say its original name was indeed Three-Nai.</gloss>
**Collected Explanations:** <gloss>Shizhen says: Sand Ginger grows in the Guangdong region. I suspect it is the same as what the ancients called "Lian Ginger." It grows three to four feet tall, the root is as large as a duck egg, and the leaves resemble garlic. A very long stalk emerges from the center, topped with a six-petaled flower that is red and white. The heart of the flower is yellow. It does not bear seeds. The herb grows in winter and dies in summer. They take the flowers and press them for oil to rub on the body to remove "wind-vapors." This description is quite similar to Sand Ginger, so I have included it here.

## Lian Ginger
<gloss>Supplement to Materia Medica</gloss>
**Explanation of Names:** Ginger Cluster (Jianghui). <gloss>Compendium</gloss> Rui-leng. <gloss>Pronounced Sui-leng.</gloss>

# Du Ruo
<gloss>Listed as a "Superior Grade" herb in the Classic; revised and incorporated from the Illustrated Classic</gloss> <note>The "Classic" refers to the Shennong Bencao Jing, the foundational text of Chinese herbology. "Superior Grade" herbs were considered life-prolonging and non-toxic.</note>

### Explanation of Names
Du Heng <gloss>Linked to the Classic and the Additional Records</gloss>; Ruo Zhi <gloss>Additional Records</gloss>; Heng Guang <gloss>Guangya Dictionary</gloss>; Mi Wu <gloss>Jiyun Dictionary; the pronunciation is noted but the definition is debated</gloss>; Mountain Ginger <gloss>Additional Records. The Records state its other names are White Lotus and Little White. Song says: This herb is called Du Heng, yet in the Ginger section there is already an entry for Du Heng—the "Earth Turnip" mentioned in the Erya. Du Ruo is actually what the Guangya calls "Chu Heng."</gloss>

They are of distinct categories, but ancient writers often used the names interchangeably. Thus, the *Nine Songs* mentions "gathering Du Ruo on the fragrant marshes," and the *Li Sao* mixes <gloss>Jiyun dictionary</gloss> Du Heng with fragrant Angelica. Commentators like Wang Yi did not distinguish between them, calling them all "fragrant herbs," which led to the names becoming muddled. Ancient formulas occasionally used it, but it is rarely used today, so few people recognize it. <gloss>Tao Hongjing, Additional Records</gloss> Zong <gloss>Jiyun dictionary</gloss> The *Records* state: Du Ruo grows in the rivers and marshes of Wuling and Yuanju. The roots are gathered in the second and eighth months and dried in the sun. <gloss>Tao Hongjing says: It is found everywhere today. The leaves resemble ginger with visible veins. The root resembles Galangal but is thinner; its flavor is spicy and fragrant, extremely similar to Lovage. Su Gong initially thought they were the same, but the leaves differ slightly. When the "Songs of Chu" mentions "The mountain dweller likes the fragrant Du Ruo," this is the plant.</gloss> <gloss>Kou Zongshi says: It is common in the Yangtze and Huai regions today. It grows in shady places. The sprouts look like Lian Ginger, and the root resembles Galangal, but it lacks a spicy flavor. Tao's description of a spicy root is the true Du Ruo.</gloss> <gloss>Ma Baosheng says: The sprouts look like Mountain Ginger. The flowers are yellow and the seeds are red, as thick as chopsticks, resembling Cardamom inside. The specimens from Lingnan and Xiazhou are best.</gloss> Fan Zi’s *Jiran* says: Du Heng and Du Ruo come from Nanjun and Hanzhong; the larger ones are superior. <gloss>Su Song says:</gloss> There is a type of Mountain Ginger in Hengzhou with stems and leaves like ginger. It has purple flowers but bears no fruit. The roots are gathered in the eighth month for medicine. <gloss>Li Shizhen says: No one recognizes Du Ruo anymore, but it is still found in the mountains of the Chu region. Mountain folk call it "Good Ginger." Its root looks like ginger and tastes spicy. Zhen Quan’s notes on Cardamom mentioned "Ranger Ginger," and the "Mountain Ginger" described in the outer categories of the Illustrated Classic of the Lingnan region are both this plant. Sometimes the large ones are called Galangal and the small ones Du Ruo.</gloss> <gloss>Li Taiji says:</gloss> When using it, do not use "Duck-Peck Herb" root, which looks similar but has different effects. After gathering the roots, scrape off the yellow-red skin with a knife, chop finely, and place in a triple-layered silk bag. Soak in honey overnight before use. At that time, it was sent as a tribute from Xiazhou. <gloss>Tao Hongjing</gloss>

### Root
<gloss>Nature and Flavor:</gloss> Acrid, mild, and non-toxic. <gloss>Xu Zhicai says: It works well when paired with Magnolia and Wild Ginger; it is incompatible with Bupleurum. Song says: Mountain Ginger is acrid and neutral, with a slight toxicity.</gloss>

<gloss>Healing Properties:</gloss> Treats "rebellious" energy in the chest and ribs, damp-wind, and "wind-stroke" that enters the brain, causing swelling of the head, pain, and excessive tearing. Taken over time, it benefits the <term>Essence (Jing)</term> <note>The vital physical reserve of the body.</note>, brightens the eyes, lightens the body, and prevents forgetfulness. <gloss>Classic</gloss> Treats fainting, redness and pain of the eyes, and removes bad breath. <gloss>Additional Records</gloss> Mountain Ginger, with the skin removed, clears wind-heat from the skin. It can be used in a bath. It also treats sudden cold, "rebellious cold" in the stomach, cholera, and abdominal pain. <gloss>Medicinal Nature; Cai Fameng; Shizhen says: Du Ruo is a "Superior Grade" herb of the Divine Farmer (Shennong). It is a vital medicine for the Kidney and Bladder meridians, yet the world does not know how to use it. What a pity!</gloss>

# Mountain Ginger
<gloss>Treatise on Medicinal Nature</gloss>

### Explanation of Names
Also named "Beautiful Herb." <gloss>Tao Hongjing says: People of the East call it Mountain Ginger; people of the South call it Beautiful Herb. Shizhen says: This is a different plant from the Mountain Ginger mentioned under Du Ruo; they share a name but are different things.</gloss>

Zhen Quan says: The roots and sprouts of Mountain Ginger are like ginger but larger, with a scent like camphor wood. People in the south eat it. There is also a "Bullet Ginger" which is yellow, firm, and very spicy; it breaks stagnant blood and Qi, and its strength is much greater than this ginger. <gloss>Su Song says: Mountain Ginger comes from Jiuzhen and Jiaozhi; it is now found in Fujian and Guangdong. Liu Xun’s</gloss> *Strange Records from the South* says: The stems and leaves are all like ginger, but the root is inedible. The flowers are similar to Cardamom but smaller. The flowers grow among the leaves in spikes like grains of wheat, and are a tender red. Southerners take the unopened buds, calling them "fetal flowers," and preserve them in salt water or sweet dregs. By winter, they turn an amber color, spicy and fragrant. They are unsurpassed when used with sliced raw fish (sashimi). They also boil the salt-cured, dried ones into a tea to treat "cold energy," which is very effective. <gloss>Li Shizhen says: Mountain Ginger grows in the south. The leaves</gloss> resemble ginger but are red and very spicy. The seeds look like Grass Cardamom, and the root is like Du Ruo or Galangal. People today use the seeds as "Flower-Grass Cardamom," but their aroma is extremely pungent.

# Lesser Galanga
<gloss>Referenced and Corrected</gloss> <gloss>Incorporated from the Kaibao Pharmacopoeia</gloss>

### Explanation of Names
<gloss>Barbarian Ginger</gloss> <gloss>From the Compendium</gloss>; the seed is called <gloss>Red Cardamom</gloss>.

> <gloss>Shizhen says:</gloss> It is produced in Gaoliang Commandery <note>Modern-day Guangdong province</note>. The roots are harvested in the second and third months; their form and scent resemble Du Ruo <note>Pollia japonica</note>, but the leaves are like Mountain Ginger. <gloss>Su says:</gloss> Those from the southern coastal regions are large, hollow, and soft. Those grown east of the river are thin, purple, and not very acrid. Essentially, they are the same. People today call the thin ones Du Ruo and the large ones Galanga, but this is incorrect. <gloss>Song says:</gloss> It is now found in various southern prefectures as well as the regions of Qian and Shu. Its leaves resemble reeds, and its flowers grow in tassels of delicate purple. The young leaves emerge curled with a slight reddish tint. These tender parts are often pickled in salt to be eaten as a vegetable; they do not lose their purple color, appearing much like Mountain Ginger flowers. <gloss>Tao says:</gloss> Red Cardamom grows in the valleys of the South Seas and is the seed of the Galanga. Its stalks are like reeds and its leaves like Mountain Ginger. The flowers form tassels, and the young leaves emerge curled and reddish. When pickled, the color remains vibrant. Some use hibiscus flowers to dye them a deeper red to enhance their effect in sobering one from alcohol—this is its primary use. <gloss>Shizhen says:</gloss> According to the *Forest of Pearls in the Dharma Garden* and the *Records of the Great Cinnamon Sea*, Red Cardamom begins to sprout after the spring. When the flowers first open, a single stalk emerges encased in a large sheath. A single tassel holds dozens of buds, pale red and as fresh as peach or apricot blossoms. Its petals droop like the crest of a bird. <gloss>Citing Li Tai</gloss>. <gloss>Shizhen says:</gloss> Both Galanga and Red Cardamom should be stir-fried before being used in medicine. Some varieties look like fire-red jewelry or intricately cut silk. Each blossom has a center with two petals, which people compare to "intertwined branches" <note>A symbol of lovers or inseparable pairs</note>. Its seeds are similar to Grass Cardamom but smaller. <insert>Supplement</insert> Some practitioners stir-fry the herb with ginger, Evodia fruits, and "east-wall soil" <note>Soil taken from the eastern side of an old wall, believed to have specific energetic properties</note> before incorporating it into formulas.

### The Root
<gloss>Nature and Flavor</gloss> Acrid, greatly warm, and non-toxic. <gloss>Zhi says:</gloss> Acrid, bitter, greatly hot, and non-toxic. <gloss>Zhang Yuan-su says:</gloss> Acrid and hot; it is pure Yang and has a "floating" quality. It enters the Spleen and Stomach meridians.

### Main Indications
Sudden cold, cold-reversal in the stomach, cholera-like disorders, and abdominal pain. <gloss>From the Additional Records</gloss>. It descends Qi. <gloss>Meng Shen</gloss>. It neutralizes alcohol poisoning, stops <unclear>vomiting</unclear>, treats "wind" disorders, breaks stagnant Qi, and heals long-standing cold pain within the abdomen, cold-wind, and cold-numbness. <gloss>Zhen Quan</gloss>. It treats muscle cramps, diarrhea, acid reflux, <unclear>vomiting</unclear>, sneezing, and aids digestion. <gloss>Daming</gloss>. It expels cold-dampness and nausea where one spits up clear water; it chases away cold-weakness. To treat a "sour" stomach or bad breath caused by summer heat, grind it with Grass Cardamom into a powder and decoct it as a drink. <gloss>Su Song</gloss>. It builds the Spleen and Stomach, eases the midsection, breaks up stubborn cold masses, removes obstructions, and treats damp-fever or seasonal illnesses that cause <unclear>distress</unclear>. <gloss>Yi Lao</gloss>. A formula for "Heart-Mouth Pain" <note>Epigastric or stomach pain</note> states: Whenever a man or woman feels a localized pain at the "heart-mouth," it is due to stagnation in the stomach or parasites. It is often triggered by anger or exposure to cold, potentially becoming a lifelong affliction. The common saying that this is "heart-Qi pain" is incorrect. Use Galanga washed seven times in wine and roasted, and Cyperus <note>Xiang Fu</note> washed seven times in vinegar and roasted. If the illness was caused by cold, use two parts Galanga to one part Cyperus. If caused by anger, use two parts Cyperus to one part Galanga. If caused by both, use equal parts. Take with rice water and <insert>Appended Formula</insert> a spoonful of ginger juice and a pinch of salt for immediate relief. Han Feixia’s *Medical Continuity* also praises its efficacy.

# Compendium of Materia Medica, Volume 34: Herbs

For those suffering from sudden cholera-like disorders <note>A term for acute vomiting and diarrhea</note>, take one tael <note>approximately 37 grams</note> of **Lesser Galanga** and boil it in three pints of water until one pint remains. Drink it all at once, and the symptoms will dissipate. 

For cold pain in the heart and spleen, use the **Lesser Galanga Pill**: take four taels of Lesser Galanga and slice it into four portions. 
1. Fry one portion with half a handful of aged granary rice until yellow, then discard the rice. 
2. Fry one portion with half a tael of aged wall-plaster soil until yellow, then discard the soil. 
3. Fry one portion with thirty-four <term>Croton seeds<note>A potent and toxic purgative used here to process the herb</note></term> until yellow, then discard the seeds. 
4. Soak the final portion in wine overnight, then fry it with <term>Blister beetles<note>Mylabris; a toxic insect used in controlled medicinal processing</note></term>. 

If Lesser Galanga is unavailable, one may substitute one tael of **Red Ginger** simmered in clear wine; although not as effective as Lesser Galanga, it is still very successful. <gloss>For cold pain of the heart and spleen</gloss> Mix the processed herbs with a paste made of rice and wine <gloss>to nourish the spleen and warm the stomach</gloss>. This formula removes cold, eliminates fatigue, expands the chest, and descends rebellious Qi. Form into pills the size of a parasol tree seed. Take fifty to ninety pills per dose on an empty stomach with ginger decoction. ○ The *Classified Collection of Proven Formulas* suggests using three mace <note>approx. 11 grams</note> of Lesser Galanga and six mace of **Ginger Resin**, ground into powder. Take three mace per dose mixed with vinegar soup <gloss>to treat heart and spleen pain and all types of food stagnation</gloss>. 

Alternatively, use equal parts of Lesser Galanga and **Long Pepper**, roasted and ground into powder. Mix with flour paste into pills the size of parasol tree seeds. <gloss>For deficiency-cold type malaria with more chills than fever and loss of appetite, use one tael each of Lesser Galanga (fried in sesame oil) and Prepared Ginger (roasted). Take five mace of the powder mixed with pig’s gall.</gloss> Take fifteen to ninety pills after meals with orange peel decoction. Pregnant women must not take this. <gloss>The *Prescriptions of the Imperial Pharmacy* suggests mixing fifteen pills with juice into a paste, taken with hot wine when the fever begins. Mixing the pills directly with gall juice is also excellent. Academician Wu Ke recorded that</gloss> during the Ding-You year of the Zhihe era, while living in Quanjiao County, a great malaria epidemic broke out. This remedy saved hundreds of people. Zhang Daheng was so ill from this that he wished to resign his post, but he was cured after taking it. Generally, the use of pig's gall acts as a guide for the two types of ginger, entering the gallbladder to remove cold and drying the "dampness" of the spleen and stomach. By balancing cold and heat, the Yin and Yang are reconciled, which produces the healing effect. Another formula uses two types of ginger—half raw and half roasted—chewed with two mace of roasted **Pangolin scales** <note>The use of pangolin is now prohibited in modern medicine for conservation</note> ground into powder, taken with wine in which a pig’s kidney was boiled. This is from *Zhu’s Collection of Proven Formulas*. <gloss>For malaria in women</gloss> that developed from a cold-induced injury: use three mace of sliced Lesser Galanga soaked overnight in betel nut and gall juice, then fry with soil from an eastern wall until black; discard the soil. <gloss>For sudden red and painful eyes</gloss>: blow powdered Lesser Galanga into the nose through a tube to induce sneezing. <gloss>For "Wind" toothache</gloss>: take fifteen pieces of fatty <term>Galls of Chinese Sumac<note>Used for their astringent properties</note></term>, grind them together, and use three mace per dose in a decoction. Drink it hot when the pain starts; it is miraculous. <gloss>From the *Yonglei Collection*</gloss>. For nosebleeds, the powder will stop the bleeding immediately. <gloss>From *Old Man Tan’s Tested Formulas*</gloss>. 

For severe toothache, take a three-inch piece of Lesser Galanga and one whole **Silkworm Moth**, grind them together and apply to the area. Spit out the saliva and rinse the mouth with salt water. This is a proven remedy for <gloss>various foul odors of the nose and sinus pain</gloss>. Grind raw Lesser Galanga and chew it. <gloss>From the *Universal Relief Formulas*</gloss>. Ji Ming suffered from this and found it truly effective. <gloss>From Wang Qiu’s *One Hundred and One Selected Formulas*</gloss>.

### Red Cardamom <gloss>From the Kaibao Pharmacopoeia</gloss>
<gloss>Nature and Flavor</gloss> Acrid, warm, and non-toxic. <gloss>Chen Shizuo says: It is bitter and acrid; eating too much makes the tongue feel coarse and destroys the appetite. Shizhen says: It is acrid and hot, belonging to the Yang principle. It is light and "floating" in nature, entering the Hand and Foot Greater Yin meridians (Lung and Spleen). The *Sheng-Sheng Compendium* says it can stir the "ministerial fire," damaging the eyes and causing blood loss; it should not be used casually in food.</gloss>

<gloss>Main Indications</gloss> Chronic diarrhea due to intestinal deficiency, excruciating pain in the heart and abdomen, cholera-like vomiting and diarrhea, and sour regurgitation. It neutralizes
<column-break/>
alcohol poisoning, aids digestion, and treats cold-related abdominal pain, nausea, bloating, vomiting, and dysentery. <gloss>Zhen Quan says: It treats cholera, abdominal pain, stomach reflux, deficiency-type malaria, and cold bloating. It dries dampness and disperses cold. ### Grass Cardamom <gloss>From the Miscellaneous Records; Superior Class</gloss> <gloss>Corrected</gloss> <gloss>Moved here from the Fruit Section</gloss> <gloss>Explanation of Names</gloss> Grass Cardamom <gloss>From the Kaibao Pharmacopoeia; also called Lou-Lan Cardamom, Jia Han’s Grass Fruit</gloss>.

<gloss>Guo Tui’s General Treatises states it is also called Doukou or Grass Cardamom. This distinguishes it from Nutmeg (Meat Cardamom). If categorized as a fruit, its flavor is not harmonious. Previous compilers put it in the Fruit Section without understanding its meaning. Its nature is hot, though it reaches the capital city with a slightly bitter and not very pleasant taste. When dried, it is pale purple and can neutralize alcohol</gloss> poisoning, which is why it was used with fruit and wine. Shizhen says: According to Yang Xiong’s *Dialects*, things that are lush and abundant are called "Kou." The name Cardamom may derive from this. Its shape resembles a bean [Dou]. The *Records of Southern Strange Things* calls it "Lou-Kou," which is likely a southern <gloss>Collected Records</gloss> says: Cardamom grows in the Southern Seas. 
transliteration without a formal character. Today, though not used exclusively as a fruit, it is still used in tea and drinks and is still called Grass Fruit. The *Sutra of Golden Light* lists it as one of thirty-two aromatic medicines, calling it "Su-Xi-Mi-Luo-Xi" <note>A transliteration of a Sanskrit name</note>. <gloss>The Old Materia Medica</gloss> says the sprouts resemble Mountain Ginger, with yellow and white flowers. The sprouts, roots, and seeds resemble **Japanese Galanga** [Du Ruo]. The *Lingnan Records* states: Grass Cardamom is found everywhere in the Lingnan region. Its sprouts resemble reeds, its leaves resemble Mountain Ginger or Japanese Galanga, and its roots resemble Lesser Galanga. In the second month, it blossoms in spikes from the base of the stem. The young leaves are curled. When it first blooms, it looks like a hibiscus flower, slightly red. The tip of the spike is deep-colored, and as the leaves widen, the flowers emerge and the color fades, sometimes becoming yellowish-white. Southerners often powder the flowers to eat as a delicacy; they especially value the tender ones, which are preserved in salt along with the spikes.

# Compendium of Materia Medica, Volume 14

...When making syrup, it does not disperse. One may also soak it with hibiscus flowers if a red color is desired. Its fruit resembles the longan fruit but is more pointed; the skin lacks scales, and the seeds inside are arranged like pomegranate segments. It is harvested in the summer months when ripe and dried in the sun. The roots and sprouts have a faint scent of camphor.

**Grass Cardamom** <note>original: "Dou Kou" (荳蔻)</note> is pungent and fragrant. **Xun** says: "Grass Cardamom grows in Jiaozhi <note>Modern-day Northern Vietnam</note>. Its root resembles ginger. The outer husk is small and thick, with seeds like pomegranate that are pungent and fragrant. The leaves resemble the flowering orchid but are smaller. In the third month, the leaves are harvested, finely shredded, pickled, and dried for use. The taste is primarily bitter with a sweet aftertaste." **Li Shizhen** says: "Although Grass Cardamom and 'Grass Fruit' <note>Amomum tsao-ko</note> are essentially the same plant, there are slight differences. Currently, Jianning Prefecture produces a cardamom as large as a longan but slightly elongated. Its skin is yellowish-white, thin, and sharply ridged. The kernels are as large as those of Amomum <term>Shrinking Sand<note>Xisharen/Amomum villosum; another type of cardamom</term></note> and possess a harmonious, pungent fragrance. The cardamom produced in Yunnan and Guangdong is as long and large as a <term>Haritaki<note>Chebulic Myrobalan fruit</note></term>; its skin is thick with dense ridges, and its seeds are coarse with a pungent, foul odor, much like the scent of <term>Blister Beetles<note>Mylabris; a toxic beetle used in medicine</note></term>. Today, people use it in steeped teas and as a common cooking ingredient. People of the South take the fresh Grass Cardamom and pickle it in plum juice and salt until it turns red, then sun-dry it; this is known as 'Red Salt Grass Fruit.' The small, newly-formed fruits are called 'Parrot Tongues.' During the Yuan Dynasty, these were considered top-tier offerings for the imperial kitchen. Southerners also harvest and use them." <gloss>Processing</gloss> says: "Whenever using it, one must remove the stem and take only the inner seeds and skin. Some use the fruit of the Fire Waxberry as a fake substitute for Grass Cardamom; its shape is round and coarse, and its scent is violently pungent and unharmonious. Many people use it mistakenly, or claim it is the fruit of Mountain Ginger; one must distinguish them carefully." <gloss>Method</gloss> Use rice to stir-fry it slowly on an iron plate until the rice turns slightly yellowish-black. Then discard the rice and take the Grass Cardamom seeds and crush them for use.

**Li Shizhen** says: "Today, people simply wrap it in dough and roast it in the fire. Once roasted, the skin is removed and the seed is used."

## White Cardamom <gloss>Song Dynasty Kaibao Era Materia Medica</gloss>
<gloss>Explanatory Name</gloss> Duo-gu <note>literally "Many Bones"</note>. <gloss>Qi Lin</gloss>. <gloss>Zangqi says:</gloss> White Cardamom originates from the kingdom of Gaguoluo <note>likely a region in India or Southeast Asia</note>, where it is called "Duo-gu." The plant's form resembles a plantain; its leaves are like those of the Wild Ginger, eight to nine feet long, smooth, and glossy. It does not wither in winter or summer. The flowers are pale yellow. The seeds grow in clusters like grapes; they are slightly green when they first appear and turn white when ripe. They are harvested in the seventh month. <gloss>Su Song says:</gloss> Nowadays it is also found in Guangzhou and Yizhou, though it is not as high in quality as those brought by foreign ships. **Li Shizhen says:** The kernels of White Cardamom resemble those of "Shrinking Sand" Amomum. When used in medicine, the skin is removed and the seeds are stir-fried.

<gloss>Nature and Flavor</gloss> Pungent, greatly warming, non-toxic. <gloss>Wang Haogu says:</gloss> Highly pungent and hot. Its flavor is thin while its Qi is thick; it is light and clear, allowing it to ascend. It belongs to the Yang category and has a floating quality. It enters the Hand Initial Yin <term>Lung Meridian</term>. **Main Indications:** Accumulation of cold Qi; it stops vomiting, nausea, and regurgitation. It aids digestion and descends Qi. <gloss>Kaibao Materia Medica</gloss>: Stagnant Qi within the joints; it relaxes the intestines and encourages appetite. It removes white ocular membranes. <gloss>Li Shizhen</gloss>: Supplements the Lungs.

<gloss>Explanations</gloss> <gloss>Zhu Zhenheng says:</gloss> Ancient formulas for treating a cold stomach where the smell of food triggers vomiting, as well as the "Six Ingredients Decoction for Vomiting," both utilize White Cardamom. Generally, the stomach governs Qi; this herb benefits the stomach, regulates the <term>Original Qi</term>, and consolidates "escaping" Qi. <gloss>Wang Haogu says:</gloss> It warms the center and removes chronic cold, treats malarial phlegm and alternating chills and fever, and resolves alcohol poisoning. <gloss>Li Shizhen says:</gloss> The Qi and flavor of White Cardamom are both thin. Its use is five-fold: First, it specifically enters the Lung meridian. Second, it disperses stagnant Qi in the chest. Third, it removes abdominal pain caused by exposure to cold. Fourth, it warms the Spleen and Stomach. Fifth, it treats sudden outbreaks of red eyes. To remove red veins in the inner corner of the eye <note>near the Greater Canthus</note> where the Sun Meridian passes, use a small amount for its powerful effect. <gloss>Li Shizhen says:</gloss> Yang Shiying noted that White Cardamom treats Spleen-deficiency malaria and vomiting with chills and fever. It can "dissolve and grind" <note>aid digestion and break down masses</note>, causing the <term>Triple Burner</term> and the <term>Nutritive and Defensive Systems</term> to circulate once more, after which all symptoms naturally subside.
