## Shrinking Sand Amomum <gloss>Song Dynasty Kaibao Era Materia Medica</gloss>
<gloss>Explanatory Name</gloss> Suo-sha <note>Original name for Amomum villosum, often called Sha Ren</note>. <gloss>Li Shizhen says:</gloss> The meaning of the name is unclear. The white lotus root found beneath the stalk is called "Mi" <note>蔤</note>, implying something "hidden" or "dense." Since this fruit is found near the root and the kernels are hidden within a shell, it perhaps shares this meaning and name. <gloss>Li Shizhen says:</gloss> This plant grows in the Western Seas, among the Western Rong tribes, and in various Persian kingdoms. It mostly arrives via the eastern routes. <gloss>Ma Zhi says:</gloss> It grows in Nanyue <note>Southern China/Vietnam</note>. Currently, it is only found among the mountains and marshes of Lingnan. The sprouts and stalks resemble Lesser Galanga, four to five feet high. Leaves are eight to nine inches long and about half an inch wide. In the third or fourth month, it flowers near the root. In the fifth or sixth month, it fruits, with fifty to seventy fruits forming a single spike. It looks like "Increase-of-Wisdom" fruit <note>Alpinia oxyphylla</note> but is round. The skin is purple-black, thick, wrinkled, and covered in tiny thorns. Inside the shell are fine prickles of yellow-red color. Between the skin is a cluster of seeds divided into eight sections, containing about forty grains like large millet. They are blackish on the outside, white inside, and fragrant like White Cardamom. Harvested in the seventh month.

# The Kernel
**Nature and Flavor:** Pungent, warm, and non-toxic. <gloss>The physician Zhen says: Pungent and bitter. Zangqi says: Sour. He says: Pungent, salty, and neutral. It pairs well with Haritaki fruit, Nutmeg, and Siberian Elm. Haogu says: Its flavor is pungent and its nature is warm; it belongs to the Yang <note>active, warming</note> category and has a "floating" <note>rising/outward</note> quality. It enters the seven channels of the Hand and Foot Greater Yin, Yang Brightness, Greater Yang, and Foot Lesser Yin <note>the Lung, Spleen, Stomach, Large Intestine, Small Intestine, Bladder, and Kidney meridians</note>. When paired with White Sandalwood and Nutmeg, it acts as a "messenger" to the Lungs. Paired with Ginseng and Black Cardamom, it acts as a messenger to the Spleen. Paired with Phellodendron bark and Poria mushroom, it acts as a messenger to the Kidneys. It also enters the Large and Small Intestines when paired with Halloysite.</gloss>

## Main Indications
Treats "deficiency labor" <note>chronic exhaustion</note>, cold-type diarrhea, and chronic indigestion. It resolves red and white dysentery, alleviates "hollow pain" in the abdomen, and descends Qi <note>reverses the improper upward flow of energy</note>. <gloss>From the Song Dynasty "Kaibao" era</gloss>. It is the primary treatment for pain caused by "cold Qi" and stops persistent dysentery. It also stabilizes the fetus <note>prevents miscarriage</note>. <gloss>According to Yang Shiying</gloss>. It treats stagnation of Qi in the Spleen and Stomach that refuses to disperse. <gloss>According to Zhang Yuansu</gloss>. It supplements the Lungs, awakens the Spleen, nourishes the Stomach, benefits the Kidneys, regulates the "Original Qi" <note>the body's foundational vitality</note>, clears stagnant energy, and disperses "cold fluids" <note>excessive internal dampness/mucus</note>.

## Pathogenic Factors
<gloss>Zangqi says:</gloss> It treats all forms of Qi stagnation, "sudden turmoil" <note>acute vomiting and diarrhea, often called cholera-like disorders</note>, and muscle cramps. It can also enhance the aroma and flavor of wine. <gloss>According to the "Daming Materia Medica":</gloss> It harmonizes the "Middle Burner" <note>the digestive center</note>, moves Qi, stops pain, and stabilizes the fetus. <gloss>According to the "Materia Medica":</gloss> It treats abdominal distention, vomiting, and uterine bleeding in women. It removes "floating heat" from the throat, mouth, and teeth, and it is said to have the power to "melt" swallowed copper, iron, or bones. <gloss>Shizhen notes: According to Han Yanzhi's "Manual of Oranges," the Kidneys dislike dryness and should be moistened with pungent flavors. The pungency of the Amomum Seed moistens Kidney-dryness. It is also said that Amomum belongs to the Earth element <note>associated with the Spleen</note> and is a primary herb for "awakening" the Spleen. It leads other medicines back to the "Cinnabar Field" <note>Dantian, the energy center below the navel</note>. Because of its fragrance and ability to disperse and harmonize the "flushing Qi" of the five internal organs—much like Earth provides the harmonizing Qi for Heaven and Earth—it is used alongside Rehmannia root in Kidney-tonifying formulas to ensure the medicine reaches the lower parts of the body. Furthermore, it is used to dissolve bones and in the refining of minerals by alchemists; however, the exact mechanism of how its nature masters these substances remains unknown.</gloss>

# Sharpleaf Galangal Fruit <gloss>From the Kaibao Era of the Song Dynasty</gloss>

【**Explanation of Names**】 <gloss>Li Shizhen says: The Spleen governs the intellect. This substance is named "Increasing Wisdom" because it benefits the Spleen and Stomach. It shares the same naming logic as the Longan <note>which is also called "Increasing Wisdom" in some texts</note>. According to the *Records of the Southern Regions*, Sharpleaf Galangal is produced in Hainan. Both the flowers and fruits grow in long spikes divided into three sections. Farmers observe the top, middle, and bottom sections to predict the success of early, middle, and late rice harvests. If the harvest will be great, all sections are full of fruit; if the harvest will fail, they are empty. It is rare for all three sections to ripen simultaneously. In medicine, however, it only treats fluid issues and does not actually increase one's intellect. Perhaps it earned this name because it "knows" <note>the word for "wisdom" and "to know" are related in Chinese</note> the quality of the coming year?</gloss>

【**Collected Explanations**】 <gloss>Ma Zhi says: Sharpleaf Galangal comes from the Kunlun regions and Vietnam. Today, it is frequently found in the southern provinces. Gu Wei’s *Records of Guangzhou* states: Its leaves resemble those of the Ginger Lily and grow over ten feet long. Small shoots grow atop the roots, about eight or nine inches high. It has no flower calyx. The stems are like bamboo arrows. The seeds emerge from the center of the plant, with about ten seeds per branch, growing in clusters. They are the size of small dates, with black kernels and white skin. Those with smaller kernels are superior. Holding them in the mouth removes foul odors and excess saliva. Some people split the fruit into four, remove the seeds, and boil the outer skin with honey to eat as a rice dumpling <note>Zongzi</note>. They have a pungent taste. Lu Xun <note>a rebel leader</note> of the Jin Dynasty once sent these dumplings to Liu Yu <note>the future Emperor Wu of Song</note>. Chen Cangqi says: The seeds resemble Forsythia fruits that have not yet opened. The leaves, flowers, and roots are no different from those of the Greater Galangal, though the seeds are smaller. Li Shizhen says: According to Ji Han’s *Flora of the Southern Regions*, it flowers in the second month and the fruit ripens in the fifth or sixth month. The fruit is shaped like the tip of a calligraphy brush, pointed at both ends, and about an inch long. Though used as a spice for wine and food, it can also be dried or made into rice dumplings. Based on this, Gu Wei’s claim that it has no flowers is incorrect. Today’s Sharpleaf Galangal is shaped like a date pit, but the skin and kernel look like those of the Grass Cardamom.</gloss>

## Flavor and Nature of the Kernel <gloss>Pungent, warm, and non-toxic</gloss>

**Main Indications** <gloss>Treats nocturnal emissions and "deficiency leakage" <note>involuntary discharge</note>, urinary dribbling, and stabilizes Qi to calm the spirit. It supplements deficiencies, benefits the Triple Burner <note>the TCM organ system governing fluid and energy metabolism</note>, and regulates all forms of Qi. For those who urinate frequently at night: take twenty crushed seeds, decoct them with salt, and drink. This has miraculous effects. It also treats "guest cold" <note>external cold pathogens</note> invading the Stomach, harmonizes the center, benefits the Qi, and stops excessive salivation.</gloss> <gloss>Li Shizhen says: It benefits the Spleen and Stomach, regulates the Original Qi <note>Yuan Qi</note>, and tonifies Kidney deficiency and urinary leakage.</gloss>

**Insights** <gloss>Wang Haogu says: Sharpleaf Galangal is primarily a Spleen medicine. It governs the "Ministerial Fire" <note>the vital energy associated with the Kidneys and Liver</note>. When used in the "Gathered Fragrance Pill," it enters the Lung channel; in "Four Gentlemen Decoction," it enters the Spleen; in "Great Wind Marrow Pill," it enters the Kidneys. This reflects the relationship between the "mother" and "child" organs. It should be used alongside tonifying medicines but should not be taken in excessive amounts. Li Shizhen says: It is highly pungent, a medicine that activates Yang and recedes Yin. It is suitable for those with weak Qi in the Triple Burner and the "Gate of Vitality" <note>Mingmen/Kidneys</note>. Yang Shiying’s *Direct Guide to Formulas* says: The Heart is the mother of the Spleen. Promoting appetite is not just about harmonizing the Spleen; because Fire <note>Heart</note> produces Earth <note>Spleen</note>, one should use Heart-tonifying medicines to enter the Spleen and Stomach. Thus, the ancients often used Sharpleaf Galangal in appetite-stimulating formulas; it is like adding a spark of fire to the soil. Furthermore, Hong Mai’s *Record of the Listener* tells of a scholar named Lu Yun who suddenly vomited blood uncontrollably. He was trembling, manic, and staring blankly. At midnight, he tried to run out the door. This continued for two nights, and no medicine worked. In a dream, the Bodhisattva Guanyin gave him a formula, promising it would uproot the disease. He awoke, prepared the medicine, and was indeed cured. The formula used one tael <note>approx. 37g</note> of Sharpleaf Galangal kernels and two qian <note>approx. 7.5g</note> of ground Cinnabar.</gloss>

**Appended Formulas** <gloss>8 New Formulas</gloss>

**Frequent Urination** <gloss>Caused by insufficient Qi in the bladder. Take Sharpleaf Galangal from Leizhou, fry it with salt, then remove the salt. Mix with equal parts Lindera root (Wuyao). Grind into a powder. Use wine-boiled Yam powder as a paste to form pills the size of a firmiana seed. Take 70 pills on an empty stomach with salted water. Grind into powder. Take three qian with warm water, or decoct one dose in water. <insert>From the Yonglei Qin Formulas</insert></gloss>

# Long Pepper <gloss>From the Kaibao Era of the Song Dynasty</gloss>

<gloss>Explanation of Names</gloss> Long Pepper <gloss>Li Shizhen says</gloss>: The name "Bibo" should properly be written as "Biba." It appears in the *Records of Southern Flora* <note>Nanfang Caomu Zhuang</note> and is a foreign term. Chen Cangqi’s *Materia Medica* writes it as "Bibo," a name transmitted from the south. The *Great <insert>Leaf</insert> Collection <insert>Essentials</insert>* states that Long Pepper grows in the Kingdom of Persia. The *Encyclopedia of <gloss>Gems</gloss>* says its leaves resemble those of the Betel Pepper <term>Piper betle</term>. Its seeds are recorded in the *Statutes of the Ming Dynasty* as "Bibo." Furthermore, Duan Chengshi’s *Miscellaneous Morsels from Youyang* notes that the Kingdom of Magadha <note>ancient India</note> calls it *Pippali*, while the Kingdom of Fulin <note>the Byzantine Empire</note> calls it *Aliheduo*.

<gloss>Collected Explanations</gloss> <gloss>Su Gong says</gloss>: Long Pepper grows in the Kingdom of Persia. Its vine-like shoots are extremely thin. Its taste is even more pungent than the Betel Pepper. People from the western regions bring it to use as a flavoring in food. <gloss>Chen Cangqi says</gloss>: Its root is named *Bibo*. It resembles the root of the Thorowax <term>Bupleurum</term> but is black and hard. <gloss>Su Song says</gloss>: Today it is found specifically in the Lingnan region <note>Southern China</note>, mostly growing within bamboo groves. In the first month of the lunar year, the shoots emerge and form stems two to four feet high. They are very straight, resembling a spinning wheel spindle, green and round like the Castor Bean plant. The leaves are two to three inches wide, resembling Mulberry leaves, with a glossy and thick surface. In the third month, white flowers bloom, about the size of a pinky finger and one to two inches long. The fruit is bluish-black and resembles a mulberry but longer. In the ninth month, the "rice" <note>seeds/fruit spikes</note> are harvested and dried in the sun. Southerners love its pungent fragrance and sometimes eat the raw leaves as a vegetable. There is also a variety brought by ships <note>imported</note> which is even more fragrant and pungent. <gloss>Li Shizhen says</gloss>: Duan Chengshi claimed that the seeds of the Green Province Ledebouriella <gloss>powdered</gloss> were Long Pepper, and that when using it, one should remove the root and use only the head after soaking it in vinegar overnight. This is incorrect. The aroma and taste of Long Pepper are exactly like black pepper, and its shape is one to two inches long. The seeds of Ledebouriella <term>Fangfeng</term> are round and large like Coriander seeds; they do not resemble each other at all. Xu <insert>appended</insert> the <insert>recipe</insert>: Toast until dry, then use a knife to scrape off the skin and husk until clean before use.

<gloss>Properties</gloss> Pungent, Greatly Warm, Non-toxic. <gloss>Li Shizhen says</gloss>: Its nature is hot and its taste is pungent; it is "Yang" and "Floating" <note>tends to move upward and outward in the body</note>. It enters the Hand and Foot Yangming channels <note>the Large Intestine and Stomach meridians</note>. However, being a <insert>medicine of</insert> pungent heat, it can exhaust and disperse vital energy and stir up "fire" in the Spleen and Lungs. Overuse causes blurred vision. It is particularly unsuitable for frequent use in cooking.

**Main Treatments** Warms the center, descends rebellious Qi, tonifies the waist and feet, kills fishy odors, aids digestion, and eliminates stomach cold, inguinal hernias, and abdominal masses. <gloss>Chen Cangqi</gloss>: For cholera, "cold Qi" <note>internal chills</note>, heart pain, and blood disorders. <gloss>Daming</gloss>: For watery diarrhea, deficiency-type dysentery, vomiting, "vinegar heart" <note>acid reflux</note>, and postpartum diarrhea. It is excellent when eaten mixed with Asafoetida. Combined with Myrobalan, Ginseng, Cinnamon heart, and Dried Ginger, it is miraculously effective for deficiency-cold of the viscera and intestinal rumbling. <gloss>Li treats nasal pain and teeth</gloss> <gloss>Li Shizhen’s</gloss> <gloss>Exploration</gloss> <gloss>Kou Zongshi says</gloss>: Long Pepper travels through the intestines and stomach. It is suitable for those suffering from "cold Qi," vomiting, and fullness or pain in the heart and abdomen. Taking too much will dissipate the "True Qi" <note>essential vitality</note>, causing emptiness in the intestines and a heavy sensation in the lower body. <gloss>Su Song says</gloss>: According to the *Veritable Records of Emperor Taizong of Tang*, during the Zhenguan era, the Emperor suffered from chronic "Qi dysentery" <gloss>precious</gloss> and did not <gloss>mistake</gloss> recover. Experts were sought, but their medicines failed. An imperial decree was issued seeking a remedy. A palace guard submitted a recipe: boiling Long Pepper in yellow cow's milk. The Emperor took it and was cured. Liu Yuxi also recorded this, noting that later trials on patients with deficiency-cold conditions were always effective. <gloss>Li Shizhen</gloss> <gloss>says</gloss>: The details for the milk decoction are found in the "Beast" section under Cow's Milk. Long Pepper is an <insert>essential</insert> medicine for headaches, chronic sinusitis <note>Biyuan</note>, and toothaches. This is because its pungent heat enters the Yangming channels to disperse "floating heat."

# Betel Pepper <gloss>Jujiang: 'Ju' is pronounced like 'Ju' (as in 'judgment'); 'Jiang' is pronounced like 'Jiang' (as in 'sauce')</gloss> Also named Betel Fruit <gloss>from the 'Comprehensive Records of Natural History' <note>Guang Zhi</note></gloss>, Local Long Pepper <gloss>from 'Materia Medica of Dietary Therapy' <note>Shiliao Bencao</note></gloss>. The seedling is named Betel Vine <note>Fuliu</note>. <gloss>Li Shizhen says: According to the scholar Ji Han, the fruit can be used to season food, which is why it is called a 'sauce' <note>Jiang</note>. It belongs to the climbing vine category. This is why Meng Shen’s 'Dietary Therapy' refers to it this way.</gloss>

<insert>Collected Explanations</insert> <gloss>The 'Tang Materia Medica' states:</gloss> Betel Pepper grows in the Ba and Shu regions <note>modern Sichuan</note>. It is what the 'Rhapsody on the Shu Capital' <note>Shu Du Fu, a 3rd-century literary work</note> describes as "spreading its flavor to Panyu." It grows as a vine with leaves resembling the King Cucumber but thicker, larger, and glossy. It has a pungent, fragrant taste. The fruit resembles a mulberry, with black skin and white flesh. Those from the Western regions are smaller and more pungent. <gloss>Su Gong says:</gloss> It grows in Sichuan. History tells us that the King of Yue in the south consumed Betel Pepper. When Emperor Wu of the Han Dynasty tasted it, he was so impressed he sent expeditions to open the Zhangke and Yuexi regions to the empire. Liu Yuanlin’s commentary on the 'Rhapsody on the Shu Capital' says it climbs trees, and the fruit is like a mulberry; when ripe, it is green and two to three inches long. People preserve it in honey and salt to eat; its fragrance is equal to lotus root silk. These descriptions are mostly similar. Liu’s account refers to the Sichuan variety, while Su Gong’s refers to the variety from the southern seas. Today, people value the vine <note>for its leaves</note> rather than the pepper sauce, so it is rarely used as a condiment. <gloss>Li Xun says:</gloss> The 'Records of Guangzhou' state it comes from the Persian Empire. The fruit looks like a mulberry root. Purple-brown ones are superior; black ones are from old roots and are unusable. Recently, mostly black ones are seen, with few brown ones, though the shape and flavor are similar. <gloss>Li Shizhen says:</gloss> Betel Pepper is found today in Guangdong, Guangxi, southern Yunnan, and southern Sichuan. Its vine is called the 'climbing vine' and grows as thick as a chopstick. People there who chew Betel Nut <term>Binglang: The seed of the Areca palm</term> take these leaves and a bit of clam shell lime <note>used to release the alkaloids in the nut</note> and chew them together. This is done to ward off 'miasma' <note>malaria or humid tropical diseases</note> and expel 'foul qi' from the chest. There is a local proverb: "With Betel Nut and a floating bubble <note>the lime/leaf mixture</note>, one can forget all worries." The fruit is indeed the Betel Pepper. Some specialized botanical texts claim Betel Pepper is the same as Long Pepper <term>Biba: Piper longum</term>. They say those from foreign lands are large and purple (Long Pepper), while those from Panyu are small and green (Betel Pepper). The older herbals are wrong to equate them. The Betel Vine and the Long Pepper plant are entirely different in appearance. Although they are related and have similar flowers, fruits, and medicinal effects, they are not the same thing. The scholar Ji Han was wrong to say they were identical. The 'Records of Jiao Prefecture' mention three types of Betel Vine: 'Zhongliu' with fragrant roots, 'Fuliu' with a pungent vine, and 'Nanfuliu' with green, pungent-smelling leaves. Today, the people of Sichuan only use the leaves to make starter for rice wine, as they are very fragrant.

<insert>Processing</insert> <gloss>Zhen says:</gloss> When the bark is thick, pound it fine. For every five mace <note>approx. 19 grams</note>, use five taels <note>approx. 185 grams</note> of fresh ginger juice. Mix them, steam for a full day, then sun-dry for use.

# Root, Leaf, and Fruit <gloss>Properties</gloss> Pungent, warming, and non-toxic. <gloss>Li Shizhen says: Its qi is hot and its flavor is pungent; it belongs to the Yang principle and has a rising/floating nature.</gloss>

<insert>Main Indications</insert> Directs qi downward and warms the center of the body. Breaks up phlegm accumulation. Treats "rebellious qi" <note>upward-moving discomfort like coughing or hiccups</note>, abdominal pain caused by worms, weak stomach with diarrhea, cholera, and vomiting. It also helps sober one up from wine and aids digestion. <gloss>Li Xun says:</gloss> It disperses stagnated qi.

<insert>Attached Formula</insert> <gloss>New</gloss> 1. For Toothache: <gloss>Take half an ounce each of Betel Pepper and Wild Ginger <term>Xixin: Asarum</term>, and five mace of large Gleditsia pods <note>Soap pod</note>. Remove the seeds from the pods and fill the cavities with green salt. Burn the pods until they are charred but retain their shape, then grind everything into a fine powder. Rub frequently on the teeth and spit out the saliva. From the 'Formulas of the Imperial Pharmacy'.</gloss>

# Nutmeg <gloss>From the Kaibao Era of the Song Dynasty</gloss>

<insert>Explanation of Names</insert> Fleshy Fruit <gloss>from the 'Compendium'</gloss>, Jajule <gloss>a transliterated foreign name</gloss>. <gloss>Song Shi says: It is named 'Fleshy' Cardamom <note>Roudoukou</note> to distinguish it from Grass Cardamom. Once the shell is removed, only the 'flesh' is used. Those with an oily color are best.</gloss>

<insert>Collected Explanations</insert> <gloss>Su Gong says:</gloss> Nutmeg grows in foreign lands where it is called 'Jajule.' It is large and thin-shelled with a pungent interior. It is said to grow in Kunlun <note>Southeast Asia/Indonesia</note> and the Roman Empire <note>Daqin</note>. Su Song says: Today, people in the Lingnan region also plant it. In spring the shoots emerge, in summer the stems grow and it flowers. The fruit looks like a cardamom pod. It is harvested in the sixth and seventh lunar months. <gloss>Li Shizhen says:</gloss> Although the flowers and fruit of Nutmeg look like Grass Cardamom, the seeds themselves are different. The exterior has wrinkles, and the interior has a marbled, variegated pattern similar to the grain of a betel nut. It is very prone to insect infestation; it can only be stored briefly if fire-dried and kept in an airtight seal.

<insert>Processing</insert> <gloss>Lei Xiao says:</gloss> To use it, one must wrap the Nutmeg in a dough made of glutinous rice flour and hot water. Roast it in hot ashes until the dough is cooked through. Remove the flour and use the Nutmeg. Do not allow it to come into contact with iron.

<gloss>Properties</gloss> Pungent, warming, and non-toxic. <gloss>Daming says it is bitter and pungent.</gloss> <gloss>Cui Gu says: It enters the Hand and Foot Yang Brightness channels <note>Large Intestine and Stomach meridians</note>.</gloss>

<insert>Main Indications</insert> Warms the center and aids digestion. Stops diarrhea. Treats abdominal bloating and pain caused by accumulated cold, cholera, and "evil winds" or "ghostly qi" <note>sudden, severe illnesses often attributed to environmental or spiritual factors</note>.

### Warming the Stomach and Removing Phlegm <gloss>To aid appetite and digestion</gloss>
Take two Nutmeg seeds and five mace <note>approximately 18 grams</note> of Pinellia <note>Banxia</note> stir-fried with ginger juice, and two and a half mace of Auklandia <note>Muxiang</note>. Grind into a powder and use steamed bread to form pills the size of mustard seeds. After each meal, swallow fifty to ninety pills with saliva. <gloss>From 'Formulas for Universal Relief' <note>Puji Fang</note></gloss>

### Sudden Vomiting and Diarrhea <note>Cholera-like symptoms</note>
Grind Nutmeg into powder. Take one mace <note>3.7 grams</note> with ginger soup and a pinch of salt. <gloss>From 'Formulas for Universal Relief'</gloss>

### Incessant Diarrhea
Roast one tael <note>approx. 37 grams</note> of Nutmeg and two and a half mace of Auklandia. Grind into powder and mix with jujube pulp to make pills the size of mustard seeds. Or, grind into powder and mix with vinegar paste to make pills; take forty to fifty with rice water. ○ Another method: Roast Nutmeg, remove the shell, and grind with flour. Take one tael of Frankincense, grind into powder, and use old rice flour paste to make pills the size of a phoenix tree seed <note>about 9mm</note>. <gloss>From 'Selected Formulas of a Hundred and One'</gloss>

### Diarrhea from Deficiency in the Elderly
Three mace of Nutmeg wrapped in dough and roasted until cooked. Remove the dough, grind the nut, and mix with one tael of Frankincense powder. Use old rice flour paste to make pills the size of a phoenix tree seed. Each dose is fifty to seventy pills taken with rice water. This formula was passed down by Professor Hou of Changzhou. <gloss>From 'Formulas from the Hall of Auspicious Bamboo'</gloss>

### Infantile Diarrhea
Five mace of Nutmeg, one and a half mace of Frankincense, and five slices of ginger. Stir-fry together until black. Remove the ginger and grind the rest into a paste. Form into pills the size of mung beans. Adjust the dose based on the child's size and administer with rice water. <gloss>From 'Mirror of the Heart for Saving the Young'</gloss>

### Diarrhea and Dysentery from Spleen Weakness
Take one Nutmeg seed, wrap it in dough mixed with rice vinegar, and roast until charred yellow. Grind the nut and dough together. Add one tael of stir-fried and ground Betel nut. Mix and take one dose for immediate recovery.

### Cold Dysentery and Abdominal Pain <gloss>For those unable to eat</gloss>
One tael of Nutmeg, peeled. Mix with vinegar and dough, wrap, and roast until dry. Grind into powder. Take one mace per dose mixed with rice porridge. <gloss>From 'Sage's Benevolent Formulas' <note>Shenghui Fang</note></gloss>

### Chronic Malaria <gloss>From 'Continued Formulas for Spreading Belief'</gloss>
Use the roasted powder. Take one mace per dose mixed with rice porridge.

# Psoralea <gloss>Song Dynasty 'Materia Medica of the Kaibao Era'</gloss>

**【Explanation of Names】** Broken Old Paper <gloss>from 'Kaibao'</gloss>, Sturdy Foreign Resin <gloss>from 'Nature of Medicines'</gloss>, Foreign Leek Seeds. <gloss>Li Shizhen says: The name Psoralea <note>Buguzhi, meaning 'Supplement Bone Fat'</note> refers to its medicinal merit. Westerners call it 'Poguzhi' <note>Sturdy Foreign Resin</note>, but common speech corrupted it to 'Poguzhi' <note>Broken Old Paper</note>. It is called 'Foreign Leek Seeds' because the seeds look like leeks, not because they are leeks from foreign lands. It grows in the Shangzhou region and Persian countries.</gloss>

**【Collected Explanations】** <gloss>Su Song says: Psoralea comes from various prefectures in Lingnan and Guangzhou.</gloss>
Nowadays, it is found in many mountain slopes in the southern regions. It also grows in Hezhou, Sichuan, but it is not as good as that brought by foreign merchant ships. The stem is three to four feet high. The leaves are small and resemble mint. The flowers are slightly purple. The fruit is like hemp seed—round, flat, and black. Harvest in September. <gloss>The 'Records of Southern Provinces' by Xu Biao says: This is the Foreign Leek Seed. Those from the southern regions are red; those from the Guangnan region are green. For medicine, stir-fry slightly before use.</gloss>

### The Seeds <gloss>Preparation</gloss>
<gloss>Lei Xiao says: This herb is dry and slightly toxic in nature. It must be soaked in wine overnight, removed, and then soaked in eastward-flowing river water for three days and nights. Steam it from the hour of the Snake <note>9-11 AM</note> to the hour of the Monkey <note>3-5 PM</note>, then sun-dry. Another method is to stir-fry it with salt and sand, then sun-dry for use.</gloss>

**【Flavor and Nature】** Pungent, Greatly Warm, Non-toxic. <gloss>Zhen Quan says: Bitter and Pungent. Li Xun says: It is incompatible with Licorice. Li Shizhen says: Avoid Rapeseed and all animal blood. It works well when combined with Walnuts and Sesame.</gloss>

**【Main Indications】** The "five exhaustions and seven injuries" <note>general terms for chronic physical and emotional overstrain</note>, wind-deficiency cold, damage to the bone marrow, coldness in the kidneys with seminal leakage, and women's blood-related disorders or threatened miscarriage. <gloss>From 'Kaibao'</gloss> It treats lower back pain in men, cold knees, dampness of the scrotum, various cold-type numbness, and frequent urination with a cold abdomen. <gloss>Zhen Quan says:</gloss> It invigorates the "Yang" <note>vital warmth and sexual function</note> and clears the hearing and vision. <gloss>Daming says:</gloss> It treats and opens the "Gate of Vitality" <note>the source of life-fire between the kidneys</note>, warms the "Cinnabar Field" <note>the energy center in the lower abdomen</note>, and gathers the spirit.

### Invention
<gloss>Su Song says: Nowadays, people often take Psoralea together with Walnuts. This method comes from a personal account by Minister Zheng of the Tang Dynasty, who said: "I was the Military Governor of Nanhai at the age of seventy-five. The region was low and damp, which damaged my internal and external health. All sorts of ailments arose, and my Yang energy was exhausted. I tried a hundred different mineral tonics to no avail. In the seventh year of the Yuanhe era <note>812 AD</note>, a ship captain from the kingdom of Holing named Li Moha learned of my condition and passed on this formula along with the medicine. At first, I was skeptical and did not take it, but Moha..."</gloss>

### Calming the Heart and Tonifying the Kidney

### Exhaustion in Men and Women
For men and women suffering from the "Five Taxations and Seven Injuries" <note>ancient terms for various types of physical and emotional exhaustion</note>, long-term coldness in the Lower Origin, all types of "wind" diseases, or painful limbs. # Turmeric
<gloss>From the "Tang Materia Medica" (Tang Ben Cao)</gloss>

<insert>Names</insert> *Shu* <gloss>pronounced "shù"</gloss>, Treasure Tripod Incense <gloss>From the "Compendium" (Gangmu)</gloss>.

<insert>Explanations</insert> <gloss>Su Gong says:</gloss> The roots and leaves of Turmeric look exactly like Wild Turmeric (*Yujin*). In spring, its flowers emerge from the roots alongside the sprouts. In summer, the flowers fade without producing seeds. The roots come in three colors: yellow, green, and white. The processing method is the same as for Wild Turmeric. People of the Western Rong <note>historical term for ethnic groups in Western China</note> call it *Shu*. Its taste is slightly pungent and mostly bitter, also similar to Wild Turmeric; only the timing of the flowers differs. <gloss>Chen Zangqi says:</gloss> True Turmeric is actually old Ginger that has been planted for over three years. It produces flowers at the base of the root, looking much like Ginger-lily. The root sections are hard, and the flavor is pungent and spicy. It can be found wherever ginger is grown, but it is rare. Some comes from the Western regions, looking like Wild Turmeric. What Su Gong described is actually Zedoary <term>Zedoary: Curcuma zedoaria, a related but different root</term> rather than Turmeric. He claimed Turmeric is *Shu* and Wild Turmeric is "Foreign *Shu*." If that were true, these three things would be indistinguishable and all called *Shu*, and their effects would be the same. However, Wild Turmeric is bitter and cold, red in color, and primarily treats "horse heat" diseases. Turmeric is pungent and warm, yellow in color. Zedoary is bitter and green. These three are distinct and used differently. <gloss>Li Tianming says:</gloss> That which grows in Hainan is Zedoary; that which grows south of the Yangtze is Turmeric. <gloss>Su Song says:</gloss> Turmeric is now found in many regions like Jiangnan, Guangdong, and Sichuan. The leaves are green, one to two feet long and three to four inches wide, with diagonal veins like small red banana leaves. The flowers are reddish-white and wither by mid-autumn. It sprouts in late spring, flowering first, then leafing. It does not fruit. The roots are yellow, shaped like ginger but rounder and segmented. Harvested in the eighth month, sliced and dried. People in Sichuan use it to treat abdominal "qi" <term>qi: vital energy or physiological function</term> and postpartum "ruined blood" <note>original: "ruined blood" (敗血 - baixue), referring to lochia or stagnant blood after childbirth</note> attacking the heart; it is very effective. The southern tribes eat it raw to ward off evil and pestilence. Note that Wild Turmeric, Turmeric, and Zedoary are so similar that Su Gong could not tell them apart. Chen Zangqi distinguished them by color and taste. Recently, merchants often sell old Ginger as Turmeric to deceive people, claiming it is superior for treating "qi" issues. There is also "Lian-ginger," which is related but a different species. <gloss>Li Shizhen says:</gloss> Nowadays, the flat ones shaped like dried ginger are called "Sliver Turmeric" (Pianzi Jianghuang), and the round ones shaped like a cicada's belly are "Cicada-Belly Wild Turmeric." Both can be soaked to dye water, but while they look like Wild Turmeric, they are not as yellow.

Root <insert>Properties</insert> Pungent and bitter, greatly cold, non-toxic. <gloss>Chen Zangqi says: It is slightly pungent and mostly bitter. It is warm, not cold. The claim of "greatly cold" is an error.</gloss>

<insert>Indications</insert> For accumulations in the heart and abdomen, "clash with the uncanny" <note>original: "zhuwu" (疰忤), a term for sudden illness attributed to malevolent spirits or environmental factors</note>, descending "qi," and breaking stagnant blood. It clears wind-heat and dissolves swellings. Its power is more intense than Wild Turmeric. <gloss>From "Tang Materia Medica"</gloss>. For abdominal masses, blood clots, and regulating menstruation. It treats bruises, stops sudden wind pain, and helps with "cold qi" digestion. <gloss>From "Daming Materia Medica"</gloss>. Treats strikes from evil, abdominal bloating, and postpartum blood attacking the heart. <gloss>Su Song</gloss>. Treats "wind-dampness" (bi) syndrome and arm pain. <gloss>Li Shizhen</gloss> says: Turmeric, Wild Turmeric, and Zedoary are similar in shape and function, but Turmeric enters the Liver meridian to treat the "blood within the qi." The ancient "Five-Bi Decoction" uses Sliver Turmeric to treat arm pain caused by wind, cold, and dampness. This shows its ability to regulate the "qi within the blood."

**Placenta Retention and Abdominal Pain:** <gloss>Where the infant cries, vomits milk, has green stools like fright-convulsions, and sweats.</gloss> One mace Turmeric, two mace each of Myrrh, Frankincense, and "Moshang" (Saussurea). <gloss>From the "Tang Materia Medica"</gloss>

# Compendium of Materia Medica, Volume 14, Herbs Section

This root is used to infuse wine, making it as yellow as gold; for this reason, it is called "Golden Stream." <gloss>Su Gong says: Wild Turmeric grows in the Sichuan region and among the Western tribes. Its sprouts resemble Turmeric, with white flowers and red tips. The root is yellowish-red and harvested across the four seasons. Because its shape resembles Zedoary and it is used to treat diseases in horses, it is also called "Horse-Delighter" (Mamixing).</gloss> <gloss>Su Song says: Today, Wild Turmeric is also found in the prefectures of Guangdong and Jiangxi, though it is not as high in quality as that from Sichuan. In the fourth month, the sprouts emerge, looking like ginger or lotus root. Su Gong noted that its fragrance is not strong. When used to dye women's clothing, the color is exceptionally bright but does not withstand the sun. It possesses a slight fragrance of Wild Turmeric. Li Shizhen says: There is a variety of "Wild Turmeric Saffron" (Yujinxiang) that uses the flower; however, this specific entry refers to the variety where the root is used. The sprouts are like ginger, and the roots are about the size of a finger, roughly an inch long. They are round with horizontal ridges resembling a cicada’s abdomen. The exterior is yellow and the interior is red. People soak them in water to extract dye; they also have a faint aroma.</gloss>

## Wild Turmeric
<gloss>Yuan Su says: Both its scent and flavor are potent; it is purely Yin in nature.</gloss>
<gloss>Dugu Ji says: The skin of this root can be used to "bind" cinnabar <note>original: "jie shazi" (結砂子), a reference to alchemical processes where plant extracts were thought to stabilize or transform minerals</note>.</gloss>

### Main Indications
Treats blood accumulation and facilitates the downward flow of Qi; promotes the growth of new flesh and stops bleeding; breaks up "evil blood" <note>original: "exue" (惡血), referring to pathological, stagnant, or clotted blood</note>, and treats blood in the urine and metal-inflicted wounds. <gloss>From the "Tang Materia Medica"</gloss>. It treats chronic blood stasis in women and "heart pain" <note>this often referred to epigastric or chest pain</note> caused by Qi blockages. For masses formed by cold Qi, grind the root with warm vinegar and apply as a poultice. It also treats abdominal bloating in horses. <gloss>Yuan Su says:</gloss> It is purely "Yin" and cooling. It targets the <gloss>Heart Channel</gloss> to manage "Original Yang." It is effective when toxins enter the stomach, causing frequent bloody stools and pain. <gloss>Li Shizhen says:</gloss> It treats pains in the heart and abdomen caused by blood and Qi disorders, cases where "spent blood" <note>postpartum lochia or stagnant blood</note> attacks the heart after childbirth (which can be fatal), and states of mania or insanity. <gloss>Su Song says:</gloss> Expanding on its uses: <gloss>Li Shizhen says: Wild Turmeric belongs to the elements of Fire and Earth, but also contains the element of Water. Its nature is light and ascending. It treats the vomiting of blood, nosebleeds, and "reverse flow" of the menses. One should take Wild Turmeric powder mixed with leek juice, ginger juice, and child's urine <note>original: "tong niao" (童尿), a common historical medicinal vehicle believed to have cooling and blood-cleansing properties</note>; the blood will then clear itself. For blood in phlegm, add bamboo sap. For persistent nosebleeds, take the powder with leek juice and "Four-Substance Decoction" (Siwu Tang). Li Shizhen says: Wild Turmeric enters the Heart and the Pericardium to treat blood diseases. An "Expert's Formula" for treating insanity and mania uses seven ounces <term>ounce: (liang) approx. 37.5 grams</term> of genuine Wild Turmeric and three ounces of Alum. Grind them into a powder and use a thin paste to form pills the size of a parasol tree seed. Take fifty pills per dose with warm water. There was a woman who was insane for ten years; after being given this, she felt something "detach" from her chest, her spirit became clear, and after a second dose, she fully recovered. This condition is caused by "phlegm-blood" resulting from fright or worry that clogs the "Orifices of the Heart." Wild Turmeric enters the heart to remove evil blood, while Alum dissolves stubborn phlegm. Pang Anchang's "Treatise on Cold Damage" states: when smallpox pustules begin to turn purple or black and sink into the body without forming pus, causing the patient to scream in distress, take one dose of Wild Turmeric powder. Boil two and a half mace <term>mace: (qian) approx. 3.75 grams</term> of Licorice in half a cup of water until dry. Within two doses, the toxin will exit through the hands and feet in the form of blisters, and the patient will recover. This is a "one-in-five-survival" emergency situation. Furthermore, Fan Shihu's "Great Collection" mentions the danger of "Tiaosheng" <note>a type of sorcery or folk poisoning involving the ingestion of substances that "come to life" in the gut</note> in the Lingnan region. This will cause the "evil matter" to be discharged. Alternatively, hold Cimicifuga or Wild Turmeric in the mouth; if it doesn't cause vomiting, it will purge the system. When Minister Li Xunyan was an official in Leizhou, he used this formula to save many lives during legal inquests.</gloss>

# Zedoary <gloss>pronounced *shu*</gloss>
<gloss>From the Kaibao Era of the Song Dynasty</gloss>
<gloss>Zedoary grows in the Western regions and various southern provinces. Its leaves resemble ginger or lotus. The seeds—specifically the Zedoary roots—grow together beneath the plant in pairs: one "good" and one "evil." The evil ones are toxic. Westerners identify them by letting sheep graze; the sheep will not eat the toxic ones, which are then discarded. Zangqi states: One type is "Peng-e," which is black; the second is "Peng-mao," which is yellow; the third is "Bolu," which tastes sweet but is highly toxic. In the *Daming* herbal, it is noted that the variety from the south is called "Southern Turmeric."</gloss>

This is a root. Those grown in Hainan are called Zedoary. Su Song says: Today, it is also found in Zhejiang. In the third month, the sprouts emerge in the wild fields. The stems are about the size of a coin and reach two to three feet in height. The leaves are bluish-white, one to two feet long, and over five inches wide, much like ginger or lotus. In the fifth month, it flowers in yellow spikes with slightly purple tips. The root resembles fresh ginger, but the Zedoary itself grows beneath the root in shapes like chicken or duck eggs, varying in size. It is harvested in the ninth month; the coarse skin is scraped off, and it is steamed and dried in the sun for use.

## The Root
<gloss>Preparation</gloss> Lei Xiao says: When using this, rub it in a sand mortar with vinegar until completely ground, then dry it by a fire and pass it through a heavy sieve. Su Song says: This material is extremely hard and difficult to pound. <gloss>Flavor and Nature</gloss> Bitter, acrid, warm, and non-toxic. <gloss>The *Daming* herbal states that it is best prepared with wine or vinegar.</gloss>

## Healing Properties
Treats severe abdominal pain, sudden stroke, demonic possession <note>original: "gui qi" (鬼氣), referring to sudden, unexplained illnesses attributed to malevolent influences in ancient medicine</note>, cholera, cold vapors, and the vomiting of sour water. It acts as an antitoxin and aids in the digestion of food when ground and taken. It also treats "blood-qi" accumulations in women and "running piglet" syndrome <note>original: "ben tun" (奔豚), a sensation of gas or energy rushing up from the abdomen to the throat, often linked to anxiety or kidney-qi disorders</note> in men. <gloss>Kaibao Era</gloss> It breaks up abdominal masses and cold vapors when ground with wine or vinegar. It treats all forms of stagnant energy, opens the stomach to aid digestion, regulates menstruation, clears bruised blood, and stops pain from traumatic injuries, internal bleeding, or stagnant "evil" blood. <gloss>Daming Era</gloss> Zhen Quan says it is used for... Haogu says: Zedoary is black in color. It breaks up the blood within the "Qi" <note>the body's vital energy</note>. When added to Qi-regulating medicines, it brings out the fragrances. Although it is a purging agent, it can also benefit the Qi. Thus, the Physician Sun used it to treat shortness of breath and included it in many powders and pills like the "Seven Fragrances" or "Nine Fragrances" formulas. It is also a medicine for the blood division of the Liver Meridian. Li Shizhen says: Wild Turmeric enters the Heart and specializes in treating the blood division. Turmeric enters the Spleen and treats the "Qi within the blood." Zedoary enters the Liver and treats the "Blood within the Qi." These are subtle but important differences. Wang Zhizhong's *Classic of Nourishing Life* states: Zhizhong suffered long-term pain in the Heart and Spleen; he took "Spleen-Awakening" medicines and used the Zedoary preparation recorded by the monk Qiyu.

<header>Compendium of Materia Medica, Volume 14, Herbs Section</header>

The records state that "Chicken-claw Sanleng" grows in the lands of Shu <note>modern-day Sichuan</note> and should be harvested in the second and eighth months. <gloss>Tao Hongjing states:</gloss> There are three or four varieties of Sanleng. "Jing Sanleng" is yellow, heavy, and shaped like a crucian carp, though smaller. There is also "Black Sanleng," which is shaped like a dark plum but larger. They are essentially of the same category, named differently according to their shape; thus, I have grouped them together. <gloss>Su Song states:</gloss> There are three or four kinds. One is "Jing Sanleng," which the people of Shu use to weave mats; this is also called "Grass Sanleng." Their medicinal properties are similar. It is no longer known where the name "Jing" <note>referring to the capital</note> originated. Today, it is found throughout the regions of Jing, Huai, Zhejiang, Nanjing, and the Yellow River valleys of Shaanxi. It mostly grows near shallow water and in marshy embankments. In spring, the sprouts emerge with leaves resembling *Sha* grass <note>Nutgrass or Sedge</note>, growing very long to a height of three or four feet. They also resemble wild rice or cattail leaves but are distinctly three-edged. In the fifth or sixth month, the stalks emerge, four or five feet high and as thick as a human finger; they are triangular as if carved into that shape. At the tip of the stalk, flowers bloom that largely resemble *Sha* grass but are large and yellowish-purple. Beneath the sprouts is the "chief" <note>the main rhizome</note>, which initially forms a clump like an Aconite tuber; some are flat. At the end of the season, a horizontal root connects several clumps together. The clumps also produce sprouts. Those that are flat and long like a small crucian carp are called "Firm Sanleng." Where the root ends and a small, round clump like a dark plum has not yet sprouted, it is called "Black Sanleng." Furthermore, those with root tips curved like talons are called "Chicken-claw Sanleng." All have black skin and white flesh and are extremely light. Some say the "Chicken-claw" variety is the one that produces only fine roots without sprouts, while the "Black" variety is the one that produces no fine roots at all. Their sizes vary. Once the skin is removed, they are all "White Sanleng." They are essentially one species, though their potency varies between "hard" and "soft" <note>strong and gentle</note>, and each is suited to a specific use. They are named for their shapes, much like the different names for Aconite or Mica; they are not actually different things. Nowadays, people mistakenly use *Xiangfuzi* <note>Nutgrass</note> for this purpose. Furthermore, in Hezhong Prefecture, there is "Stone Sanleng," with a yellowish-white root shaped like a glue-plug and green leaves like cattails. The sprouts reach a foot high and are also three-edged. In the fourth month, it blooms with white flowers like knotweed. The roots are harvested in the fifth month and are also used to dissipate accumulated Qi. The "Sanleng" used in my collected recipes is mostly "Red Sedge" root from Huainan; it is particularly abundant in Taizhou. Its body is extremely hard and heavy, and when sliced, it reveals a fish-like shape. Its leaves are flat and its stems are round, lacking the three edges. I do not know why it was named "Sanleng." Even the Imperial Physicians do not consider this an error. Because the habit has persisted for so long, those who use the root do not recognize the sprouts, and those who harvest the herb do not investigate its use. I record this discrepancy so it can be identified. Currently, the "Sanleng" available is simply the lower root, mostly shaped like a crucian carp. **Shizhen states:** Sanleng grows mostly in abandoned ponds and wetlands. It grows in clusters in the spring and withers in the summer and autumn. At the top of the tall stalk, several leaves grow, and yellowish-purple flowers bloom in six or seven branching spikes. Inside are tiny seeds. Its leaves, stalks, flowers, and fruits all have three edges, identical to the leaves and flowers of *Xiangfuzi* <note>Nutgrass</note>, though larger. The stalks are smooth, and the triangular shape is like a weaver's shuttle. Inside the stalk is a white pith; when sliced, the fibers are soft and tough like vine. The *Zilin* <note>an ancient dictionary</note> says: "The *Li* grass grows in water; its roots can be carved into vessels." This refers to the stalk, not the root. *Baopuzi* <note>the Daoist text</note> mentions reed roots transforming into something else; this also refers to this plant. Its roots are mostly yellowish-black. To prepare them, one must remove the fibrous "whiskers" and skin, revealing a shape like a crucian carp. It is not that the original root is a carp, but that it resembles one.

Those with Qi deficiency must not use it.

Postpartum "evil blood" <note>lochia/stagnant blood</note>, blood clots, to promote menstruation, to induce labor, to stop pain, and to benefit the movement of Qi. <gloss>Kaibao Herbal:</gloss> Treats abdominal bloating, breaks up accumulated Qi, and dissipates masses and tumors. # Nutgrass (Xiangfuzi)
<gloss>Intermediate Grade</gloss> <gloss>Named in the "Additional Records" as Sparrow-head Fragrance. Also called Attached Seed, Menstrual Fragrance, and Water Sanleng. Recorded in various historical illustrations. Commentaries provided by Tao Hongjing, Su Gong, Su Song, Kou Zongshi, and Li Shizhen.</gloss>

The *Additional Records* mention *Sha* grass <note>original: "shacao," referring to the Nutgrass plant</note> but do not specify whether to use the sprouts or the root. Later generations have all used the root, calling it *Xiangfuzi* ("Fragrant Attached Seed"), often remaining unaware of the name *Sha* grass. This grass can be woven into bamboo hats and raincoats; it is coarse and does not hold water. Therefore, its Chinese character is derived from the radicals for "grass" and "sand." It is also called the "Raincoat Plant" because its hanging fibers resemble the straw raincoats worn by the ancients. The *Erya* <note>the oldest surviving Chinese dictionary</note> refers to it as *Tui* or *Shanghe*, noting that the fruit of the *Sha* grass is called *Ti*. It is also called *Tai* or "The Commoner’s Necessity," as it provides the material for hats required by laborers. Its roots grow attached to one another in a continuous chain and can be blended into perfumes, hence the name *Xiangfuzi* (Fragrant Attached Seed). In ancient times, it was called "Sparrow-head Fragrance." The *Annals of Jiangbiao* record that Emperor Wen of Wei sent envoys to the Kingdom of Wu to seek "Sparrow-head Fragrance," which is this very plant. Its leaves resemble those of the Sanleng (Bur-reed).

The *Additional Records* state that *Sha* grass grows in fields and in the Ba Mountains. Because it grows in low, damp places, it is colloquially known as "Water Sanleng" or "Water Bajian." Common folk call it "Thunder God’s Head." In the *Golden Light Sutra*, it is called "Moon Fragrance." It is widely recorded in botanical texts. The layman Baolu says it should be harvested in the second and eighth months. 

**Tao Hongjing states:** This is no longer used in medical prescriptions. Ancient poets often mentioned it, but those without knowledge might confuse it with common sedge, which is different. 

**Su Gong states:** The root of this grass is called *Xiangfuzi*, also known as Sparrow-head Fragrance. It is found everywhere. Its leaves are similar to Sanleng, and it is used in blended fragrances. 

**Su Song states:** It is found everywhere today. The sprouts and leaves are like those of shallots but thinner. The root is as large as a thumb. According to the botanical illustrations from the Tianbao era of the Tang Dynasty, the properties of "Water Sanleng" are similar to this. It says Water Sanleng grows in the ponds and marshes of Boping Commandery. The sprouts are called *Xiangleng* and the roots are *Shajie* (Sha-knots), also called *Caofuzi* (Grass Attached Seed). In the damp lowlands of Henan and Huainan, it is called "Earth Dragon Root," and in the Shu region, it is called "Water Yi." Today, in Fuzhou, it is most prized. It is called "Three-edged Grass" and used to make shoes. It grows everywhere. The sprouts, flowers, and roots are all harvested. Some call it *Xiangfuzi*. People use it frequently. Although it grows among *Sha* grass, some roots have the "attached" nodules and some do not. It has a thin, purple-black skin and is not very hairy. If you scrape off the skin, the inside is white. Some mistake the root itself for the medicine, which is an error.

**Li Shizhen states:** The leaves of *Sha* grass are like old leeks but are hard, smooth, and glossy, with a spine like a sword. In the fifth or sixth month, a single stalk emerges. This stalk is three-edged (triangular) and hollow. At the tip of the stalk, several more leaves emerge, and it produces bluish flowers in spikes, resembling millet, containing small seeds. The root has fine whiskers, and beneath these whiskers, one or two seeds (tubers) form, which then spread to grow more. These tubers have fine black hairs; the large ones are like "sheep dates" and are pointed at both ends. Once harvested, the hairs are singed off, and the root is dried and crushed. This is a primary medicine in daily use today. Tao Hongjing did not recognize it, and other commentators were brief. It is unknown why ancient and modern medicinal use differs so much. One cannot discard a medicine from the *Materia Medica* simply because it is currently unrecognized; who knows if it will not become a vital medicine in another era, just as Nutgrass has?

# The Root
<gloss>Preparation</gloss> It is said that once harvested, it should be dried in the shade and pounded in a stone mortar. **Crucially, avoid the use of iron tools.** **Li Shizhen states:** Once harvested with the sprouts attached, sun-dry it and use fire to singe off the sprouts and hairs. When ready for use, wash it clean with water and rub it on a stone to remove the skin. It can be soaked in boy’s urine <note>a traditional processing method to enhance cooling and blood-moving properties</note>, washed and dried, and then pounded for use. It may be used raw, stir-fried, or soaked in wine, vinegar, or salt water; each method follows the specific requirements of the formula, as detailed below. Furthermore, boiling it with *Fulicao* <note>an unidentified herb, likely used for processing</note> removes its bitter taste.

<gloss>Aroma and Flavor</gloss> Sweet, slightly cold.

# Formula for Edema from Qi Deficiency
One *jin* <note>approximately 500 grams</note> of Nutgrass <note>original: "Xiangfuzi"</note>. Soak in boy's urine <note>traditionally used as a cooling agent and to direct medicine to the kidneys</note> for three days. Roast it and grind into a powder. Form into pills using a paste. Take forty to fifty pills each time with rice water, twice a day. <gloss>Heart Methods of Danxi</gloss>

# Abdominal Masses in the Old and Young
For alternating chills and fever with pain: Nutgrass and Arisaema <note>original: "Nanxing," a pungent herb used to resolve phlegm</note> in equal parts. Grind into powder and form pills the size of a parasol tree seed using ginger juice paste. Take twenty to thirty pills with ginger broth. <gloss>Formulary of Benevolent Grace</gloss>

# Hernia and Abdominal Pain
Also for "Small Intestine Qi" <note>a traditional category involving lower abdominal pain or scrotal swelling</note>: Two *qian* <note>approximately 6-8 grams</note> of Nutgrass powder. Decoct with one *qian* of Seaweed <note>original: "Haizao"</note> in wine. Take on an empty stomach and eat the seaweed. <gloss>Essential Formulas</gloss>

# Toothache
For dental pain: Five *liang* <note>approximately 155 grams</note> of Nutgrass and two *liang* of fresh ginger. Extract the natural juice of the ginger and soak the Nutgrass in it overnight. Stir-fry until yellow and grind into powder. Add two *qian* of blue salt <note>a type of rock salt</note>. Rub onto the teeth several times; the pain will stop immediately. <gloss>Business of the Universe</gloss>

# Stabbing Pain from Blood and Qi
Grind into powder. Take two *qian* per dose, mixed with rice water. <gloss>Fine Formulas for Women</gloss>

# Winter Daphne
<gloss>From the Compendium of Materia Medica</gloss>
<gloss>Shizhen <note>Li Shizhen, the author of the Compendium</note> says: It grows in the mountains everywhere in the south. The branches and trunk are lush and spreading, the leaves are thick and do not wither during the four seasons. Between winter and spring, it blooms in clusters about three to four *fen* long, shaped like cloves. There are three colors: yellow, white, and purple. The *Gegu Lun* <note>a 14th-century treatise on antiques and curiosities</note> states: The Winter Daphne grows three to four feet high. There are several varieties: those with leaves like loquats, those like bayberries, and those with "ball" or "twisted" branches. Only the "climbing branch" variety has purple flowers with an intense fragrance. The loquat-leaf variety produces seeds. It originally came from Mount Lu. During the Song Dynasty, people began to cultivate it, and it became famous. The "twisted branch" variety has nodes that are bent as if broken. Its root is soft and fragrant.</gloss>

## The Root
<gloss>Flavor: Sweet and Salty. Toxicity: None. Primary Indications: For scrofula <note>chronic swelling of the lymph nodes</note> and wind-dampness. Use the white-flowered variety; grind it with water and pour it into the affected area.</gloss>
<gloss>Shizhen: This information comes from the *Collection of Medical Works*.</gloss>

# Jasmine
<gloss>From the Compendium: Collected Explanations</gloss>
<gloss>Shizhen says: The *Record of Plants and Trees* by Ji Han calls it "Muli." The *Record of Famous Gardens in Luoyang* calls it "Molie." Buddhist scriptures call it "Moli." In the collection of Wang Guiling, it is "Meili." These are all transcriptions of a foreign word <note>likely the Sanskrit "Mallika"</note>; there is no "correct" character, as people simply used characters that matched the sound. Wei Jun called it the "Escort Guest," while Zhang Minshu called it the "Distant Guest." Yang Shen’s *Danyuan Record* says the capital's people use it as a substitute for plum blossoms.</gloss>
<gloss>Shizhen says: Jasmine originally came from Persia and was transplanted to the South Seas <note>Southeast Asia</note>. Today, the people of Guangdong cultivate it. It dislikes the cold and does not thrive in the central regions. It has weak stems and many branches. The leaves resemble the Gardenia but are thin. The flowers do not produce fruit. There are varieties with double petals, red flowers, and climbing vines. All bloom at night and have a lovely fragrance. Women wear them as hair ornaments or mix them into face creams. They can also be used to scent tea or distilled into a liquid to replace "Rose Water" <note>an imported Persian perfume</note>. There is another variety similar to Jasmine but with larger petals and a pure, sharp fragrance called "Dog Tooth" or "Snow Petal." The "Cunxiang," "Royal Jasmine," and "Henna" of Hainan are all of the same class and are appended below.</gloss>

### Royal Jasmine
<gloss>Shizhen says: Royal Jasmine <note>original: "Suxin"</note> also came from the Western Regions. It was called "Yexiruo" flower, which is the same as the "Yeximi" <note>likely "Yasmin" or Jasmine</note> recorded in the *Miscellaneous Morsels from Youyang*. The branches and stems are green, and it blooms in the summer with a fragrance like Sweet Osmanthus.</gloss>

### Henna
<gloss>Used to dye fingernails; the color is even deeper than that of the Balsam flower <note>original: "Fengxianhua"</note>.</gloss>

The flower has a pungent and hot flavor and is non-toxic. It is primarily used by steaming it with oil to extract its essence, which is made into face creams and hair oils to promote hair growth, moisturize dryness, and scent the skin. It can also be added to medicinal teas. <gloss>Shizhen</gloss>

The root has a hot flavor and is toxic. It is used for treatments by grinding one inch of the root with wine. If consumed, the patient will fall into a coma for one day; if two inches are used, for two days; and three inches for three days. It is used for those suffering from fractures, dislocations, or those needing bones reset, as they will not feel any pain under its influence. <gloss>Wang Ji</gloss> <note>This likely refers to the "Maliuhua" or a similar potent anesthetic herb often discussed alongside fragrant flowers in this volume.</note>

# Tulip / Saffron <gloss>Song Dynasty *Kaibao Bencao*</gloss> <insert>Corrected</insert>

<gloss>Yuxi says: Master Chen stated that this herb is the "Tulip" <note>original: "Yujinxiang"</note>. Its leaves are like those of the Turmeric plant, but the flowers are small and purple, and it smells of musk. <gloss>The Buddhist hymns say: Xu Shen’s *Analytical Dictionary of Characters* explains that "Yu" is a fragrant herb; ten leaves form a bundle, and one hundred and twenty bundles are boiled to create the scent.</gloss> It should not have been categorized under the "Tree" section; it is now moved here.</gloss>

**Names:** Tulip <gloss>From the *Southern Materia Medica*</gloss>, Purple Curcuma Scent <gloss>From the *Compendium*</gloss>, Grass Musk <gloss>From the *Compendium*</gloss>, *Tujumo* <gloss>The Sanskrit name, likely Kunkuma</gloss>.

<insert>Collected Explanations</insert> 
> Zangqi says: The Tulip grows in the Roman Empire <note>original: "Daqin"</note>. In the second and third months, it produces flowers. It is the finest of all herbs, blended to brew wine for summoning the spirits. It was a tribute brought by people from distant lands, hence the name "Yu," referring to the Yulin Commandery. 
> Shizhen says: The Han Dynasty’s Yulin Commandery corresponds to modern-day areas in Guangxi and Guizhou. The *General Gazetteer* records that Lucheng County in Liuzhou produces the Tulip, which is this very plant. The *Golden Light Sutra* calls it *Tujumo* scent. This is the Tulip flower, which shares a name with the Turmeric root <note>also called "Yujin" in Chinese</note> used today, but they are different things. The Tang Dynasty *Materia Medica* mistakenly combined the two. According to Zhao Guze’s *Six Scripts*, the character "Yu" <note>鬱</note> depicts items gathered in a vessel and stirred with a ladle. The character is composed of elements representing a mortar, a jar, and a stand. "Yu" refers to the process of extracting the scent from flowers and leaves for wine, not necessarily to a specific place; the place-name Yulin likely comes from this herb.
> According to Guo Li: The "Yu" herb resembles an orchid. Yang Fu’s *Strange Things from the South* says: It comes from the Kingdom of Kashmir <note>original: "Jibin"</note>. People plant it to offer to the Buddha; after a few days, when it withers, they harvest it. Its color is a true yellow, resembling the tender lotus inside a hibiscus flower. It can be used to scent wine. Furthermore, the *Book of Tang* states: During Emperor Taizong’s reign, the Kingdom of Kapisa offered Tulip. Its leaves resemble Lilyturf, and it flowers in the ninth month. The flower looks like a hibiscus, colored purple and blue, with a fragrance reaching dozens of paces. It flowers but does not seed; those wishing to plant it must use the root. These accounts are similar, though flower colors vary, suggesting there may be several varieties. The *Ancient Music Bureau* poems mention "scents of Tulip and Storax," which refers to this plant. Lady Zuo of the Jin Dynasty wrote a "Panegyric to the Tulip," describing it as: "A wondrous herb named Tulip, surpassing all from foreign realms. Its fragrance is intense and sharp, delighting the eye and soothing the heart. Its virtue is its scent, cherished by the virtuous."

The flavor is bitter and warm, and it is non-toxic. <gloss>Zangqi says: It is balanced.</gloss> It is primarily used to treat "Gu" poisoning <note>toxins from ritual magic</note> and various wild toxins, as well as "evil Qi" <note>pathogenic energy</note> in the heart and abdomen. It is used to treat "Ghost Infestation" <note>likely a term for wasting diseases or sudden illness</note> and various other ailments, often combined with other incenses. <gloss>Zangqi</gloss>

# Fragrant Thatch <gloss>Song Dynasty *Kaibao Bencao*</gloss> <insert>Corrected</insert> <gloss>Merged with "Fragrant Hemp" from the Song *Illustrated Classic*</gloss>

**Names:** *Xunshiluo* <gloss>From the *Golden Light Sutra*; Sanskrit: Usira, likely Vetiver</gloss>, Fragrant Hemp <gloss>Shizhen says: Su Song’s *Illustrated Classic* had a separate entry for "Fragrant Hemp," stating it comes from Fuzhou and is decocted for baths. Su Gong says this is actually Lemongrass <note>original: "Xiangmao"</note> found in the Jiannan region. People in Fujian call it "Mao" (thatch) but it looks like "Ma" (hemp), hence the name. They are now merged into one entry.</gloss>

<insert>Collected Explanations</insert>

> Su Gong says: Fragrant Thatch grows in the various prefectures of the Jiannan region. Its fragrance is quite excellent. This is indeed Lemongrass. 
> Su Song says: Today, it is also found in the prefectures of Shaanxi, Henan, and eastern Bian. In the third month, shoots emerge resembling barley. In the fifth month, it opens white flowers, though some are yellow. Some bear fruit while others do not. The roots are harvested in the first and second months, flowers in the fifth, and fruit in the eighth. It is also called "Mao-Xiang." The root resembles thatch but is clear and long. It is excellent for bath decoctions, especially when paired with Lovage <note>original: "Gaoben"</note>. It is also used in compounding incense with Shell-incense and Cyperus.
> Shizhen says: There are two types of Fragrant Thatch. This is one variety. The "White Fragrant Thatch" is a different variety from the southern foreign regions. The Tang *Materia Medica* did not understand this distinction and mistakenly included notes about White Thatch flowers under this entry. I have now separated them into their respective categories.

The flower has a bitter and warm flavor and is non-toxic. It is primarily used to treat "Middle Evil" <note>sudden collapse or stroke</note>, to warm the stomach and stop vomiting, and to relieve cold pain in the heart and abdomen.

**Attached Formula** <gloss>New</gloss>

> **For Chronic Cold Fatigue and Lingering Illness:** <gloss>Take 4 *liang* <note>approx. 124g</note> of Fragrant Thatch flowers and 4 *liang* of Mugwort leaves. Char them while retaining their medicinal properties, then grind into a fine powder. Mix with millet rice to form pills the size of parasol tree seeds. Initially, take 20 to 30 pills with a decoction of Cnidium seeds. If slight vomiting occurs, it is not a concern. Afterward, take with date soup for immediate effect.</gloss>

# Seedlings and Leaves <gloss>From the *Kaibao Materia Medica*</gloss>

## White Thatch Fragrance <gloss>Supplement to the Materia Medica</gloss>
<gloss>Collected Explanations</gloss> **Chen Cangqi** <note>A Tang Dynasty pharmaceutical scholar</note> states: White Thatch Fragrance grows in Annan <note>Modern-day Vietnam</note>. It belongs to the same category as the "Arranged Fragrance" (*Paixiang*) used today. It is not the common White Thatch found along roadsides, nor is it the "Thatch Fragrance Flower" of the northern territories.

**Root** <gloss>Flavor and Nature: Sweet, balanced, and non-toxic.</gloss> <gloss>Main indications</gloss> Used for chills; it makes the body fragrant. ## Arranged Grass Fragrance <gloss>Compendium of Materia Medica</gloss>
<gloss>Collected Explanations</gloss> **Li Shizhen** says: Arranged Grass Fragrance comes from Jiaozhi <note>Northern Vietnam/border regions</note>. Today it is also cultivated in the regions south of the Five Ridges. It is a grass root, white in color, and shaped like fine willow roots. Many people sell counterfeits. **Fan Chengda** states in his *Treatise on the Fragrant South* <note>Guihai Yuheng Zhi</note>: Arranged Grass Fragrance looks like White Thatch Fragrance but has a scent as powerful as musk. It is used in blending incense, and no other fragrance can match it. There is also "Muskwood" from Champa <note>Zhancheng, in modern Vietnam</note>, which is the heartwood of old, decayed trees; its scent is very similar to musk.

**Root** <gloss>Flavor and Nature: Pungent, warm, and non-toxic.</gloss> <gloss>Main indications</gloss> Expels foul odors and wards off evil or malevolent influences. <gloss>Shizhen</gloss>

<gloss>Appendix</gloss> **Lingxiang** <note>Likely Lysimachia fœnum-graecum, or Fenugreek-scented grass</note> <gloss>Tao Hongjing says: According to Chen Cangqi, it grows in the mountain valleys of the South Seas. Boiled in water, it treats "water-floating qi" (edema). Decoct with soil-ginger and mustard seeds as a bath to treat severe wind-itch (rashes). ## Rosemary <gloss>Supplement to the Materia Medica</gloss>
<gloss>Collected Explanations</gloss> **Cangqi** says: The *Extensive Records* states it comes from the Western Sea. He and Cao Zhi both wrote rhapsodies about it. Its general form is a plant with tall, soft stems and delicate branches. The leaves are small and the flowers are purple. It bears fruit and does not wither even in severe frost. It is harvested and the leaves are stripped and placed in sachets to be worn; the fragrance is extremely strong, sharing the same "qi" as the modern Arranged Fragrance.

<gloss>Flavor and Nature: Pungent, warm, and non-toxic.</gloss> <gloss>Main indications</gloss> Treats malevolent air and scents clothing. People in ancient times often cultivated it. It is similar to modern Orchid Fragrance (*Lanxiang*) and Lingling Fragrance.

## Aina Fragrance <gloss>Supplement to the Materia Medica</gloss>

## Thread Incense (Incense Sticks)
<gloss>Compendium <note>Li Shizhen says</note>. Modern methods for blending incense are numerous, but only "thread incense" <note>the precursor to modern incense sticks</note> is suitable for clinical use in treating sores and wounds. The ingredients vary. Generally, it uses Dahurian Angelica, Sichuan Lovage, Notopterygium, Sweet Pine, Kaempferia, Clove, Patchouli, Lovage, Galangal, Fennel, Forsythia, Rhubarb, Baikal Skullcap, Cypress wood, and Liquidambar resin. These are ground into a powder, mixed with elm bark and flour to make a paste, and then kneaded. It is pressed into threads like wire or coiled into shapes and characters, suspended by iron or copper wires <note>Shizhen says</note>.</gloss>

**[Flavor and Nature]** Acrid, warm, non-toxic.

**[Main Indications]** Used to "smoke" (fumigate) various sores and ringworm. <note>Shizhen says</note>

## Patchouli
<gloss>Song Dynasty <note>*Jiayou Materia Medica*</note> **Correction**: <insert>Should properly</insert> be categorized under the Herbs section. Its original name was **Fragrant Grass** <note>original: "Xuncao"</note>.</gloss>

<gloss>Li Shizhen says: The leaves of beans are called *huo*. These leaves resemble them, hence the name. The *Weixi* records state: In the south, they use *Douluopo* <note>Sanskrit: Dronapushpa</note> fragrance to boil in water for bathing; this is the same plant. The *Lotus Sutra* calls it *Duomoloba* <note>Sanskrit: Tamalapatra</note>. The *Golden Light Sutra* calls it *Bodaluo* <note>Sanskrit: Patra</note>. These are all transliterations of Sanskrit words. The *Mahaparinirvana Sutra* also calls it *Jazun* fragrance <note>Collected Explanations <note>Tao says</note>. Following...</note></gloss>

The *Extensive Records* says: Patchouli grows in coastal countries. Its beans are like the *Duliang* plant. The leaves resemble water mint and can be placed among clothes for fragrance. Ji Han’s *Flora of the Southern Regions* says: It comes from the countries of Jiaozhi, Jiuzhen, Wuping, and Xinggu <note>regions in modern Vietnam and Southern China</note>. The officials and commoners plant it themselves. It grows in clusters; it is harvested in the fifth or sixth month and dried in the sun, at which point it becomes fragrant. <note>Su Song says</note> Patchouli is abundant in the Lingnan region. Many families cultivate it. In the second month, it sprouts. The stems and stalks are very dense and grow in clusters. The leaves resemble mulberry leaves but are smaller and thinner. It is harvested in the sixth or seventh month. One must wait until they turn yellow to collect them. The entire flower spike and stem are used.

The records of Gai, Qi, and Mo all state: People from the Kingdom of Funan <note>an ancient kingdom in mainland Southeast Asia</note> claim that five different fragrances all come from a single tree. The root is Sandalwood, the knots are Aloeswood, the flowers are Cloves, the leaves are Patchouli, and the resin is Frankincense. Therefore, the old Materia Medicas grouped these five together. However, in Lingnan today, Patchouli is clearly a type of grass. This matches what Ji Han described. Fan Ye’s *Incense Recipes* says that Patchouli <note>original: "Linghuo"</note> must be dried before use. The ancients used it to blend incense. The Funan story about the five fragrances coming from one tree seems to be a deception. <note>Shizhen says</note> Patchouli has square stems with nodes and is hollow inside. The leaves slightly resemble eggplant leaves. Masters Jiegu and Dongyuan only used the leaves and discarded the stems. Today, people use the stems as well, primarily because the leaves sold on the market are often adulterated. The *History of the Tang Dynasty* says: The Kingdom of Dunxun produces Patchouli. If you plant a branch, it grows; the leaves are like *Duliang*. This is the plant. Liu Xinqi’s *Records of Jiaozhou* says Patchouli resembles a turnip. Those who blend incense say this because the *scent* is similar, not because the *shape* is the same.

**[Flavor and Nature]** Acrid, slightly warm, non-toxic. <gloss>Li Yuansu says: Acrid and sweet. Also says: Acrid and bitter. Its "qi" is thick and its "flavor" is thin. It is light and rises; it is Yang. Li Gao says: It can rise and descend. It is Yang. It enters the Lung and Spleen meridians.</gloss>

**[Main Indications]** Edema caused by "wind-water" toxins, expels evil qi, and stops "cholera" <note>In TCM, "Huoluan" refers to acute, violent vomiting and diarrhea, not necessarily the specific bacterial disease</note> and abdominal pain. <note>*Supplementary Records*</note> It is an essential medicine for vomiting and nausea caused by Spleen and Stomach issues. It aids the stomach qi, opens the appetite, and encourages eating. <gloss>Yuansu says: Warms the center. Circulates qi. For Lung deficiency with cold or heat congestion in the "upper burner." Excellent for rinsing the mouth to treat alcohol breath. [Exposition]: Because its fragrance aids the Spleen and Stomach, Patchouli can stop vomiting and improve appetite. Wang Haogu says: It is a medicine for the Lung and Spleen meridians. Therefore, it is used in "Qi-Smoothing" formulas. Combined with Lindera (*Wuyao*), it clears the spirits. Combined with Astragalus...</gloss>
