# Fragrant Grass <gloss>Middle Grade, from the *Miscellaneous Records*</gloss> Lingling Fragrance <gloss>From the *Kaibao Era Records* of the Song Dynasty</gloss>

### <gloss>Explanation of Names</gloss> Hui Grass <gloss>Miscellaneous Records</gloss>, Fragrant Herb <gloss>Kaibao Era</gloss>, Swallow Grass <gloss>Compendium of Materia Medica</gloss>, Xunqin Grass <gloss>Jade Register</gloss>
> Li Shizhen states: The ancients burned this fragrant herb to summon the gods; thus it is called *Xun* (Fumigation) or *Hui* (Harmony). The *Book of Han* says, "The *Xun* herb burns itself because of its fragrance"—this is the plant. Some say the ancients weeded fields and used this herb to fumigate the soil, which is why it is called *Xun*. In the *Treatise on the Southern Wilderness* by Shen Chengda, it is said that Lingling is modern Yongzhou, but it does not produce this fragrance; rather, it is abundant in places like Rongzhou and Yizhou. The locals weave it into mats, which are warm and pleasant. I have carefully investigated this: the old seat of Lingling was in modern Quanzhou, which is the source of the Xiang River and where this fragrance grows in abundance. People commonly call it "Guangzhou Lingling Fragrance," and this is the true herb. Regions like Yongzhou and Wugang were historically part of Lingling. Nowadays, people in Zhenjiang and Danyang harvest it in season, wash it with wine, and sell it. Its scent is powerful and intense. It is often mentioned alongside the Orchid (*Lan*). The *Songs of Chu* <note>a classic anthology of Chinese poetry</note> mentions "nurturing nine *wan* <note>about 15 acres</note> of orchids and planting a hundred *mu* <note>about 16 acres</note> of *Hui*," showing the ancients cultivated it. The *Broadened Expositor* says *Lan* and *Hui* are the same, calling the leaves *Hui*. However, Huang Tingjian <note>a Song dynasty poet</note> argued that a single stem with many flowers is *Xun*, while a single stem with one flower is *Lan*. This was likely because he did not recognize the actual Fragrant Grass and used the flowers to distinguish them. Zheng Qiao's *Commentary on the Materia Medica* says *Lan* is *Hui* and *Xun* is Lingling Fragrance; this is also mere speculation and lacks clarity. In truth, the Orchid and Fragrant Grass are two species within the same category.

### <gloss>Collected Explanations</gloss>
> <gloss>The *Miscellaneous Records* states:</gloss> Fragrant Grass, also known as *Hui* Grass, grows in low, damp places. It is harvested in the third month and dried in the shade. Those with fallen leaf-nodes are best. It also says it grows in mountain plains and marshes. Tao Hongjing <note>a 5th-century polymath</note> says: The *Musical Records of Master Xiang* states the leaves resemble hemp and grow in opposite pairs. The *Classic of Mountains and Seas* mentions that on Floating Mountain grows a grass with hemp-like leaves, red stems, and black fruit, with an aroma like *miwu* <note>Selinum</note>; it is called *Xun* and can cure leprosy. Today, common folk call "Swallow Grass" (which looks like thatch but is fragrant) "Fragrant Grass" and cultivate it, but this is incorrect. Scholars often mention *Hui* without knowing what plant it is; they grasp the name but lose the reality. <gloss>Chen Cangqi states:</gloss> Fragrant Grass is indeed Lingling Fragrance; *Xun* is the root of the *Hui* plant. The *Records* state: Lingling Fragrance grows in the valleys of Lingling with leaves like basil. The *Records of the Southern Yue* say locals call it Swallow Grass or *Xun* Grass, which is the Fragrant Herb. The *Xun* Grass of the *Classic of Mountains and Seas* is this very plant. <gloss>Su Song states:</gloss> Lingling Fragrance is found today in many prefectures across Hubei and Hunan. It grows in low-lying damp areas, with hemp-like leaves in opposite pairs and square stems. It blooms in the seventh month and is extremely fragrant. The ancients called it *Xun* Grass. People in Lingnan <note>Southern China</note> make smoking baskets and dry it over a fire until it turns yellow, which is best. In the Yangtze and Huai regions, there is a local variety that can be used for incense, but it is not as good as the southern ones. Even when withered, its scent remains intense. Ancient formulas used *Xun* Grass, not Lingling Fragrance by that name. Today, makers of incense, face creams, and bath powders all use it. It is very common in the city markets.

### <gloss>Nature and Flavor</gloss> Sweet, balanced, non-toxic.
> <gloss>The *Expositor* says:</gloss> Bitter, non-toxic. <gloss>Zhen Quan says:</gloss> Acrid, warm, non-toxic. Do not take in large quantities as it causes wheezing. <gloss>The *Jade Register* says:</gloss> It can subdue sulfur, orpiment, and sal ammoniac.

### <gloss>Main Indications</gloss> Brightens the eyes and stops tearing. Treats seminal emission, removes foul odors and "evil qi." Treats typhoid headaches, rising qi, and back pain. <gloss>Miscellaneous Records</gloss> Used entirely to treat nasal polyps and congestion. <gloss>Zhen Quan</gloss>
> Lingling Fragrance primarily treats "evil qi," abdominal pain and fullness. It descends qi and makes the body fragrant. It is especially effective when combined with other aromatics in a decoction or steeped in wine. <gloss>Kaibao Era</gloss> Treats wind-evil attacking the heart, taxation-exhaustion, and childhood malnutrition/parasites. When decocted with Perilla and Asarum, it treats tooth swelling and pain. <gloss>Daming</gloss>

### <gloss>Discourse</gloss>
> Li Shizhen states: Fragrant Grass is aromatic and its qi is acrid and dispersing, reaching upwards. Thus, it is used for "evil qi" in the heart and abdomen, toothache, and nasal congestion. <gloss>Li Xun says:</gloss> It treats abdominal bloating due to blood and qi disorders; decoct the Fragrant Grass in wine for the patient. <gloss>For women:</gloss> Steep it in oil to dress the hair; its fragrance is unsurpassed. <gloss>Kou Zongshi states:</gloss> The Spleen and Stomach delight in fragrance; fragrance can "nourish the nose." However, excessive consumption causes wheezing because it consumes and disperses the "true qi" <note>the body's vital energy</note>.

### <gloss>Attached Formulas</gloss>
> Diarrhea from recent Cold Damage <note>Typhoid</note>: <gloss>Green Onion Decoction: Use two *liang* <note>approx. 75g</note> each of Fragrant Grass and Angelica, and four *liang* of Coptis. Boil in six *sheng* of water until two *sheng* remain. Take three doses a day. From *Fan Wang’s Formulas*</gloss>
> Fox-bewitchment syndrome <note>a TCM condition involving mucosal ulcers</note> from Cold Damage: <gloss>When the anus is affected, use four *liang* each of Fragrant Grass and Coptis. Shred them and soak overnight in one *dou* <note>approx. 2 liters</note> of juice from white stallion manure. Boil until two *sheng* remain and divide into three doses. From *The Small Grade Formulas*</gloss>
> "Bean Wind" <note>a type of dizziness</note>: <gloss>For dizziness, phlegm reversal, nausea, and lack of appetite: use genuine Lingling Fragrance, Patchouli, and Nutgrass root, each... </gloss>

<gloss>Zang Qi states: It grows by marshes. Women mix it with oil to gloss their hair, hence the name "Orchid Luster" (Lanze).</gloss>
<gloss>Tao Hongjing’s *Records of Jingzhou* says: In Duliang, there is a mountain with clear water below it where Orchid Grass grows, hence the name Duliang Fragrance.</gloss>
<gloss>Shizhen states: Duliang is modern Wugang Prefecture. It is also produced at Duliang Mountain in Xuyi County, Linhuai. Fragrant Orchid is a "fragrant herb" that can ward off evil. Lu Ji’s *Commentary on the Classic of Poetry* says that in Zheng customs, in the third month, men and women hold orchids by the river to perform purification rituals. The name "Female Orchid" may come from the *Huainanzi*, which says if a man plants orchids, they are beautiful but not fragrant; they require a woman to plant them. Because the leaves resemble chrysanthemums and women and children love to wear them, they are called "Child’s Chrysanthemum." Tang Yao’s *Treatise on Classics and Formulas* says families in the south plant it. During the summer, they place it in their hair to prevent the head from swelling, hence the name "Head-Cleansing Grass." This matches the "Luster" meaning. In ancient times, Lan and Hui were common terms for fragrant herbs; like Lingling Fragrance, any virtuous fragrant herb was called "Lan" (Orchid).</gloss>

However, the one with round stems, long nodes, glossy leaves, and bifurcated tips is Orchid Grass. The one with slightly square stems, short nodes, and hairy leaves is Swamp Reed. <meta>This page continues the catalog of aromatic herbs in Volume 14 of the Compendium of Materia Medica. It focuses on Lan Cao (Eupatorium fortunei), specifically addressing a long-standing historical confusion between this fragrant herb and the ornamental Orchid (Cymbidium). Li Shizhen provides a rigorous philological and botanical critique to distinguish the "True Orchid" of antiquity from modern varieties.</meta>

The older plants grow to three or four feet tall. The flowers bloom in spikes, resembling the flowers of Water Mint <note>original: "Jisu"</note>, appearing in red and white. Inside are tiny seeds. In his *Treatise on the Preparation of Medicines*, Lei Xiao stated that "Great Swamp Reed" is actually Orchid Grass, while "Small Swamp Reed" is the plant known as Swamp Reed <note>original: "Zelan," referring to Lycopus lucidus</note>. The *Book of Rites* mentions wearing it at the waist with sashes, and how the autumn orchid was fashioned into pendants. The *Miscellaneous Records of the Western Capital* records that during the Han Dynasty, orchids were planted in palace ponds to ward off evil spirits, or mixed into powders and stored in clothes and books to repel moths. Both of these practices refer to these two types of "Orchid." Today, people in the Wu region <note>the lower Yangtze delta</note> call it "Fragrant Grass." In the summer months, it is harvested, processed with wine and oil, tied into bundles, and sold as a hair treatment or worn as a pendant. This matches the descriptions of the "large-leaved" variety in the *Additional Records*. Various scholars did not realize that these two "orchids" are two species of the same genus, though their medicinal functions differ in terms of "Qi" <note>vital energy</note> and "Blood"; thus, there has been no settled conclusion. The errors made by Master Kou and Master Zhu were particularly severe, so I have provided a correction below. Some say the cultivated variety is Orchid Grass and the wild one is Swamp Reed, which is also an acceptable distinction.

<gloss>Correction of Errors</gloss>
<gloss>Kou Zongshi stated: "The descriptions of Orchid Grass by various authors differ, and they seem not to recognize it, leaving no settled conclusion. Today, it is found quite often in the valleys of Jiangling, Ding, and Lizhou. It is absent from the flat fields outside the mountains. It mostly grows in shaded areas and secluded valleys. The leaves resemble Lilyturf <note>original: "Maidong"</note> but are broader, tougher, and one to two feet long, remaining green through all four seasons. The flowers are yellow-green with fine purple spots on the central petals. Those that bloom in spring are Spring Orchids and have a deep color; those in autumn are Autumn Orchids and are pale. When they bloom, the whole room is filled with fragrance, distinct from any other flower." Zhu Zhenheng stated: "Orchid leaves receive the energy of 'Metal' and 'Water' but seem to possess 'Fire.' People know the value of the flower's fragrance but do not realize the leaves have medicinal power. The leaves can disperse long-accumulated stagnant 'Qi' very effectively. This is the plant I keep by my seat." Li Shizhen notes:</gloss>

What Master Wang <note>referring to Wang Ji</note> described is the modern "Orchid Flower" <note>Cymbidium</note>, not the Orchid Grass of antiquity. There are several types of orchids. The poet Huang Shanting claimed that a single stem with one flower is an "Orchid," while a stem with multiple flowers is a "Hui." This was because he did not recognize Orchid Grass or Swamp Reed, and thus forced a distinction upon the Orchid flowers. Orchid Grass and Swamp Reed are of the same class. Thus, Lu Ji said that the Orchid resembles Swamp Reed but is broader and longer. The *Songs of Chu* <note>original: "Li Sao"</note> describes it as having "green leaves, purple stems, and white branches," noting it can be worn, sat upon, used as a straw mat, or used in a bath. The *Book of Odes* mentions "men and women holding orchids," and Ying Shao's *Popular Customs* mentions harvesting fragrant plants for spring rites on the Dragon Boat Festival. The *Book of Rites* says "feudal lords offer Xun, and high officials offer Lan," and the *Book of Han* says "the orchid burns itself because of its fragrance." However, modern orchid flowers have leaves but no stems <note>stalks with leaves</note>; they are for enjoyment, not for wearing. For wearing, pounding into medicine, or bathing, it is logical to use Orchid Grass. Thus, Master Zhu Xi's *Corrections on the Songs of Chu* states: "The fragrant herbs of the ancients must have had fragrant leaves and flowers, and their scent did not change whether dry or wet; thus they could be worn. Modern Orchids and Hui have fragrant flowers but the leaves have no scent; they are weak and wither easily, and cannot be worn. It is clear they are not what the ancients referred to." The ancient Orchid was a relative of Swamp Reed, which is the same as modern Sweet Basil <note>original: "Lingling Xiang"</note>. It looks like thatch grass but has two kinds of flowers; I do not know when the confusion began. Xiong Taigu's *Jiyue Collection* states: "The orchid of common folk grows in deep mountains and remote valleys; it is certainly not the 'Water-Swamp Orchid' of ancient times." Chen Lizhai's *Leisurely Readings* says: "The orchid of the *Songs of Chu* is thought by some to be Duliang Fragrance, by others Swamp Reed, and by others 'Holland' <note>He-lan</note> fragrance; Swamp Reed should be considered the correct one." The plants grown by people today that look like Lilyturf are called "Secluded Orchids" <note>You Lan</note>, but they are not the true Orchid. Thus, Chen Zhizhai wrote the *Tale of the Stolen Orchid* to mock this. Fang Xugu's *Poetry on Orchids* says: "Ancient Orchid Grass is modern Qianjin Grass, commonly called 'Child Daisy.' What people call 'Orchid' today has leaves like shepherd's purse but tenderer; the root is called 'Earth Teasel' <note>Tu Xuduan</note>. Because the flowers are clustered and fragrant, it gained the name Orchid." Yang Sheng’an said: "The world takes plants resembling Sweet Flag <note>Changpu</note> to be the Orchid; the 'Nine-Acre Garden' <note>a reference to Qu Yuan's orchid fields</note> has been slandered for a long time!" Furthermore, Wu Caolu wrote a very detailed account of the Orchid, saying: "The Orchid is a top-grade medicine in the medical classics. It has stems and leaves; it is a branching plant. Modern so-called Orchids have no branches and no stems. Because Huang Shanting praised them, the world mistakenly points to them as the Orchid of the *Songs of Chu*. Master Kou’s *Materia Medica* followed this common error and rejected old descriptions as wrong. Medical classics are for practical use; how can we allow such errors? Can the modern 'Orchid' fruit really promote urination, kill parasites, and remove phlegm? Its cultivation is most popular in Fujian. Master Zhu Xi was from Fujian; would he not recognize his local products? Instead, he analyzed it this way. Even now, commoners take the 'non-orchid' to be the Orchid—how hard this confusion is to resolve! Alas! Seeing the clear analysis of these scholars, the errors of Kou and Zhu are obvious. Those in the medical profession who use Orchid Grass should no longer have any doubts."

<meta>This page continues the botanical and medicinal analysis of aromatic herbs, transitioning from the discussion of Orchid Grass (Eupatorium) to its close relative, Swamp Reed (Lycopus). It addresses the physiological causes of "wasting-thirst" syndrome and provides detailed instructions for preparing traditional hair oils before diving into the specific properties of Swamp Reed.</meta>

When the flavor enters the mouth, it is stored in the spleen and stomach to circulate its essence, vital energy <note>Qi</note>, and fluids. When stored in the spleen, it causes the mouth to taste sweet; this is triggered by the consumption of rich, fatty foods. This energy overflows upward and transforms into "wasting-thirst" <note>original: "Xiao Ke," a condition similar to modern diabetes</note>. This is treated with Orchid Grass to remove stagnant energy. Wang Bing <note>a famous Tang dynasty commentator</note> noted that this works because its pungency has a dispersing quality. When Li Dongyuan treated wasting-thirst with his "Fluid-Engendering Drink," he used orchid leaves, likely basing his formula on this principle. Details can be found under the entry for Swamp Reed. Furthermore, this plant can be soaked in oil and applied to the hair to remove dandruff and grime, leaving a fragrance. This is what the *Records of the Grand Historian* refers to when describing the subtle scent of "fragrant oil" detected when a silk robe is unbuttoned. The *Collection of Treasures* and the *Almanac of the Four Seasons* provide a method for making this fragrant oil: use clear oil to soak four ingredients—Orchid, Patchouli <note>original: "Huoxiang"</note>, Cloves <note>original: "Lishexing," literally 'tongue-leaving fragrance'</note>, and Alfalfa leaves. Wrap them in fresh silk and soak in sesame oil. Mix with lard in a copper cauldron. Once it stops boiling, add a small amount of Sweet Wormwood. Cover the jar with silk and pour the liquid out through a narrow-spouted vessel for use.

# Swamp Reed <gloss>Middle Grade of the Divine Husbandman's Classic</gloss> Corrected <gloss>Incorporating "Earth Grass" from the Jiayou Era</gloss>
### Alternative Names: Water Fragrance <gloss>Wu Pu</gloss>, Duliang Fragrance <gloss>Divine Husbandman's Classic</gloss>, Tiger Puss <gloss>Additional Records</gloss>, Dragon Date <gloss>Divine Husbandman's Classic</gloss>, Child’s Chrysanthemum <gloss>Compendium</gloss>, Wind Medicine <gloss>Compendium</gloss>. The root is named Earth Bamboo Shoot <gloss>Jiayou Era</gloss>.

<margin>Jing says: It grows by the side of marshes (Ze), hence the name Swamp Reed (Zelan). It is also called Duliang Fragrance. Shizhen says: This herb can also be used to make fragrant hair oil.</margin>
The name does not only refer to its growth near marshes. People in Anhui call it "Wind Medicine." Wu Pu’s *Materia Medica* calls it Water Fragrance. Master Tao says it is also called Duliang Fragrance. **Collective Explanations** <gloss>The *Additional Records* state: Swamp Reed grows near large marshes in Ru’nan. Harvest on the third day of the third month and dry in the shade.</gloss> Today, it is commonly called Child’s Chrysanthemum, which further proves that Orchid Grass and Swamp Reed are two species of the same plant. Its root is edible, hence the name Earth Bamboo Shoot. <gloss>The *Collection* states: It grows in low-lying water margins. Leaves resemble the orchid. In the second month, it sprouts with red joints and four leaves growing opposite each other.</gloss> Hongjing says: It is found everywhere now, mostly in low, damp ground. The leaves have a faint fragrance and can be boiled for oil or used in bathwater. Many people cultivate it, though the leaves vary slightly. Today, there is another very similar kind found in the mountains, but its stem is square and its leaves are small and tough, lacking fragrance. Since the name is "Swamp" Reed, the mountain variety is incorrect, yet pharmacists still use it. Master Cai says: Swamp Reed has square stems and purple joints; the leaves resemble Orchid Grass but are not very fragrant. This is the variety used in the capital today. Master Tao’s description actually refers to Orchid Grass, which has round stems and fragrant white flowers, quite different from Swamp Reed. Master Yuan says: Today it is found in Jing, Xu, Sui, Shou, Shu, Mei, Wu, and Hezhong. The roots are purplish-black like madder roots. In the second month, it sprouts two to three feet high. The stems are bluish-purple and square-edged. The leaves grow in opposite pairs like mint and are faintly fragrant. In the seventh month, it flowers with purplish-white blossoms and purple calyxes, also resembling mint. Harvest the shoots in the third month and dry in the shade. Households in the Lingnan region often plant it. The variety from Shouzhou has no flowers. It is generally similar to Orchid Grass, but Orchid Grass grows near water with glossy leaves and small purple roots, peaking in the fifth or sixth month. Swamp Reed grows in marshes and damp ground; its leaves have fine hairs and are not glossy. The stems and leaves become slightly pungent in the seventh or eighth month. This is the difference. Master Xia says: To use it, one must distinguish between "Male" and "Female" types. The "Great Swamp Reed" has round stems and leaves with greenish-yellow roots; it generates blood and regulates energy. The "Small Swamp Reed" has square stems with pointed roots; it breaks up stagnant blood and clears obstructions. Zongshuang says: Swamp Reed branches out as soon as it leaves the ground. The back of the leaf is like a cattail but pointed and long. It is an error to say its leaves resemble the ornamental orchid. Today's orchid leaves resemble Lilyturf <note>Ophiopogon</note> and are not similar at all. Shizhen says: Wu Pu’s description is the true Swamp Reed. The "Great Swamp Reed" mentioned by Lei Xiao is actually Orchid Grass, while his "Small Swamp Reed" is this Swamp Reed. The variety mentioned by Kou Zongshuang is similar but incorrect; his criticism of Wu Pu stems from his own mistake of confusing the ornamental Orchid flower with the medicinal Orchid herb. See the "Orchid Grass Corrections" below for details.

# Compendium of Materia Medica

## Volume 14

Energy <note>Qi</note> produces blood. When this energy is potent, it can break up stagnant blood and clear internal accumulations. This aligns with the properties of the two types of "Orchid" <note>referring to *Zelan* and *Lan-cao*</note> used in treatments. The effectiveness of Swamp Reed <note>original: "Zelan"</note> is even more reliable than common Orchid Grass. Since blood is generated from energy, we say it "regulates energy to produce blood." Furthermore, the philosopher Xunzi stated that "Swamp Reed and Fragrant Angelica <note>original: "Baizhi"</note> nourish the nose," referring to how the fragrant scent of these herbs opens the passages of the lungs.

### Indian Aster <gloss>From Rihuazi</gloss>

<gloss>Explanation of Names</gloss> **Purple Chrysanthemum.** <gloss>Shizhen says: Its leaves resemble the Orchid but are larger; its flower resembles the Chrysanthemum.</gloss>

<gloss>Collection of Explanations</gloss> <gloss>Chen Zangqi says: Indian Aster grows near marshes, similar to Swamp Reed but with a stronger scent. The *Songs of Chu* used "vile weeds" to symbolize "vile men"; people see its purple flowers and call it Purple Chrysanthemum, hence the name. In common speech, the larger variety is called "Ma" (Horse) Aster. Su Song says: It is named for its resemblance to Orchid and its purple color. There is also a "Mountain Aster" growing on slopes, resembling the leaves of *Liu Jinu* (Artemisia), but without the opposite leaf pattern. The flower center is slightly yellow. It is excellent for breaking stagnant blood. Li Shizhen says: Indian Aster is abundant in damp lake areas. In the second month, it sprouts with red stems and white roots. The leaves have serrated edges like Swamp Reed but lack the fragrance. Southerners harvest the shoots and dry them as vegetables or for steaming with rice. By summer, it reaches two or three feet high and blooms with purple flowers. After blooming, it produces small seeds. There is no basis for the *Songs of Chu* categorizing Indian Aster as a "vile weed."</gloss>

**Roots and Leaves** <gloss>Flavor and Nature</gloss> **Pungent, neutral, non-toxic.**

<gloss>Main Indications</gloss> **Breaks up old stagnant blood and nourishes new blood. Stops nosebleeds, vomiting of blood, and bleeding from wounds. Treats "wine jaundice" <note>jaundice caused by excessive alcohol</note> and various toxins from fungi or insects. Freshly crushed and applied to snake bites. Treats malaria and acute abdominal pain.**

<gloss>Invention</gloss> <gloss>Shizhen says: Indian Aster is pungent and neutral, entering the "Yangming" blood level. Therefore, its blood-treating powers are equal to Swamp Reed. Recently, people have used it to treat hemorrhoids with success. In spring and summer, use the fresh plant; in autumn and winter, use the dried. Boil in plain water without salt or vinegar and eat it. Drink the juice as well. Alternatively, boil in wine, dry, grind, and form into pills with rice paste to be taken daily. Use the decoction with a little salt to wash the area daily. The *Collection of Medical Achievements* says: To treat hemorrhoids, crush the root and apply it; remove it once the flesh appears level.</gloss>

# Aromatic Madder <gloss>pronounced "róu"</gloss> ○ <gloss>Revised entry: moved from the Vegetable Section to this Herb Section</gloss> 
### Also known as Fragrant Vegetable <gloss>same as Fragrant Ear</gloss>, High Fragrant Vegetable, <gloss>Gold Silkworm Herb</gloss>

<margin>
Li Shizhen’s *Compendium* notes: The name *ru* was originally written as *róu*, similar to the *róu* in *róusū* (a type of perilla). It possesses a fragrant aroma and its leaves are soft, which is why it was named "Soft" (*róu*). The character for *róu* includes the component for "soft." It is colloquially called "Bee Herb" because its flower clusters resemble a beehive.
</margin>

<insert>Collected Explanations</insert> <gloss>Tao Hongjing says:</gloss> Every household grows this as a vegetable to be eaten raw. In the tenth month, it is harvested and dried. <gloss>Su Song says:</gloss> It is found everywhere, though it is somewhat rarer in northern regions. It resembles White Turnip but the leaves are much finer. Both Shouchun and Xin'an produce it. In those areas, there is another variety called "Stone Aromatic Madder" which grows on rocks; its leaves are even finer, yellowish in color, and it has an even more intense pungent fragrance. This variety is considered superior for medicinal use. People in the Wu region use it as a substitute for Wormwood (*Yinchen*). <gloss>Kou Zongshi says:</gloss> It grows in wild fields throughout Jingzhou, Hunan, Hubei, and Sichuan. In the capital areas of Bian and Luo, people plant it in gardens. During the summer months, it is served as a vegetable. The leaves are like Wormwood, and the purple flowers form clusters on the edges of the spikes. Each spike contains forty to fifty flower pods, looking like Schizonepeta (*Jingjie*) spikes, but with a distinct fragrance. <gloss>Li Shizhen says:</gloss> There are both wild and cultivated varieties. People in the Central Plains plant it in the third month and call it "Aromatic Madder" to use as a food item. Zhu Danxi <note>a famous Yuan Dynasty physician</note> argued that only the large-leaved variety is good, but the small-leaved variety is actually more fragrant and potent, and is more commonly used today. It has square stems, pointed leaves with serrated edges—somewhat like Chaste Tree (*Huangjing*) leaves but smaller. In the ninth month, it produces purple flower spikes with tiny seeds. The small-leaved type grows only a few inches high. <gloss>Wu Hui says:</gloss> When harvesting, remove the roots and keep the leaves. Chop them and dry them in the sun. Do not let them touch fire. If one takes ten ounces over a lifetime, they will never suffer from <gloss>constipation/blocked Qi</gloss>.

# False Perilla
<gloss>From the *Divine Husbandman's Classic of Materia Medica*, Middle Grade</gloss> <gloss>Correction: Moved here from the Vegetable Section</gloss>

<meta>This page continues the botanical and medicinal profile of herbs from the previous page, moving from Aromatic Madder to a detailed examination of Schizonepeta (Jingjie). Su Song <note>a prominent Song Dynasty scholar and pharmacologist</note> states: The medical official Chen Yi says that people south of the Yangtze River believe False Perilla and Schizonepeta are two different things. Su Gong <note>a Tang Dynasty editor of the Materia Medica</note> argued that the name "Ginger Mustard" in the *Classic of Materia Medica* was a mistake for Schizonepeta, and that calling it "False Perilla" was also incorrect. Shizhen says: According to the *Materia Medica of Wu Pu*, False Perilla is another name for Schizonepeta. Its leaves resemble those of smartweed but are finer. In the Shu region <note>modern Sichuan</note>, people eat it raw. Wu Pu lived near the end of the Eastern Han Dynasty, a time not far removed from when these records were compiled; his words are likely accurate. Therefore, Su Gong of the Tang followed this theory. When Chen Shiliang later raised doubts that they were two separate things, it was merely his own speculation. The names *Wei* <note>original: 薇</note>, *Jiang* <note>original: 薑, "Ginger"</note>, and *Jie* <note>original: 芥, "Mustard"</note> all refer to its aromatic and pungent nature, as they belong to similar categories of plants. <gloss>The *Additional Records* state: False Perilla grows in the rivers and marshes of Hanzhong. Su Song says: It is now found everywhere. The leaves look like Goosefoot but are finer. When it first sprouts, it is fragrant and pungent and can be eaten. People use it as a raw vegetable. It was rarely used in ancient formulas, but in recent times, it has been included in medicines in the same way.</gloss> Shizhen says: Schizonepeta was originally a wild plant, but because it is so useful now, it is widely cultivated. The seeds are sown in the second month. When the seedlings grow, they can be stir-fried and eaten; they are fragrant and pungent. The stems are square, and the leaves are fine, <gloss>The *Evidence* <note>referring to the *Materia Medica for Practical Use*</note> says: One name for it is "Xisui," but this is an error; "Xirou" is a separate entry.</gloss> narrow, and a pale yellowish-green. In the eighth month, it produces small flowers on spikes that form seed pods. The pods resemble those of Purple Perilla. Inside the pods are tiny seeds like those of Tansy Mustard; they are yellowish-red. The spikes are harvested along with the seeds for medicinal use. <gloss>This entry is found in the Herb Category.</gloss> Shizhen says: Wang Ji’s *Compilation of the Materia Medica* claims that False Perilla is the same as White Swallow-wort <term>Baiwei: Cynanchum atratum</term>, but this is also an error. White Swallow-wort is actually a type of Perilla, as seen later in the text.

### Schizonepeta Spikes
The "qi" <note>energetic property</note> and flavor are acrid, warm, and non-toxic. <gloss>It is said: If eaten as a vegetable for too long, it triggers thirst and irritates the spirits of the five internal organs. # Compendium of Materia Medica, Volume 14

When using Schizonepeta <note>original: 荆芥, *Jingjie*; a medicinal herb in the mint family</note> for Wind-related illnesses, one must avoid eating fish. Yang Chengzhai once witnessed a person die almost instantly from this combination. Shizhen notes: Schizonepeta is a medicine used daily, yet its contraindications are so severe. Therefore, I have recorded this in detail as a warning. Also note: <gloss>Appended Formulas</gloss> <gloss>4 old, 27 new</gloss>

The *Treatise on the Mutual Resonance of Things* states that if pufferfish is boiled with Schizonepeta three to five times, changing the water each time, it becomes non-toxic. Why does this account differ from all other books? Generally speaking, those who care for their health should strictly observe the previous warning as a precaution.

### Head-Wind <note>A term for chronic or severe headaches often attributed to "Wind" pathogens</note>

For severe cases: After the eighth lunar month, take Schizonepeta spikes and make a pillow out of them, or spread them under the bed. Remove them on the first day of spring. <gloss>From *Formulas Worth a Thousand Gold*</gloss>

For Wind-Heat headaches: Take equal parts Schizonepeta spikes and Gypsum <note>original: 石膏, *Shigao*; a cooling mineral</note> and grind into a powder. Take two mace <note>approximately 7.5 grams</note> per dose, mixed into tea. <gloss>From *Yonglei Kanfang*</gloss>

For Wind-Heat causing red eyes: Schizonepeta spikes, chopped green onion roots, and one ounce of white salt. <gloss>From *One Hundred and Twenty Varieties*</gloss> Use one ounce of Schizonepeta spikes and one ounce of Alum <note>half raw and half prepared</note>. Grind into powder and make pills the size of millet using paste. Coat them with Sal Ammoniac <note>original: 硇砂, *Naosha*</gloss>. Take twenty-nine pills per dose with ginger soup, twice a day. <gloss>From *Collected Works of Medicine*</gloss>

### All Types of Partial Wind <note>Referring to hemiplegia or facial paralysis</note>

For a deviated mouth and eyes: Use one pound of fresh Schizonepeta and one pound of fresh Mint. Grind them together in a mortar until pulverized. Squeeze the juice through raw silk and simmer it in an earthen vessel until it becomes a thick paste. Strain out one-third of the residue. Dry the remaining two-thirds in the sun and grind into powder. Mix the powder with the paste to form pills the size of a parasol tree seed. Take thirty pills per dose with plain broth, once in the morning and once in the evening. Avoid foods that "stir the Wind" <note>such as seafood or spicy foods</note>.

### Lockjaw from Stroke

Grind Schizonepeta spikes into a powder. Take two mace with wine; recovery is immediate. This is called "Schizonepeta Powder." Jia Sidao <note>a late Song Dynasty official</note> said: "This formula comes from the *Conversations of Lord Hui*. I have recorded its use many times with great success. When my son, named Shun, was critically ill with this condition, he recovered instantly after taking it. It is truly a pill of rebirth." <gloss>From *Tested Formulas*</gloss>

### Postpartum Stroke

"Hua Tuo's Wind-Curing Powder" <note>original: 愈風散, *Yufeng San*</note>. This treats women who suffer from postpartum Wind-stroke, lockjaw, and tetanic spasms where the body bends backward like a bow <note>opisthotonos</note>; or postpartum blood fainting where the patient is unconscious with rigid limbs; or when the eyes are upturned, and they suffer from vomiting and diarrhea to the point of death. Use Schizonepeta spikes, lightly toasted and ground into powder. Take three mace per dose, mixed with "bean-drenched wine" <note>wine in which hot black beans have been soaked</note> or child's urine. If the jaw is locked, pry the teeth open to pour it in. If the jaw is completely clamped, pour it into the nose. The effect is miraculous. Generally, after childbirth, the body is strained, leading to sweating and "loose pores," which makes it easy for Wind to invade. Shizhen says: This formula is praised for its excellence in many books. Yao Sengtan's *Collection of Proven Formulas* uses it with wine and calls it "As-If-Sacred Powder," saying the effect can be seen as soon as the medicine is swallowed. Chen's collection calls it "Juqing Gubai Powder." Xiao Cunjing's formulas use a decoction of old copper coins to take it, calling it "A Pinch of Gold." Wang Kuang’s *Guide to Faraway Places* adds equal parts Angelica and decocts it in water. Xu Shuwei's *Formulas of an Accomplished Physician* says: "This medicine has truly extraordinary effects, a work of the divine. # Mint <gloss>From *Tang Materia Medica*</gloss> <insert>Revised</insert> <gloss>Moved here from the Vegetable Section</gloss> <gloss>Pronounced *Bo-he*</gloss> <gloss>Also named *Zuolan*, *Suhe*, *Wu-zuo*, *Southern Mint*, *Money Mint*</gloss>

<gloss>Shizhen says: "Mint" is the common name. Chen Shiliang's *Materia Medica of Food Properties* calls it *Zuolan*. Yang Xiong's *Ganquan Ode* calls it *Zuolu*. Lü Shen’s *Lexicon* calls it *Weitai*. Thus, we can see the many names for Mint. Sun Simiao's *Formulas Worth a Thousand Gold* calls it *Fanhe*, which is a phonetic error. Modern medicinal use favors those from Suzhou; therefore, Chen Shiliang called it "Wu-Mint" to distinguish it from "Hu-Mint." Song Shi’s *Jiayou Materia Medica* says the world calls this "Southern Mint" because there is another variety called "Borneo-camphor Mint." Some say that pediatric formulas often use "Money Mint," whose leaves are small and round like coins; it is excellent for polishing gold and silver vessels. It grows everywhere. The stems and leaves resemble Perilla but are pointed and long. The roots do not die in winter. In summer and autumn, harvest the stems and leaves and dry them in the sun. Ancient formulas rarely used it, or only used it in broths with shallots. In recent times, it has become a primary medicine for treating Wind-Cold, so many households plant it. There is also "Hu-Mint" <note>Foreign/Spearmint</note> which is similar but tastes slightly sweeter; it grows in the Jiangsu and Zhejiang regions, where people use it for tea. It is commonly called "Silla Mint" <note>referring to the ancient Korean kingdom</note>. Recently, monasteries in the Bian and Luo regions have planted one or two varieties. This is what the *Single Formulas of the Tianbao Era* calls "Coin-Linked Grass." There is also "Stone Mint," which grows among mountain rocks in the southern mountains; its leaves are tiny and turn purple in winter, but no special medicinal effects are recorded. One account says people plant mint and also eat it raw; a creeping variety has similar effects. Shizhen notes: People plant it frequently. In the second lunar month, the old roots sprout. These are divided around the Qingming festival. The leaves grow opposite each other; at first, they are long and round-tipped, but they become pointed as they grow. People in Yuezhou and Lake regions often use it as a tea substitute. The variety planted in Suzhou has small stems and a fragrant aroma. Those from the riverbanks are coarser, and those from Sichuan are coarser still. For medicine, the Suzhou variety is superior. The *Record of the Mutual Resonance of Things* says: When harvesting mint, one must water it with manure water the night before and harvest after rain; then it will be cool in nature. Otherwise, it will lack its cooling, pain-relieving properties. Wild mint has purple stems, but the aroma and flavor are similar.</gloss>

# Asiatic Pennywort
<gloss>Middle Grade in the *Classic*. Also named *Baba* or Foreign Mint.</gloss>

I respectfully note that the *Formulas of the Tianbao Era* say: Connected Coin Herb grows in damp lowlands of Xianyang, as well as in the marshes of Linzi and Jiyang. It is very fragrant. Locals say the round leaves resemble mint. It is extremely common in the Danyang region of Wu and Yue, where people often eat it as a vegetable. In Liucheng, Hebei, it is called "Sea Hook"; it prefers growing near water and does not die in winter. It is also found in Xianyang and Jiyang. Some call it Foreign Mint. It is found everywhere. Taken alone, it treats ailments of the lower abdomen in women. Zhen Quan says: Asiatic Pennywort is common in the South, growing in dark, damp places, not just in Jingzhou. It looks like a small water lily, but the surface is smooth and clean. Each leaf grows individually. People today call it Connected Coin Herb based on its appearance.

Shizhen says: Following Su Gong’s note on mint, one variety is a vine with similar effects... The *Illustrated Classic* says: Foreign Mint is similar to common mint, but the taste is slightly sweeter. It grows near rivers and lakes. People there often use it as a tea, and it is commonly called "Silla Mint" <note>original: 新羅薄荷, *Xinluo bohe*</note>. This is the "Connected Coin Herb" used in the *Tianbao Formulas*. Based on these two accounts, Asiatic Pennywort is indeed Foreign Mint, which is a vining variety of mint. Furthermore, the *Classic of the Erya* and the *Jade Register of Acridity* state: Ground Coin Herb is an herb of the immortals. It grows...

## Perilla <gloss>Middle Grade in the Supplementary Records</gloss> <gloss>Revised</gloss> <insert>Moved here from the Vegetable Section</insert>

#### Explanation of Names
<gloss>Purple Perilla <gloss>Supplementary Records</gloss>, Red Perilla. <gloss>Shizhen says: The character "Su" (蘇) comes from the word meaning "to revive" or "comfort" (穌), because its nature is to soothe, promote the flow of qi, and harmonize the blood. It is called Purple Perilla in medical formulas to distinguish it from White Perilla. Since Perilla belongs to the "Ren" <note>Beefsteak plant</note> family but has a more acrid taste like cinnamon, the Erya dictionary calls it "Cinnamon-Ren."</gloss></gloss>

#### Collection and Notes
<gloss>Tao Hongjing says: If the underside of the leaf is not purple and lacks fragrance, looking like the "Ren" plant, it is called "Wild Perilla" and is not fit for medicinal use. Su Song says: Purple Perilla is found everywhere. Those with leaves that are purple on both sides are best. Harvest leaves in summer and seeds in autumn. There are several varieties like Water Perilla, Fish Perilla, and Mountain Perilla, all belonging to the "Ren" family, but each has its own entry. Shizhen says: Both Purple and White Perilla are sown in the second or third month, or grow from seeds left in the ground. The stems are square, and the leaves are round with pointed tips and serrated edges. In fertile soil, both sides of the leaf are purple; in poor soil, the top is green and the bottom is purple. Those that are white on both sides are White Perilla (the "Ren" plant). When Purple Perilla is tender, the leaves can be gathered and eaten as a vegetable, or pickled with salt and plum brine; they are very fragrant. In summer, they are made into a cooked infusion to drink. In the fifth or sixth month, the whole plant including the root is harvested, the roots are singed with fire, and then dried in the shade so the leaves do not fall off. In the eighth month, it bears small purple flowers in spikes. The seed pods resemble those of Schizonepeta. In the middle of the ninth month, harvest the seeds, which are tiny like mustard seeds and yellow-red. They can be pressed for oil just like "Ren" oil. The "Book of Essential Agriculture" says: Perilla can be planted along field borders and roads to block livestock. The seeds are harvested for lamp oil, which burns very brightly, or used to coat vessels. The "Source of the Alchemical Laboratory" says: Perilla oil can soften the "Five Metals and Eight Minerals" <note>metals and stones used in alchemy</note>. The "Records of Shazhou" state: In the lands of the Qifu captives, they do not grow the five grains but eat only Perilla seeds. Thus, Wang Zhen said Perilla has the merit of protection (as a hedge) and the utility of lamp oil; it is indispensable. Today there is a variety called "Flowering Purple Perilla," with finely toothed, wrinkled leaves like cut velvet. It is extremely fragrant, but the stems and seeds are no different. People call it "Huihui Su" <note>Crested Perilla</note>. Su Fu says: Mint roots and stems truly resemble Perilla, but the leaves are different. Perilla stems are mild; when using them in medicine, one must scrape away the green outer skin and slice them.</gloss>

# Stems and Leaves <gloss>Taste is acrid, property is warm, and it is non-toxic. Li Tingfei says: Do not eat with carp, as it causes toxic abdominal masses <note>original: "Jia," referring to hard masses formed by stagnation</note>.</gloss>

<insert>Main Indications</insert> Lowers uprising Qi <note>vital energy moving the wrong way, often causing coughing or vomiting</note>, removes cold, and is particularly good for warming the "middle" <note>the digestive system</note>. <gloss>From the Supplementary Records</gloss> Treats chills and fever and all types of "cold Qi" <note>ailments caused by environmental or internal cold</note>. <gloss>Meng Shen says</gloss> Tonifies the center and benefits the vital energy; treats abdominal bloating; stops "sudden turmoil" <note>original: "Huoluan," acute vomiting and diarrhea</note> and muscle cramps; opens the stomach to promote appetite; stops beriberi <note>original: "Jiaoqi," leg swelling or weakness</note>; and clears the large and small intestines. <gloss>Rihua says</gloss> Opens the Heart meridian and benefits the Spleen and Stomach. Drinking it as a decoction is superior. It pairs well with orange peel. <gloss>Su Song says</gloss> Generally used to release the exterior <note>induce sweating to break a cold</note>, disperse wind-cold, move vital energy, and widen the chest. It dissolves phlegm, benefits the lungs, harmonizes the blood, warms the digestive center, stops pain, calms asthma, and stabilizes the fetus <note>prevents miscarriage</note>. It also detoxifies fish and crab poisoning and treats snake and dog bites. <gloss>Shizhen says</gloss> Adding Perilla leaves to soups kills all toxins from fish and meat. <gloss>Chen Cheng says</gloss> Su Song noted that if treating wind-toxin, using the stem alone with the nodes removed is most effective. <gloss>Shizhen says</gloss> Perilla is an essential medicine in modern times. Its acrid taste enters the "Qi level," while its purple color enters the "Blood level." Therefore, when paired with orange peel and Amomum seed <note>original: "Sharen"</note>, it moves Qi and stabilizes the fetus. With Agastache <note>original: "Huoxiang"</note> and Lindera <note>original: "Wuyao"</note>, it warms the center and stops pain. With Cyperus <note>original: "Xiangfu"</note> and Ephedra <note>original: "Mahuang"</note>, it induces sweating and releases the muscles. With Atractylodes <note>original: "Cangzhu"</note> and Angelica <note>original: "Danggui"</note>, it harmonizes and disperses the blood. With Papaya and Magnolia bark <note>original: "Houpu"</note>, it disperses dampness and relieves summer heat, treating sudden turmoil and beriberi. With Platycodon <note>original: "Jiegeng"</note> and Bitter Orange <note>original: "Zhike"</note>, it benefits the diaphragm and widens the intestines. With Apricot kernel and Radish seed <note>original: "Laifuzi"</note>, it dissolves phlegm and calms asthma. <gloss>Wang Ji says</gloss> Emperor Renzhong of the Song Dynasty ordered the Hanlin Academy to determine the best medicinal beverage; they reported that "Perilla Infusion" <note>original: "Zisu Shushui"</note> was number one because it lowers floating Qi in the chest. However, they did not realize that long-term use can leak one's "True Qi" <note>the body's essential vital energy</note>. <gloss>Zongshi says</gloss> Perilla is fragrant and slightly acrid-sweet; it can disperse energy. People today drink Perilla tea morning and night, but it is not beneficial for those without an actual medical need. <insert>Correction of Errors</insert> <gloss>Shizhen says</gloss> Perilla is mainly used for chicken <note>as a digestive aid</note>, though the original classics do not mention this. In the Southern Qi records, Lu Cheng treated Li Daonian, who had developed an abdominal mass from eating white poultry eggs; this is one such example. If those with a "cold" Spleen and Stomach take it, it often causes diarrhea without them realizing the cause. <gloss>Wang Ji says</gloss> A patient once took Perilla for a mass and reportedly vomited up a small chick to be cured. <gloss>Shizhen says</gloss> According to my research into the Southern Qi books, the claim about the chick is an error; Su Song has already investigated this thoroughly. Details are under the entry for Garlic.

### Water Perilla
<gloss>Classified as Middle Grade in the Classic</gloss> <gloss>Revised: moved from the Vegetable Department to this location</gloss> <gloss>Also named:</gloss> Chicken Perilla <gloss>Wu</gloss>, Fragrant Perilla <gloss>From the Handbook of Emergencies</gloss>, Dragon-Brain Mint <gloss>From Daily Use</gloss>, Mustard-Ju <gloss>pronounced 'Ju'</gloss>, Perilla-Merge Record. Shizhen says: This herb resembles Perilla but grows in pairs by the water's edge, hence the name Water Perilla. Its acrid fragrance makes it suitable for seasoning food. Because its acrid taste is like mustard, it is also called Mustard-Ju. The Song Dynasty work *Formulas of the Radiant Grace Pharmacy* contains a "Dragon-Brain Mint Pill" specifically for treating blood diseases. Yuan Dynasty scholar Wu Rui stated in his *Materia Medica for Daily Use* that this is actually Water Perilla; he must have had a source for this. The *Tang Records* by Wang Yi on "Boiling Herbs" states that mint is actually Chicken Perilla, and those growing on Dragon-Brain Ridge in Dongping are of the best quality, hence the name. However, Chen Jiamo in the *Primer of Materia Medica* states that it is named after mint planted at the Suzhou Prefectural School in a place called Dragon-Brain. Why are these accounts so different?

<gloss>Collected Explanations</gloss> The *Supplementary Records* say: Water Perilla grows in the marshes of Jiuzhen <note>a historical commandery in modern-day Vietnam</note>; harvest in the seventh month. Hongjing says: It is not used in formulas, so few recognize it. Jiuzhen is far away and no one can visit to check. Su Song says: This Perilla grows in low-lying marshes by the water. The sprouts resemble *Rao* <note>Thistle-like herb</note>, with two leaves growing opposite each other. It is very fragrant. People of Qing, Qi, and Hejian call it Water Perilla. South of the Yangtze, it is called *Rao* grass. In Wu-Hui, it is called Chicken Perilla. Master Tao [Hongjing] was mistaken to list Chicken Perilla separately in the Vegetable Department. Baosheng says: The leaves resemble *Baiwei* <note>Swallowwort</note>, with two leaves opposite each other. Flowers grow between the nodes and are purplish-white. The taste is acrid and fragrant. Harvest the stems and leaves in the sixth month and dry in the sun. [Su] Song says: Water Perilla is found everywhere, mostly by water. Southerners often use it as a vegetable. It is abundant north of the river, but people there do not eat it. Also, people south of the Yangtze say Chicken Perilla and Water Perilla are two different species. Chen Cangqi says *Rao* grass is its own thing and not Water Perilla. Water Perilla stems have "goose teeth" <note>serrated edges</note> and the scent is fragrant and acrid. *Rao* grass leaves have hair, are slightly longer, and have a foul smell. Also, in the notes on *Yinchen* <note>Artemisia</note>, it says that the *Yinchen* used in the South has stems and leaves that look like garden *Yinchen* but grow three to four feet high. The scent is extremely fragrant, and the taste is sweet and acrid; it is commonly called Dragon-Brain Mint. Zongshi says: The scent and taste of Water Perilla are different from Purple Perilla; it is acrid but not harmonious. Its shape is exactly like *Rao*, but the surface is not purple, and it has serrated edges like goose teeth. [Wu] Rui says: Water Perilla is Chicken Perilla, commonly called Dragon-Brain Mint. Shizhen says: Water Perilla and *Rao* grass are of one category but two species. They are distinguished by scent: Water Perilla is fragrant, while *Rao* grass is foul-smelling. Water Perilla sprouts in the third month. The square stems are hollow. The leaves resemble *Rao* but are slightly longer with serrated edges and a wrinkled green surface. They grow in opposite pairs. The scent is very strong. In the sixth or seventh month, it flowers in spikes like Perilla, water-red in color. Inside the spikes are tiny seeds like mustard seeds. It is easy to plant and grows from old roots, or grows wild in fertile soil, reaching four to five feet in height.

### Motherwort Stems and Leaves
<gloss>Flavor and Nature</gloss> Acrid, slightly warm, non-toxic. <gloss>Main Indications</gloss> For children: aids digestion <note>original: "Sha Gu," literally 'kills grain'</note>, removes food stagnation, and eliminates bad breath. Wards off "evil toxins" and "evil Qi." Long-term consumption communicates with the spirit, lightens the body, and resists aging. <gloss>From the Classic</gloss> Primarily for vomiting blood, nosebleeds, and excessive uterine bleeding. <gloss>From the Supplementary Records</gloss> Treats lung atrophy, bloody dysentery, and vaginal discharge. <gloss>Rihua says</gloss> Primarily for all Qi-related disorders and abdominal masses. <gloss>Zhen Quan says</gloss> Cooked in clear wine or the juice extracted by boiling in wine; frequent consumption treats "head-wind" <note>chronic headaches</note>, dizziness, and postpartum "wind-stroke" <note>sudden collapse or neurological issues</note> where "evil blood" does not stop. In such cases, taking it is wonderful. <gloss>Meng Shen says</gloss> Eat it as a raw vegetable to remove stomach acidity. <gloss>Shizhen</gloss>

### Invention

Shizhen says: The medicinal power of Water Mint <note>original: *Jisu* (雞蘇), likely a variety of Mentha arvensis or Mentha aquatica</note> is specialized in regulating the blood, lowering uprising Qi <note>counter-flow energy that causes coughing or vomiting</note>, clearing the lungs, warding off "evil" <note>pathogenic influences or contagious diseases</note>, and aiding the digestion of grains. The *Formulas of the Peaceful Benevolent Dispensary* contains the "Dragon-brain Mint Pill" <note>Dragon-brain refers to the cooling, camphor-like scent of high-quality mint</note> used to treat vomiting blood, nosebleeds, blood in saliva, coughing up blood, blood in the stool, bloody urine, bad breath, a bitter or sweet taste in the mouth, a fishy sensation in the throat, and various diseases caused by "evil heat." Although the many ingredients of that formula are not recorded here, the method is exceptionally effective for blood diseases.

### Appendix of Formulas <gloss>6 old, 9 new</gloss>

**Vomiting or passing blood:** Decoct the juice from the stems and leaves of Water Mint and drink it. <gloss>From Master Mei’s Formulas</gloss>

**Vomiting blood or coughing:** Roast "Dragon-brain" Mint and grind into a powder. Take one *qian* <note>a traditional unit of weight, approx. 3.75g</note> with rice water to achieve results.

**Unstoppable nosebleeds:** <gloss>Master Mei’s Formulas</gloss> suggest taking five portions of Water Mint mixed with a walnut kernel the size of a date seed; insert this into the nostrils to stop the bleeding. <gloss>Formulas from the Divine Benevolence</gloss> <note>original: *Sheng Hui Fang*</note> uses two *taels* of Water Mint and one *tael* of *Saposhnikovia* <note>original: *Fangfeng*</note> ground into powder. Take two *qian* per dose with warm water, and also plug the nose with the leaves. <gloss>Formulas for Universal Relief</gloss> <note>original: *Pu Ji Fang*</note> uses Dragon-brain Mint and Rehmannia root <note>original: *Shengdihuang*</note>, among other ingredients.

**Heat in the brain and sinus congestion:** For lung congestion with excessive nasal discharge: use Water Mint, Ginseng, Ophiopogon <note>original: *Maimendong*</note>, Bamboo shavings, Mulberry bark (dry-fried until yellow), Licorice (honey-toasted), and Rehmannia root. Grind equal parts into powder and take with cold water.

**Wind-heat headaches:** When heat accumulates in the Upper Burner <note>the chest and head area</note> leading to "wind-air" and phlegm-syncope headaches: use five *taels* of Water Mint leaves (toasted), three *taels* of *Evodia* <note>original: *Wuzhuyu*, here referring to the seeds with skins removed</note>, and one *tael* of *Caryopteris* <note>original: *Qianghua*</note> (fried with vinegar until charred). Grind into powder and form into pills the size of parasol tree seeds using refined honey. Take twenty pills per dose after meals with *Schizonepeta* <note>original: *Jingjie*</note> decoction. <gloss>From Formulas from the Divine Benevolence</gloss>

**Sudden deafness or ear blockage:** Crush fresh Water Mint leaves and wrap them in silk or cotton to plug the ear. <gloss>From Meng Shen’s Dietetic Materia Medica</gloss>

**To make hair fragrant:** Use a decoction of Water Mint to wash, or use its ashes; this is the same as the previously mentioned formulas.

**Dim vision in summer months:** For eyes with excessive discharge or tearing: crush fresh Dragon-brain Mint leaves and squeeze the juice through raw silk. Use the juice as eye drops. <gloss>From Formulas from the Divine Benevolence</gloss>

**Sudden Turmoil Disorder with exhaustion:** <note>original: *Huoluan* (藿亂), a condition of sudden vomiting and diarrhea, often translated as cholera-like distress</note> Use three *taels* of Water Mint in two liters of water. Decoct until one liter remains and divide into three doses. <gloss>From Formulas from the Divine Benevolence</gloss>

**Poisoning from various fish:** Boil a thick decoction of "Fragrant Mint" <note>original: *Xiangsu*</note> and drink it. <gloss>From Simplified Formulas</gloss>

**Wasp or bee stings:** Crush mint to extract the juice and apply it to the site. <gloss>From Simplified Formulas</gloss>

# Mosla <gloss>From the Supplement to the Materia Medica</gloss>
<note>original: *Jining* (薺薴), likely Mosla chinensis, a small aromatic herb</note>

**Explanatory Names:** Smelly Perilla <gloss>Shizhen says:</gloss> Green-white Perilla. <gloss>Shizhen says: When Hua Tuo explained Water Perilla, he mentioned its names were Smelly Perilla and Green-white Perilla. He was actually referring to this plant, but mistakenly identified it as Water Perilla. Its shape resembles Water Perilla but it smells like White Perilla, and its color is green; hence the two names.</gloss>

**Collection and Explanation:** <gloss>Zangqi says:</gloss> I note that Su Gong said the people of the Jiangzuo region call Water Perilla "*Jining*." However, Water Perilla leaves have serrated edges and a fragrant, pungent scent. *Jining* leaves are slightly longer, covered in hairs, and have a foul odor, though they can still be eaten as a raw vegetable. Shizhen says: *Jining* grows everywhere on flat ground. The leaves resemble Wild Perilla but are slightly longer and hairy with a bad smell. Mountain folk eat it, though the flavor is not very pleasant.

**Nature and Flavor:** Pungent, warm, non-toxic.

**Primary Indications:** Dispels wind and cold Qi; treats scrofula <note>swollen lymph nodes</note>, sores, scabies, and hemorrhoids. <gloss>Shizhen says:</gloss> Boil into a juice and consume. It grows among mountain rocks, featuring small leaves and purple flowers, reaching one or two feet in height. People in the mountains use it.

## Pavilion Mountain
<note>original: 亭山 (Tingshan); likely referring to a specific library, studio name, or a geographical classification for the collection.</note>
